HARTLEY COLLIERY ACCIDENT,

Jaw. 16Ta, 1863. Old Winter blows and whistles hard To keep his fingers warm; while I Shut out the cold night, frosty stained, Bleak earth, and bitter sky, And to the fireplace nestle nigher And gaze on pictures in the fire. It has a soft, blithe, murmuring glow, As if it crooned a cradle song. Yet whispers of some awful woe, Are on each flaming to, That may have licked up human life, Quick, ruddy as a murderer's knife. I see the dead men underground, Just as they found them, rank on Old mothers, young wives. red-eyed, round The corpses brought to bank; I see the mournful phantoms dlt From out the namith of Hartley pit.

• 'Vs brave to die in battle's flash For the dear country we adore, Struck breathless 'mid the glorious crash, When tanners wave before The fading eyes, and, at the cars, We are caught by following Victory's cheers. And sailor blood that on the waves Can feil the mother's heaving breast. This sailer blood no wailing craves Over its place of rest. When souls first taste eternity In those last kisses of the sea. And death oft comes with kind release To win a smile from those who lie Where they may feel the blessed breeze, And look up at the sky. And drink in with their latest sigh, A little air for strength to die. But 'tis a fearful thing to be Instantly buried alive, fast bound In cold arms of eternity That clasp the breathing round, And hold them though their comrades call, And siig with.efforts useless all. A tear for those who in that night Went down so unavailingly ; A cheer for those who fought our tight And missed the victory; Peace to the good, true hearts that gave A moral glory to that grave, We know not how, amid the gloom, Some Jewel of the Just outshone, With precious sparkle lit the tomb, And led the hopeless on To hope, and showed the only way To find God's hand and reach the day. We know not how, in that quick hour, Some poor, uncultured, human clod May have tut forth its one sweet flower Acceptable to God, Or how the touch of Death revealed Some inner beauty life concealed. We know not how the Dove of Peace Came brooding on the fluttering breast To make the fond life yearning cease And fold them up for rest. And into shining shape the soul Burst, like the flame from out the coal. We only know that watchfires burned Long in their eyes for human aid, And failed, and that to God they turned, And all together prayed, And that the deepest mine may be, In prayer. God's whlspering gallery. Dear God : be very pitiful To those poor, toiling slaves of men, Be gracious, If their hearts be dull With darkness of their den ; 'Lis hard for flowers of heaven to grew Down where the earth flower cannot blow. Their lives are as the candle snuff, Black in the midst of its own light. Let hard hands plead for spirits rough, They work so much in night. Be merciful ; they breathe their breath So close to danger, pain, and death. The love mist in a father's eye, Will rise and soften much that's rude /n his poor children—magnify The least faint gleam of good. 0, find some place for human worth It; Heaven when it has failed on earth. GERALD MASSY.

The truest help we can render to an afflicted man is not to take his hoiden from him, but to cell out his best strength, that he may be able to bear the butden.—Phillips Brooks. A short time since a dieorderly Eueeralder faithfully pro- mised the magistrates of a certain borough that if they would let him off be " wouldn't be five minutes in the town after he was out of it!" Don't live your life alone, without forming friendships and love; your nature needs love, you were made for it, and other natures need you. You are robbing yourself, you are robbing others if you live like a hermit. Therefore go out Into God's world and live your life for others. Conscience is your magnetic needle. Reason is your chart. But I would rather have a cre•-v willing to follow the indications of the needle, and giving therneelyee no great trouble as to the chart, then a crew that bad ever so good a chart and no needle at all—Joseph Cook. Dr. Hawks, a popular New York divine, once asked the vestrymen of his church to incline(' his salary beceuse of his increased family expense?. "Don't trouble yourself,e said the vestrymen ; "the Lord has said he will care for the young ravens when they cry." "I know that," said the clergymen," but nothing is said about the young Hawks." Peace is better than joy. Joy is a very uneasy guest, and is always on tiptoe to depart. It tires and wears us out, and yet keeps us ever fearing that the next moment it will be gone. Peace is not so It comes more quietly, it stays more contentedly, and it nrver exhecste our streegth, nor gives us one anxious, fencasting thought. 1 herefore, let us have peace. Jones was riding, and saw a board nailed open a post in the yard of a farmhouse, with a sign peinted on it, "This Farm for Sail." Always ready for a little pleasantry, end seeing a woman In checked eurabonnet picking up an apron- fal of chips at the wood-poe in front or the house, he stepped and asked her very vlitety 'shed the farm was to sail. She went on with her work, but replied to his question Instanter: "Just as soon as the man comes along who can raise the wind." The late Mr. Bush need to tell this story of a brother barrister:—&s the coach was about starting before breakfast, the modest limb of the law approached the landlady, a pretty Qualceress, who was rear the fire, and said he could not thick of going without giving her a kiss.—" Friend," said she, "thee must not do it."—" Oh, by heavene I will!" replied the barrister.—" Well, friend, as then blast sworn, thee may do it, but thee must not make a practice of it." A bald-headed gentleman was recently importuned by acme young ladies to present them with his photograph. He complied with the request; but instead of presenting them with a picture of his handsome features, sent a very striking view of the bsck of his head. The joke was duly enjoyed, but the projector was mach surprised shortly after to see copies of the picture in the windows of a print shop On inquiring of the attendant, he found to his horror that the sharp photograoher bed published it as "A remarkable picture of the moon." A Passim( yoa Viceronv.—A. correspondent of the New York Nation tells the following aneceote:—An Englishman named Thompson fought as a volunteer in the Texan army at the battle of San Vacinto. He was walking meditatively over the field among the Mexican dead, soon after the battle, when he was accosted by Dr. Shepherd, my inrormaut, with, "Well, Thompson, how is this for a victory ?" "No vic- tory at all," was the reply. "Why, what's the matter? Haven't we killed enough ?" "Oh, yes, it will do; but I have always wanted to be in a battle where they are all killed on both sides!" Wosnams op Fietortans Wotex.—A short time ago there was made in Genoa a model of the famous statue of Colum- tons, each hair of the head and beard being individually worked. The windows of Goldsmiths'-stpet present a dazzling variety of designs of most exquisite finish—bas- kets of fruit and flowers, monuments, towers and churches, whilst of smaller designs, in that branch of the art which is devoted to personal adornment, there is literally no end. You see ears of barley so light that the horns droop like the originals under the faintest breeze, insects with wings of gossamer lightness, flowers of every variety, with delicately veined leaves and distinct petals, half opened pods with per- fectly modelled peas within, shoes too dainty even for Cin- derella, half closed umbrellae, gondolas, bracelets in which the rare designs of the richest laces are faithfully repro- duced ; indeed, there is no limit to the profuse variety in design, as there Is nothing lacking in elaborate finish. Like the prophet who has no esteem in his own country, these beautiful ornaments, which look as if they were the work of fairy fingers, find little favour at home, and are produced chiefly for foreign markets, a considerable trade, however, being done with the, passing tourist.—Cassell's Fa-nzilu Magazine. AN A CTOll'B PROTEST.—Very early in its history mankind discovered that it had a dramatic instinct, long before it occurred to anybody that in the business of acting there was a very Strong flavour of the forbidden fruit. The writer of the Book of Job might not have been greatly scandalised had someone proposed to enact his dramatic narrative ter the general edification; nor did the pious founders of the Miracle Plays think that they were fostering a great moral evil when they made simple peasente the actors of the most terrible of tragedies. At Oher-Ammergau to-day, many people who regard a theatre with miss,ivirg, if rot aversioa, are profoundly moved by the story of the Divine Paulen, unfolded, not by preachers, but by trained artistes. For the same class, the dramatisation of the "Pilgrim's Progress," by Dr. George MacDonald and his clever family, is void of offence. 'Yet the actors who personified the creations of eEschylue and Sopbocles, would have been astonished could they have foreesetn that their profession would be alternately patronised, petted, and preached at; outlawed in the lar:ci of Shakpvere ; refuted the rites of decent burial in the land of Moliere ; and not safe even now from misconstruction. Reflecting on the viciesitudes of his art, an actor might be tempted to the conclusion that "holding the mirror up te Nature" was the most thenlless of occupatiors. He is re• petit by the delight his craft affords to thr,uf,ands, and by tile appreciation it has Won from some of the noblest of hunizn intellects; hut WM a wave of prejudice, a little higher than usual, dashes in hi a face, he is distracted by the Insoluble pezzie thet a large section of the community still Oita-es ism to hove e,me pereenel responsibility for the perpetuity of eyil.— Hen 7 y Irtziwg in Good Words.

Pink•eye disease continues among horses at Durham and in the chinty, and serious losses have been sustained. At a celliery between Derlington and Auckland the whole of the horses have suffered, and nearly a dozen were lost. The recently issued agrigultaral report of the province of Ontario enumerates the number of thorough-bred cattle in the province as follows:—Shorthorns,ls,3Bs; Davons, 1,438; Hereforee, 841; Aberdeen or Angus, 2W; Grelloways, 1,189; Ayrshircs, 4,496; total, 23,619. Mr. Wm. Ashburner, on purchasing the Horton Hall estate in Gloucesterehire, removed his highly-bred herd of ehorthoins to that place. It is now stated that he intends in the coarse of the coming spring to have the herd taken bark to their former quarters at Conishead, Grange. A men in lowa has invented a new fastening for horse collars. It is lucky that the horse's collar does not fasten to a button in the back of his shirt, because if it did, judging from human experience, when it flew off after he had broken his thumb-nail trying to crowd it into anew button-hole, he would just kick the stuffing out of anything he was hitched to even if it was a freight car. 'TREF, PLANTING IN THE ISLE OF MAN.—By direction of Sir Henry Loch, K a, her M;jestyB Commissioner of Woods and Forests, a large extent of Crown lands in the Isle of Man is about to be planted with forest and orna- mental trees. About 500 acre.e are now being so planted on the mountain called Archallgan, where cabins have been erected by the contractors for the accommodation of the men. Mews. Little and Bellantyne. Knowefield Nurseries, Carlisle. have been entrusted with the contract, and already the drat instalmcnt of a quarter of a million of young trees has been shipped from the Carlisle Nurseries for the work. VIE NEW ACT ON CORN RETURNS (45 and 46 Vic.) came into operation on the Ist January. According to its prnvisinost the respective weights of grain per imperial bushel will now be as follows, viz, wheat, 60Ib. to the ins- renal bushel (same as before); barley, 501 b. to the imperial bushel (as against 471 b. previously); and oats, 391 b. to the imperial bushel (as against 331 h. before). The corn inspec- tors have strict orders to enfot ce the provieion of the Act, which requires all buyers of Britishegrown corn to make their returns be a stated time each week, under a penalty of £2O f neglect, and the making of a false or fraudulent return will he treated as a misdemeanour. Mis. THOMAS DAY.—We learn with interest that Mr. Day ia celebrating the jubilee of his connection with a business, now of very large proportiona indeed. Perhaps we should rather say that the large staff he employs, who have long looked up to their chief with hearty goodwill and respect, are celebrating it for Hun. Messrs. Day, son, and Hewitt, of Doreet-street. Baker-street, London, arc known wherever Queen's so' .jects speak English--and that is a world-wide account of them. This celebrity they have achieved no doubt mainly by admirable energy and organi• cation devoted to a business which is needed wherever a horse or caw or sheep or pig is kept. Their success is due to the great width and extent of the interest whieh they serve—to the enterprise which advertises them wherever the Enelish lanetkage is in use— and to the hearty co-operation of the staff whose goodwill they have secured. Above all —and this, except the personal interest we have already ex- pressed in the culmination of so long and honourable a career, is the only reason which the Agricultural Gazette can have for referring to the firm—their success has been owing to the usefulness and excellence, especially for eg rictalturiats, of the goods which they dietribute.—ely; iCzti- tura Gazette.—Advt. LARGE CORN Getenes.—Mr. F. Heishell, of Knoxville, Tennessee, send to the New Fork Times a sample ear of corn grown by him, which has grains an inch long. The ear weighed 41b,, and shelled a quart of grain. Forty average ears of it will shell a bushel. This seems to be a very vain. able variety. Mr. Heiehell writes ef it as follows:—" There are instances in which, by in and in breeding for a number of years. one man has produced ears of corn 15iin. in length, and another has by great care produced a variety of corn hearing from four to eleven ears to the stalk. These are certainly remarkable results, and the authors of them most assuredly deserve the thanks of mankind. But there is Another point of excellence in corn that is of as much, or more, importance than either the length of ear, or the num- ber of ears on a stalk, and that is the depth or length of the grain. I have been experimenting in that direction for the last four or five years, and I flatter myself that I have, even in that short time, produced a very superior corn. The ear is not of more than usual length, and it rarely bears more than two ears to the stalk or four ears to the hill ; but the cob is quite la-re, and is covered with grains (in tha best specimens) a fall inch in length. I have picked over only a small portion of my crop, and have two or three bushels of such ears. As I write I have before me one of them that measures just 10in, in length and 10iin. in circumference, and the grain a long inch." LORD CARNARVON'S ADVICE TO FAIIIIERS ON SREEP FEEDING.—The following letter has been written from High- clere Castle by the Earl of Cameroon :—" The continuance of this wet weather is so serious to all farmers that I will ask your leave to say a word on one part of our prospects. We know, and can more or less measure, the extent of the mis- chief as regards the wheat, which it has been impossible to sow. With good management, I hope that the loss there need not be very great ; hut it is impossible not to feel anxiety for the sheep in acme of the wet and heavy lands. Unless there hat been during the last two months good management, there will be, I fear, danger, if not certainty of sickness. But we are approaching the moment of greatest risk as the lambing time draws near; and if DOW and during that period the ewes are allowed to run down, it will, I be- lieve, be impossible to get them up,' or to save the lambs. The loss in sech case will be mon serious both to the indi• vidnal farmer and to the country, where the amount of stock is already much below the mark. It may, on the other hand: be added, as an inducement to the prudent agri- culturist, if any he needed, that he who can save and suc- cessfully carry his ewes and lambs over this winter may reasonably count upon a very large profit. The plain moral, therefore, of what I have now said is this—that those who detire to avoid any great loss, and to make considerable prefir, must spare no expense in feeding their ewes now. With z alight verbal alteration one may say, as the Father of Agricultural Poetry has well sang eighteen hundred years ago:— Now minister the cake with bounteous hand, And open let the stacks all winter Etend. , The temptation to economise in these small matters Is greater than would be supposed. I have seen many sheep kept, and their food stinted ; I have seen on neighbouring land and under identical conditions, a few sheep kept and generously treete.i. In the first case there has been heavy loss; in the eecarei, large profit. Of course money spent on feeding, without general good management, will be money wasted. There is no magic in food if it is not judiciously need and seconded by other precautions. Moreover, they who Lave let their sheep go down may find it too late now to bring them into a satisfactory condition. I have of late had some experience of whet I am now writing about, and have had inreresting illustrations of the truth of what I say; and simple and commonplace as the observation may seem, I am convinced that generous feeding at this season Is one, at least, of the secrets of eueceesful sheep-farming; and *at for want of it more money is sometimes wasted than is supposed. This is my excuse for stating what to many will appear a self-evident truth."

FARMERS ON Fetzer TOPICS.—An interesting conversation toek place at Barnstaple last week, at a gathering in connec- tion with the Western Counties' Agricultural Co-operation Association. Mr. J. Wreord, J.P., presided, and in calling on Mr. Olver, Bedrnin, asked him to explain, if he could, how it was that farming in Cornwall was so prosperous.— Mr. Olver raid one duty they should all perform was to test the different classes of seeds, to find which were the most suitable to their particular soils and climates, and, when they had discovered the best, they should communicate with Mr. Martin, the manager of the society, who would secure a quantity of it for use. He had been experimenting in different seeds for a long time, and he was certain that, so far as swedes were concerned, nothing would succeed in Cornwall so well as wbat was known as the Cornish short tops. Mr. Olver, in answer to the Chairman, said he did not know exactly how it was that agriculture prospered in Cornwall. One reason, however, was that perhaps in Corn- wall they did not live so high nor spend so much. (Laugh- ter.) And then Cornishmen were a "go-ahead" lot. They used their wits, and if they did not make better use of them than did the Midland counties men of theirs they would be In a fix 5u31 as they were in the Midlands. A farmer, to be staccEssful, must he as shrewd as a merchant. In Cornwall, perhsps, they had a little freer land, and other advantages, and they used all the new inventions in machinery. On every little farm would be found mowers and reapers and sowers; and, with regard to cattle, instead of depending on buying and selling, they always reared for themselves. His experience was that people took to the market only what they did not care to keep, so that for good stock they should depend on rearing and not on buying. (Hear, hear.) Then they had a lot of little streams which they used to turn a small wheel, with which a great deal of work was done. They did their own grinding, and used the wheel in every poesible way. The double-furrow plough had also been a wonderful saving to them. He believed it was by keeping a little of everything (and let it be good), using plenty of manure, and not selling all the corn they raised, but using it on the farm, that they did so well in Cornwall. Perhaps, after all, Devonshire men did equally well, but were not so saving.—Mr. Martin spoke of the adulteration in grass seeds, and the difficulty in getting good reliable permanent grass seed.—Mr. Olver, in proposing a vote of thanks to the Chairman, said the latter had land which was a credit to the county, atd if every man cultivated his bit of land like the Chairman did his, they would not want to go to America for anything. But then the Chairman had security, it being his own land, and it was security which the tenant wanted. (Hear, hear, and applause.) It was all very well to talk about trying this and that, but what they wanted to try first was the effect of security. If he were to die the next trey he knew very well that the whole money value which he had put into his farm would go from his wife and family. This ought not to be. But he believed the time was fast approaching when the tenant would get security for the in- vestments in land, and if the present Government did not P Cve them this the next would have to do so, They did not watt a long Act—simply a few words saying "tenant farmers to have security for what they put into the land." Thi3 ought and must Come.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 27, 1883
SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

The blood of animals of an herbivorous nature that have been acclimatised in elevated regions has been found by M. P. Bert to be richer in oxygen than the blood of the simi- lar animals inhabiting lands near the level of the sea. The Wiener Gewerbe Zeitung states that a chemist of Vienna has invented a new kind of glass, which contains no silex, potash, soda, lime, or borax. In aopearance it is equal to the common crystal, but more brilliant; it is perfectly traneparent, white, and clear, and can be cut and polished. It is completely insoluble in water, and is not attacked by fluoric acid, but it can be corroded by hydrochloric and nitric acid. When in a state of fusion it adheres to iron, bronze, and zinc. Mr. A. Le Neve Foster has, in the Trafalgar Collieries of the Forest of Dean successfully carried out an electrical arrangement for the: transmission of power. An electric motor is used to drive a pump in the underground workings. A dynamo-machine is placed at the surface for generating the current, which is connected with the pump, a distance of 300 yards along the workings. The total vertical lift of the electric pump is 115 feet, while the length of the pipe through which the water is forced is 500 yards. The total eclipse of the sun which will take place on the Bth of May next will Last six minute; and no longer one will probably occur within the next 100 years. It will be partially visible in many places, but few will see it in its entirety, as its path lies almost entirely through the ocean, touching land nowhere but at a little island in the South Pacitle called Caroline Island, which is out of the track of any established commerce or travel. The French G )vern- ment has determined to send an expedition to that island; it is almost certain an American party will go thither, and it is more than prubehle a grand international gathering of astronomers will take place at Caroline Island, to take part in this scientific quest. THE ORBIT OF THE GREAT COMET —Professor Frisby, Of the Naval Observatory, Washington, hes:completed A Cal- culation of the orbit of the great comet of 1882, from oh- servations made on September 191.11, October Bth, and Nov. 24th, and finds the orbit to be a very lengthened ellipse, I having a period of about 793 years, and probably identical with a very large comet seen 371 B.C. and 363 AD., just about the time of the death of Constantine. Its perihelion distance is only about 700,000 miles from the centre of the sun, and it extends outward at aphelion to about 90 times the sun's distance from the earth. He gives the following ! results of his calculation, which he believes to be very near I the truth, although on account of the extreme length of the orbit the time may be somewhat uncertain. Time of peri- helion pasts igo, September 17th, 22 282 Greenwich mean F rime; longitude of node, 316 dog. 1 min. 791 sec. ; distance from perihelion to node, 69 deg. 31 min. 1219 sec.; inclina- tion to ecliptic, 141 deg. 59 min. 52 16 sec ; angle of eccen- , Welty, 80 deg. 7 min. 42 70 sec ; logaritum of half major axis, -1 9331386; logaritnm of perihelion distance. 7 8904769; time of revolution, 793689 years.—New York Times. ELECTRICITY FROM CosanusTioN.—Dr. Brand, of La Rochelle, has given us A means of generating electricity by the act of combustion. His electro-generetive torch, or caadle, gives up a current of electricity in the act of burn. lug. It is prepared by making a paste of coal dust and mo- lasses, and moulding it into a stick, which serves as the in- flammable wick of a candle. This rod is then covered with asbestos in a thin sheet, and dipped into fused nitrate of potash until a good :thick coating of the nitrate adberes Ashes are mixed with the nitrate to make the candle burn more uniformly. On the wick being ignited it burns away ; and a current of electricity is drawn from the candle by wires inserted into the nitrate and the coaly wick. The cur- rent given by this device when it is ignited is comparatively feeble and not of much practical value as yet; but Dr. Brand is working in quite a new direction— namely, the prepara- tion of electro-generative fuels—and, of course, be may die. cover something worth finding. For example, if we had a fireplace so constructed that, on burning any ordinary fuel in it so as to give us heat, it would at the SAtlle time develop an eleetric current sufficient to ring electric belle, or charge an accumulator, and give us light, the novelty might prove very useful in certain circumstances. This is, we under- stand, Dr. Brand's present aim, and it would be a happy ter- mination to his researches, which are based on the discovery of Becquerel, the great French phesiciet„ who found that red-hot carbon plunged into nitrate of potash forms an elec- tric battery. - -

FOOD" PRESERVATION.—The preservative action of car- bonic acid on meat has been demonstrated by Professor Kolbe, of Leipsic. He hung pieces of beef, including fat and bone, in cylindrical tinned iron vessels, which were kept in a warm room of the laboratory, where the temperature at mid-day rose to 32 deg. C. Each piece was hung from the cross-bar; a plate for dropping liquid stood below; just over this wee a tubular passage for entrance of carbonic acid ; the cylin- drical lid of the vessel entered an annular trough holding glycerine, and had a tuhulure in the middle. When nearly all the air was supposed to be driven out through the latter tubulure by the entering gas, the elastic tubes connected to both tubulures were pinched with screws. After eight days In the vessel the beef was not distinguishable from fresh beef In aspect or taste after cooking, and the gravy was like that from fresh beef. After a fortnight the beef had be- come somewhat gray externally, and only a fine palate would distinguish the gravy from that of fresh meat. Sometimes beef and gravy had a weakly acid taste, which was easily remedied with a little carbonate of potash. After three weeks the beef was still of the same good quality, only softer than fresh beef, and requiring less time to cook. It was quite free from bad smell even after from four to five weeks, bat the cooked gravy then no longer Lilted so good as fresh cravy. The experiment ceased at that point, and it is believed to establish that carbonic acid is an excellent means of preserving beef from putrefaction, and maintaining Its good taste for several weeks It is noteworty that mut- ton under like treatment began to smell badly after eight days; veal, also, could not be kept so long as beef. Fowl and game have not yet been operated upon; but fish, lobsters, oysters, and fruit could be kept for a short time. Further tests arc to be made of this new food antiseptic. THE REMARIE&BLE DISCOVERY OF ZINC ORE IN NORTH DERBYSIIIRE.—The extraordinary "find" of blends (zinc ore) at the Magpie Mine, near Bekewell, in the High Pesk of Derbyshire, continues to excite much interest. The Magpie Mine has been worked for nearly 400 years, with the exception of a short interval from 1843 to 1869. In the latter year two Sheffield gentlemen—Alderman Fairburn and the late Mr.ltavison Barker—stimulated by the large returns of ore which disclosed themselves in the old books, resolved to re-open the mine. Associating themselves with other gentlemen, they put down a powerful pumping engine, weighing 12 tons, and other machinery, which occupied a year and a half. The depth of the mine at that time was 228 yards. They commenced to pump in 1870, telling 1,800 gallons a minute out of the werkings at an expenditure of 80 tons of coal per week. After two years' incessant labour, during which 09,000 worth of ore was raised, the water was still master of the situation, and it was thought advie. able to suspend pumping and get rid of it by driving a level. This work was commenced in 1873, and finished In 1831. The level is driven at a depth of 196 yards, is nearly 2,000 yards long, and cost £14,000. All this time the proprietors had received no return for their money. A few weeks ago the workmen came upon an Immense natural cavern, 22 yards lorg, extending for ten yards above the water. The cavity was large enough to contain the whole of the dibris taken out in driving the level for six months—many hundreds of thousands of tons weight. Twenty yards beyond this cavern was discovered the vein of zinc ore, five feet wide, and widening as it is cut. Mr. Simmons, the first captain of the mine, can see his way already to over 50,000 tons of this ore, samples of which have been sent to Messrs. Vivian, the well-known ex- perts in Wales, and others. Offers have been made to the company by three large firms, who are willing to contract for the whole quantity that can be raised at 183. 64. a ton. As the cost of getting the ore is only 255. a ton, there is no difficulty in working to a profit. All the land in the neighbourhood belongs to the Duke of Devonshire except a few small fields, and, singularly enough, it is underneath these fields that the ore has been found. The discovery of "zinc ore" is without a parallel in Derbyshire, and opens out an interesting field of inquiry for the geologist. The Magpie Mine is not far from the well-known Darley Dale Mine, the richest in Derbyshire, where Mr. E. M. Was, the proprietor,has cleared 00,000 a year for ten years.

pected, most important, as without it the dog would lose its handsome appearance; colour, too, is thought a great deal of, and markings also—the former being of the deepest jet where black, and of a dark reddish hue, without a white hair, where tan; and it is necessary that each colour be clearly defined. The markings are :—Tan along the jaws and under the chin, a spot over each eye and on each cheek, inside the ears, fore legs, half-way up the legs. a spot on each side of the chest, on the breast; the feet tan colour, with a black pencil mark up each toe; and half-way up be- tween the knee and foot should be a round black spot, known as the thums mark; under the tail and inside the legs should be tan, and all the rest black. Manchester ter- riers tequire to be kept very clean, and should be groomed with a hair glove not too hard in texture. Prheoes.—TerE Potrrza.—This variety of pigeons is known from the large distended crop, which causes the head to be thrown backwards. Hence it has been called the Cropper, and now the Pouter, but there can be no ques- tion that during the last generation it has been very con- siderably improved, not only so far as its crop is concerned, hut also as to its length of limb, its slenderness of holy, feathering, colour, and markings. Certainly there is no handsomer bird when standing upon a good block, in a bell- shaped pen, than a tall, good-shaped, rich-coloured, and well made Pouter. This variety is regarded by many as , the highest of all the fancy pigeons, and even lovers of Carriers, who may be inclined to place their favourites first, give the Pouter the second position. It sells for almost if not quite as high prices, and £5O is not an unreasonable sum for a really first-class bird. In Scotland it is undeni- ably the first favourite, and it is indeed a treat to visit a large show there, as the numbers and quality of these birds shown is sometimes wonderful. Tne leg, or as it is called in pigeon parlance, the limb, requires to be lone, well placed, and well feathered. It should also be muscular and firm, as this improves the appearance of the bird very much, and without it there is a want of proportion. The shank should be long in proportion to the thigh, and the foot well set on. Seven inches is reckoned a very good length, and, of course, any tendency to cow-hock in the legs or turning in of the toes is objected to. The thighs and shanks are covered with soft email feathers, with longer feathers spreading out at the toes. The crop in good specimens ie round and exactly even, not tending to hang at one side or the other. When inflated it stands out well in front, and only in front, as any bulging behind is deemed a great fault. But it is also well up so that the bek is buried, and the point then to be desired is that it shall flow easily into the lines of the body, for a lumpy crop is most objection- able. At one time the tails were bred very long, but as this had the effect of tipping the bird forward, it spoiled its car- rieee, and of late a more reasonable length bee been accepted. Colour is an important element, and without it an otherwise good bird may be spoiled. There are five standard colours, namely—Black-pied, blue-pied, red-pied, yellow-pied, and white; the last-named being a self colour. The pie& are so marked all over the body, except a white mark across the crop, forming a perfect crescent. In rear- ing pouters the best way is to give each bird to a pair of dragons or Antwerps, and Wright recommends that eve-y morning a belus should be given made of oatmeal and bone- dust, mixed up with a few drops of Perrish's chemical food. Pouters need to have larger nest boxes and pans than almost any other variety, and a roomy aviary is indispen- sable. They are not then very difficult to breed ; but, of course, it Is not easy to obtain the very highest exhibition specimens, which can only be the result of careful, skilful, and long-continued breeding. In addition to the larger variety, there :ire pigmy pouters, which are similar in every way. except that the latter are very much smaller, and per- haps have not such well-developed crop. If more fashon. able, many more would be seen, but now they are somewhat rare

CAGE BIRDS.—THE Monireseeenv.--Nightingales are favourite inmates of the aviary in consequence of their song, more than of their personal appearance, which is not neatly co beautiful as is that of many others of our British birds. The plumage is flesh coloured and gray, with a little touch of yellow here and there, and consequently there is not much to describe in their personal appearance. They are proud in carriage and deliberate in action, and are really beautiful singers, though somewhat variable in this respect. They must be caught from April to September, for being migratory birds they leave our shores during the autumn season. In confinement they may be allowed to fly freely, but they do not sing E 0 well as when In a cage, where they are less liable to interruptions, and where they also live longer, being fed with gteater care and regularity. The cage should not be a very small one, and the size we should recommend would be not less than 18 or 20 inches long, 12 Inches wide, and 15 inches in height. Many are friendly and will sing almost anywhere, whilst others are very diffi- cult to manage, and, as we have already indicated, very variable in their temperament. The song of the nightingale is very musical, and it is for this reason that he has been called "the king of songsters." The compass, flexibility, harmony, variety, and strength of voice possessed by this bird is really wonderful. "Sometimes dwelling for minutes on a strain composed of only two or three melenchely tones, he begins in an undervoice, and swelling it gradually by the meet superb crescendo to the highest point of strength, he ends it by a dying cadence, or it consists of a rapid succession of more bril- liant sounds, terminated, like many other strains of his song, by some detached ascending notes. Twenty-four different strains or couplets may be reckoned in the song of a fine nightingale, without including its delicate little varia- tions, for amongst these, as among other musicians, there are some great performere and very middling ones." Not only is this so, but the nightingale possesses the quality of being able to augment the number of his friende, as he is capable, after a time, of forming strong attachments. When he has once made friends with the person who takes care of him, he will know his step, welcome hiea with a cry of joy, and has been known to pine to death on the loss of his bane. factor. Se far as feeding is ',concerned, well cooked mutton or beef, mixed with hard boiled eggs—oneethird of the latter to two-thirds cf the former is the beet. This must be chopped as fine as possible, and be fresh and free from fat. Only a small quantity must be given at one time, but they require to be fed often. If a large quantity is put into the cage, it gets dry and stale, so that the birds do not relish it. In addition to this, ants eggs, a meelworm, or a cockroach may be given once or twice a day, but it is necessary to be careful in not giving too much of these things. Cleanliness is a very important element, not only in the cage itself, but also providing a bath for the bird every other day at least. The caka we have often recernmended made from peameal, lard, sugar and eggs, is else a capital thing, and nightingales are very fond of it. But whatever the food may be, it is moat important to see that it is kept sweet and good, and that the cage is cleaned out regularly. Whilst this is being done let the inmates have a fly round the room, and the ex- ercise will do them good.

CITIIISTUNITY ITS OWN EVIDENCE.—The Christian reve- lation is no mere announcement of certain propo,sitions or dogmas to be accepted on its own authority, or because they are authenticated by physical signs and wonders. It is its own evidence. It shines by its own light. It appeals to the faculty in us of spiritual discernment, and he who be- lieves it, believes it not in assent to external evidences, or In unintelligent acceptance cf mysteries, but because it has quickened his spiritual vision, opened up views of God and divine things' which carry conviction of their truth into his intellect, while they captivate the affections and bring peace to the conscience.— Good Words. FLOWERS OF TILE CORNFIELD.—Amongst all the locali- ties that various plants favour, none bear away the palm for brilliancy from our cornfields. Our hedgerows are gay with the pure white blossoms of the sloe or the delicate pink of the rose; the moorland is dotted over with the golden stars of the asphodel, the white tufts of the cotton grass, the brilliant yellow of the furze, or the rich sheet of crimson of the heather-bells; while the river bears on its surface the silver chalice of the water-lily, or reflects in its waters the clusters of purple blossom of the loose-strife; but the corn- field has an intensity of colour all its own, for here we find In perfection the glorious corn•flower, one of our finest blue flowers, the intensely scarlet poppy, and the great golden discs of the corn marigold. Such a nosegay as a good hand- ful of these three flowers' would make should form a good test for the detection of colour-blindness, and their repre- sentation not only taxes the powers of the colour-box to the uttermost, but leads us in despair to cast aside our poor pig- ments as we revel in the splendour and intensity, the won- derful depth and force of colour of any one of the three flowers in the bunch we have gathered. Nature paints with tints no human art can rival, and the nearest approach one can make to the colour of a poppy looks mere brickdnat when laid by the silken splendour of the petals of the way- side weed.—From "Familiar Wild Flowers" for January. Slam ME num.—The usual crowd of autumn liars were gathered together in the store, occupying all the grocery seats—the only gross receipts that the proprietor took no pride in—when a little, blear-eyed, weazen-faced Individual sneaked in by the back door and slunk Into a dark corner. "That's him," said the ungrammatical bum- mer with a green patch over his left eye. " Who is it ?" asked several at once. "Why, the chap who saved a train from being wrecked," was the reply. "Come, tell us about it," they demanded, as the small man crouched in the dark- ness, as if unwilling that his heroic deed should be brought out under the glare of the biasing kerosene lamp. After much persuasion, reinforced by a stiff horn of applejack, be began—" It was just such a night as this—bright and clear —and I was going home down the track, when, right before me, across the rails, lay a great beam. There it was. Pale and ghastly as a lifeless body, and light as it appeared, I had not the power to move it. A sudden rumble and roar told me that the night express was thundering down, and soon would reach the fatal spot. Nearer and nearer it ap- proached till, just as the cow-catcher was about lifting me, I sprang aside, placed myself between the obstruction and track, and the train flew on unhermed." The silence was so dense for a moment that one might have heard a dew drop. Presently somebody said, " What did you do with the beam ?" "I didn't touch it," he replied ; "hut it touched me." " Well," persisted the questioner, "if you couldn't lift it, and didn't touch it, how in thunder did the train get over it?' " Why, don't you see," aeid the sad-faced man, as he arose from his seat and sidled towards the door, "the obstruction was a moonbeam, and I jumped so that the shadow of my body took its place, and—" Bang flew a ham against the door ; and if it ILO struck the body of the retreating hero, there would have been a rnneh bigger grease-spot frescoed on the panel.—Drake's 17-ave!ler's May«;ine.

DOGS.—THE MANCHESTER TERRIER.—Thee beautiful and attractive terriers hardly receive the attention they de- serve, although there is no doubt that they are amongst the handsomest of show dogs. The contrast between the jet black and the shining tan, combined with their graceful forms and elegant marking, gives them a very striking ap- pearance. They are nearly always cropped in the ears, and though an attempt has been made to do away with this prac- tice the opponents have not as yet succeeded. On the ground of prevention of unnecessary pain, we should be glad to hear of their success, as we cannot think it right to inflict pain for the gratification of a whim, or as a tribute to fashion. Where there is a.decided advantage to the animal concerned, or even to its owner, then we reluctantly consent to it, but not otherwise. This, however, is not a popular view of the subject, and fashion very largely rules such matters. Manchester or Black and Tan Terriers are often used for rat killing, and are capital as watch dogs, as they are always on the alert, very active, and attach themselves greatly to their owners, although their nature is to be ner- vous and shy with strangers. They are perhaps a little noisy, and, having a decided aversion to shabbily-dressed strangers, are on this account useful inmates of a house lonely situated or not over well protected. They are capital as ladies' pets, are very clean in their habits, easily con- tented, and not quarrelsome. For these reasons, as for their good looks, they can be recommended. The defi- nition of this breed of dogs is as follows :—The shape of the head should be very narrow and long, without any fulness at the jaws or brows; the skin should be drawn tight over the hones, and be very clean cut with a flat skull, not at all apple-headed nor arched ha the slightest degree; the eyes keen and black, with no moisture at the corners, nor any approach to full eyes, as in pugs and spaniels; the muzzle lean and very long, but not weak ; the teeth very level; the lips should close tight over the teeth, without any looseness of flesh or skin; the ears are usually cropped to a sharp point, and, of course, both done alike; the chest should be deep, the ribs long, but the chest should not be wide, as it causes a clumsy appearance; the neck should he lengthy and well set on, gradually be. coming thicker at the shoulders; the loins should be mus- cular, but not tucked up in the flank; the legs reonite to be straight and light in bone ; the feet well formed, arched and round, and the toe nalle as black as a ; the coat ought to be glossy, short, and tins. hat not fine in texture; the t:il --nt be thin ^,rd ra a t•airi., and he r7.rriNl straight, Out N.ther low; siaetry 1., a.l might be ex-

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

THE CONSPIRACY TO MURDER DUBLIN OFFICIALS. The magisterial inquiry into the Fenian conspiracy to assassinate Irish Government officials was commenced in Dublin on Saturday, 20 of the 21 men recently taken into custody being placed in the dock. The other man, Robert Farrell, was put in the witness box. He said that he had for seven or eight years been a member of the Fenian Brotherhood, and he described various meetings of that society and the part taken in them by the prisoners. About 18 months ago he had a conversation with Daniel Curley, one of the prisoners, as to becoming a member of the "inner circle." He told witness that the -sinner circle was to be composed of the chosen men of the organisation. The busi- ness for which the inner circle was to be formed was chiefly to assassinate Government officials. After this Curley told him he was to stop the Chief Secretary's (Mr. Forster's) carriage, and that two other men named "would do the renaainder." Witness let the carriage pass, as he did not know it, and then Peter Doyle (a prisoner) said it was all up, and Curley seemed to be vexed over the mistake. The witness described other failures of the murderous design, and was then questioned with a view to its being shown that the Phosnix Park murders and the attempt on the life of Mr. Justice Lawson were crimes as to which overtures had been made to him. He also told how he received orders to take part in the attack on Mr. Field, the Dublin juror, and described Le facts of the attempted assassination. "There was," said the witness, " never an ord_r for assassination issued from the Fenian Society. The orders used to he given from the assassination con- spiracy. Joseph Mullett (one of the prisoners) was the man who was responsible for this conspiracy." Farrell added ' that this assassination society was established from the , Fenian Brotherhood. He grew sick of the business, as he saw it was a sham and a delusion, and only good for those who lived by it. He repeatedly tendered his resignation, and Mullett placed him in his present position through his threats. The inquiry was adjourned for a week. SUPPOSED FURTHER CLUE TO OUTRAGE ORGiANISATIONS.

The Press Association's special correspondent in Dublin, telegraphing on Thursday evening, says :—Some important evidence has been obtained, within the last couple of months, regarding the perpt trators of some of the outrages committed daring the past two years in the West of Ireland. The fact that two men are awaiting their trial in Galway Gaol for the murder of a bog bailiff named Connors, on the estate of Lord Dunsany, is already known, but it is also a fact that the murderers of Mr. Blake and his servant Thady Flynn near Loughrea last year, and of Mr. Bourke and Corporal Wallace at Rahassane, will shortly engage the attention of a judicial tribunal. A man who is believed to have been engaged in the first of these two murders, and who is now in America, is being sought, for, and if he is found, as there is every reasoß to hope, it is expected Olathe will disclose the names of his associates. A number of Irish detective,, acting on information collected by the Royal Irish Constabulary, have been pursuing a close inquiry in the vicinity of the scenes of these murders, and it is stated that they are now in pos- session of information which, it is hoped, will enable them to lay their hands upon the whole of the members of the organisation which promoted those frightful crimes and others in the district. The extreme punishment which has been visited recently on the perpetrators of certain murders has evidently caused something like a panic among the local outrage organisations, some of thc members of which, by suddenly leaving the country or by taking some other extraordinary steps, have drawn upou thems,lves the notice of those who have been watching for nearly a year for a clue. In connection with these discoveties by the police it is also stated on good authority that the murderers of Lord Mountmorres are in view, and that the next month or two will witness the indictm4nt of several of the men engaged in these crimes. THE PH(ENIX PARK MURDERS.

It is understood that the result of the late inquiry at the Castle is to reduce the number of men supposed to have taken part in the Pluenix Park murders to 10, four of whom are alleged to have been the actual perpetrators, the other six being posted in the immediate locality to guard against a surprise. All ten are amongst those in custody, and they will no doubt be formally charged before the magistrates with the perpetration of this dreadful crime.

It is stated that Mr. D. M. O'Conor, MV. for county Sligo, will, owing to delicate health, accept the Chiltern Hundreds, and that Mr. M'llermott, Q.C., will come forward as a moderate Liberal candidate.

Dr. Commins, M.P., had convenal,a meeting nominally of his constituents at Boyle, on Sunday, and attelided for the purpose of delivering an address. The Lord Lieutenant, however, had caused the meeting to be "proclaimed " under the Crimes Act, and Dr. Commins advised the crowd to return quietly to their homes. Mr. Parnell appears to have cast his eye upon new possi- bilities for the amelioration of the condition of Ireland. He writes that he is about to visit some Dutch peat factories, the products of which bring high prices in Ireland ; and he expresses the opinion that the introduction of the industry into his own country would be attended with advantage:

Mallow election has resulted in the return of the Nation- alist candidate, Mr. O'Brien, by 161 votes against 89 recorded for Mr. Naish, the new Solicitor-General for Ire- land.- Tho result, though matter for regret, was not unex- pected. At the general election Mr. Johnson polled 189, and his Conservative opp,nent 72 votes. In the cases of Messrs. Dayitt, Healey, and Quinn, charged with delivering speeches inciting to violence, judgment was given in the Dublin Court of Queen's Bench on Wednesday, ordering Messrs. Davitt and Healy to be bound over to good behaviour in sums of £l,OOO each, with two sureties of £5OO each, and Mr. Quinn in the sum of £5OO, with two sureties of £250. The defendants were allowed a week in which to comply with the order. A letter has been addressed by the Pope to Archbishop Maccabe on the condition of Irelona. In this document his Holiness urges the Irish prelates to continue to keep their faithful people entirely apart from those who, led away blindly by their own passions, think they can serve their country by steeping themselves in crime, by drawing others into the same depraved courses, and imprinting a foul stain on their country's cause. .

DARING OUTRAGE NEAR KILLARNEY.—A daring. outrage has been committed by a" Moonlight " party at Annabeg, seven miles from Killarney. A marriage was about to take place between the daughter of a farmer, named Moynihan, and a cattle dealer, named Culloty. Moynihan's residence was entered on Friday.night by the assailants, who obliged the girl to swear she would never wed Culloty. On leaving they fired several shots. The motive for the outrage is that Culloty was boycotted for purchasing a farm from Lord Kenmare. Dounrat EXECUTION IN IRELAND —Sylvester Poff and Thomas. Barrett, two " Moonlighters," who were convicted at Cork Assizes of shooting a man, named Thomas Browne, in broad daylight, were executed at Tralee Gaol, on Ines- day. On the scaffold each man declared his innocence, and each has left a solemn declaration to the effect that he had no hand in the crime, and did not know who did it. The two mut were twice tried, and on the first occasion the jury disagreed. The chief evidence against them was that of a boy who witnessed the murder, and said that it took place in the afternoon while many persons were passing to and fro.

div.p: A CONTENTED MAN.—In summer, when the mercury bolted up among the nineties, the judge would come to the front door with beads of perspiration standing out all over his red face, and would look at the sky and say, "Splendid! perfectly splendid! Noble weather for the poor and for the ice companies and the washerwomen! I never saw sich magnificent weather for dryin' clothes. They don't shake up any such climate as this in Italy. Gio3lllo me my um. breller. Harriet, while I sit out yer on the steps and enjoy it." In the winter wheti the mercury would creep down 15 degrees below zero, and the cold was nearly severe enough to freeze the inside of Vesuvius solid to the centre of the globe, Pitman would sit out on my fence and exclaim, "By gracious, Adeler ! did you ever see sich weather as this! I like an atmosphere that freezes up yer very marrer. It helps the coal trade an' gives us good skeetin'. Don't talk of summer time to me. Gimme cold, and give it to me stiff." When there was a drought Pitman used to meet me in the street and remark, "No rain yet, I see! Magnificent, isn't it? I want my weather dry, I want it with the dampness left out. Moisture breeds fevers and ague, an' ruins yet' boots. If there's anything I despise, it's to carry an um. breller. No rain for me, if you please." When it rah:cc] for a week and flooded the country, the judge often dropped in to see me and observe, "I dunno how you feel about this yer rain, Adeler, but it snore seems to me that the heavens never drop no blessin's but when we have a long wet spell. It makes the corn jump an' cleans the sewers an' keeps the springs from gittin' too dry. I wouldn't give a cent. to live in a climate where there was no rain. Put me on the Nile, and I'd die in a week. Soak me through an' through to the inside of my bones, and I feel as if life was bright and beautiful, an' aorrer of no account." On a showery day, when the sun shone brightly at one moment and at the next the rain poured in torrents, the judge has been known to stand at the window and exclaim, "Harriet, if you'd 'eve asked me how I liked the weather, I'd 'ave said, just as it is now. What I want is weather that is streaked like a piece of fat an' lean bacon—a little shine an' a little rain. Mix 'em up an' give us plenty of both, an' I'm yer man." The judge is always happy in a thunderstorm, and one day, after the lightning had knocked down two of his best apple trees and splintered them into fragments, and the wind had torn his chimney to pieces, I went over to see him. He was standing by the prostrate trees, and he at once remarked, "Did you ever know of a man havin' sich luck as this ? I was goin' to chop down them two trees to.morrer, an' as that chimney never draw'd well, I had concluded to have it rebuilt. An' that gorgeous old storm has fixed things just the way I want 'ern. Put me in a thunderstorm an' let the lightnin' play around me, an' I'm at home. I'd rather have one storm that 'd tear the inside out of the American Continent then a dozen of yer little dribblin' waterin'-pot ehowere. If I can't have a riopin' and roarin' storm, I don't want none." They say here in the village, but I don't believe it, that one day the judge was upon his roof fixing a shingle, when a tornado struck him, lifted him off, carried him a quarter of a mile, and dashed him with ouch terrible force against A fence that his leg was broken. As they c4rried I:im honue, he oonned his eyes larguidly and said, "Immortal Moses ! what a storm that was ! When it 0(4.8 how, it suits me ,f it blows her']. l'd give both legs if we could have a squall like that every day. I—l--" Then he fainted. If contentreent is heopineee, then the lire of Pit inAn is one uninterruned condition of blios —.By Max Ackler, in. " Gleanings from Popular Authors" for J•inuary.
DISTRICT NEWS.
ALTRINCHAMI

HALE UNITAIZIA.N CIIAPEL.—On Tuesday evening, a soirée. was held in the Building Society's Rooms, Altrin- cham, on the occasion of the departure from the Hale Uni- tarian Chapel of the Rev. I'. Lloyd Jones, who is about to take charge of the Beaufort-street Demestic Mission, Liver- pool. At the same time a welcome was given to the Rev. C. D. Badland, M.A., his successor to the pastorate of Hale Chapel. The chair was occupied by the Rev. J. E. Odgers, M.A., Altrineham, and among those present were the Revs. S. A. Steinthal, Dendy Agate, B.A. (Gorton), L. Scott (Denton), and several other ministers; Mr. Alderman Hey- wood, Mr. John Hadfield, Godfrey Worthington, Dr. Emrys Jones, Mr. A. E. Paterson, and others.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

LYM3I CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH TEA PARTY. - The annual tea party, in connection with the above-named place of worship, took place on Wednesday, when about 120 persons partook of tea. After tea a meeting was held, presided over by the Pastor (the Rev. J. Bedell), and he was supported by the Revs. J. lionge, T. W. Pinn, M.A. (Stockport), Messrs. R. Dutton, George Wood and William Woodburn.—The Chairman, in addressing the meeting, re- ferred to their financial position, which, he said, was in a very satisfactory state. During the year the money col- lected had been as follow :—Chapel anniversary, £2O 18s. id; Sunday school anniversary, £lB 63. Pd.; nais- sionary contributions, £23 103. 11d. ; weekly offering, £195 19s. 3d.; total, £258 15s. With respect to their Sunday school the average attendance in the morning had slightly increased on that of last year, and that of last year was an increase on the previous year. In the morning the average attendance had been 43, and in the afternoon it had been 167; the highest number present on any afternoon was 201; and the number at present on the register was 227. The scholars had collected for the missionary cause £lO, and the second class on the boys' side of the school had decided upon doing what they could to help on this cause, and the result of their efforts was that they had collected the sum of £2, and he hoped that this would act as an incentive to other classes in the school. Last July the school, along with three others, had a trip to Llandudno. which proved a source of much pleasure, and instead of being a heavy bur- den upon the school, as some supposed it would, it had left a slight balance in the treasurer's band. This winter they had had three entertainments, and judg- ing from the number of friends who had attended them they had been very popular, and from these they also had a little bilance. It was intended that three more of these entertainments should he field. As for the Band of Hope, so far as he could learn it was being carried on, and was in a prosperous condition. There was a monthly tract distri- bution, which was worked by nine friends in as may dis- tricts, and there were two or three other districts waiting for friends to come forward and take them. This cost £9 per year, and towards this some kind friends had contributed between £5 and £6, and he hoped that the remainder would be generously contributed by other friends. He then pro- ceeded to speak of the church work, which, lie said, was in a satisfactory condition.—Mr. Dutton next addressed the meeting, and reviewed the work of the church during the past year, and said there. were many bright snots to be found which were encouraeing to them.—The Rev. J. Yonge spoke of a disposition to worldliness which he noticed to be growing in the church, and mentioned an instance of a church which, he said, was not a hundred miles array, that had advertised and was giving a panto- mime on three evenings. He deprecated this kind of thing, and hoped that the time would never come when Congrega- tional churches would-go in for that kind of thing. Sunday schools were not places for dancing and theatrical perform- ances.—Mr. Geo. Wood and Mr. Woodburn also addressed the meeting, which closed in the usual way.—The follow- ing ladies gave trays :—Mrs. Rowson, Mrs. Boyd, Mrs. Bickley, Mrs. Chorley, Mrs. Dyson, Miss Forrest, and Miss Bedell.

div.head: NANTWICH.
div.p: NANTWICH.

A petition for liquidation has been tiled in the Manches- ter County Court by Frederick Kelly, of Yew Tree Terrace, Stockport-road, Lewnshulme, near Manchester, commercial clerk, formerly trading as a licensed victualler, at the Red Lion Hotel, Nantwich, Cheshire. Liabilities £3OO.

div.head: OVER.
div.p: OVER.

CONCERT.—An amateur concert was held in the Board School, Over, for the purpose of raising the balance requisite for the painting of the window for St. John's church. The chief vocalists were Miss Wood, Miss Ather- ton, Miss Eavenscroft, and Miss Lilia Ste!fox. Mr. Weave and Mr. Mason, accompanied by Mr. E. Singleton and Mr. Dodd. The attendance was only moderate, and the profit in proportion.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

TEISPERANCE.—Now that the Blue Ribllon Army is mak- ing efforts of no small magnitude in Winsford to gain a footing, and rear a cause, it is no wonder that the different religious persuasions should seek to keep and guide those whom for so long a while they have had in training. The Primitives of Station-road held a temperance meeting' on Tuesday with this end in view. Messrs. Hind, Saul,Gibson, Newall, Pinches, Rogerson, Leech, &c., spoke, while the choir rendered good service. There was a good attendance. ENTERTAINMENT.—On Friday last Mr. B. J. Malden gave his dioramic entertainment called" Under the British flag." There were splendid views of about 100 places including Gibraltar, Cyprus. Malta, St. Helena, The Cape, Ceylon, Calcutta, Melbourne, Quebec, the Egyptian Campaign, Jzc., &c., which were followed by some beautiful statuary and comic scenes. The great and descriptive power of Mr. Malden added greatly to the entertainment. There was a very good audience, and the proceeds, after deducting ex- penses, will be added to the fund for the relief of the poor in the town.

UNITED FREE METHODIST CHURCH MISSIONARY SER. VICES.—On Sunday last two sermons were preached in the High•street Chapel. by the Rev. J. W. Chicholin, of Liver- pool, in aid of the Home and Foreign Missions. In the morning he preached from Matthew 2ad chanter, 2nd verse, and in the evening from St. Luke 23rd chapter, 42nd and 43rd verses, when his eloquent discourse was attentively listened to by a large congregation. In the afternoon a juvenile missionary meeting was held, when addresses and recitations were given by the scholars and friends. Mr. Reuben Stubbs presided. On Monday the annual meeting; was held, over which Mr. Shafer, the Mayor of Over, pre- sided. There were also in the rostrum the Revs. W. Symms, J. Wright (circuit ministers), C. S. Reader (Wesleyan), J. W. Chicholin (deputation), Mr. R. Stubbs, and a few others. After a hymn was sung and prayer, the Rev. J. Wright read the report. The Winsford and Sandbach circuit last year raised £B2 15s. 4d., of which amount Winsford sent £26 Os. 5d.; Station-road. £4 Bs. 5d.; Sandbach, £lO is. 5d.; Holmes Chapel, £8 9s. 4d.; Weaver, £4 75.; Clive Green, £4 7s. 9d.; Over, £2 125.; Middlewich, £8 9s. 5d.; Elworth, £4 183. 3d.; Brereton, £8 10s. 9J.; juvenile contributions through missionary cards, £l2 Ds.

div.head: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.
div.p: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

Alfred Lings, landlord of tbe Stamford Arms Hotel, and John Hunt, Griffin Hotel, Bowdon, were each fined at Altrinc- ham Petty Sessions, on Monday, £2 5s 6d each for haling in their possession a number of unstamped measures. DEATH OF A CHESHIRE MAGISTRATE. Mr. Meadows Frost, J.P. for Cheshire and Flintshire, and residing at Meadows, Lee Hope, near Chester, died at his residence on Saturday morning. Mr. Meadows Frost was twice mayor of Chester, and for many years was in the Corporation. THE. CHESTER MANSLAUGHTER CASE. On Saturday, Martha Anderson, of 22, Charles-st., Chester, was brought up at Chester City Police Court charged with the man- slaughter of James Douglas, 27, an ironmonger, on the 16ch December. A number of witnesses were called, and the pri- soner was remanded for a week.

At the Chester City Police Court, on Monday, John Caw- ley, of Sbordely Hall, was charged with having been drunk in charge of a horse on Saturday night, and also with hav- ing assaulted the police and members of the Salvation Army. The defendant, who was on horseback, charged several times into the ranks of the army in Eastgate-street. The defen- dant was fined £4 and costs. CRESEIR.E DAIRY FARMERS' Assoc'Anow. A general meeting of the members of this association was held at Chester, on Saturday. Mr. James Tomkinson, Liberal can- didate for West Cheshire, presided, among those present being, Mr. H. J. Tollemache, M.P., Captain Cotton, ctc. A long discussion took place upon the question of electing a new secretary, some members arguing in favour of a paid officer and others in favour of the post being continued as an honorary one, some strong observations being made as to the manner in which the duties had been discharged in the past.—Mr. Finchett propossl, and Mr. Gouldbourne se- conded, a motion in favour of electing a paid secretary.—As an amendment, Mr. Henry Davies moved, and Mr. James Owen seconded, that an honorary secretary should be ap- pointed.—Mr. Finebett's motion was carried by a large majority.—On the suggestion of Mr. Rigby, a committee, composed of Messrs. Rigby, Finchett, Aston, Allwood, Dut- ton, Charmley, and Fearnall was appointed to consider and draw up a definition of the dnties and remuneration of the secretary, and other objects of general utility.—After a warm discussion as to the remuneration of the late secretary, the matter was referred to the same committee, with Messrs. Phillips, Cooke, Tomkinson, Hulse, and Captain Cotton added to it.

At Brechin, on Wednesday, Mrs. Knowles, landlady of the Crown Hotel, was charged with having supplied drink to two ploughmen last Sunday. It was contended that the ploughmen were bona-fide travellers, and it was stated that this belief was prevalent among Scotch hotel-keepers. The Bench decided that farm servants were not travellers, and lined Mrs. Knowles 50s.

A Lloyds' telegram received on Thursday morning states that the ship Marathon, of Liverpool, 1,335 tons register, has foundered in the North Atlantic Ocean, and the whole of her crew, 35 in number, have, it is feared, perished. The vessel left Bombay in June last, with a full cargo of up- wards of 2,000 bales of cotton, valued at £50,000, and was seen on the 9th September near the Cape. de Verde Islands, all well, but nothing further has been heard of her. It is supposed that she foundered during the heavy gales in October in the Atlantic. Herr Lee, professor of languages, committed suicide at Gloucester by throwing himself in front of a passenger train on Saturday morning last. A young lady named Mary Lewis has committed suicide by throwing herself from the Crumlin Viaduct, Cardiff, into the gully below, a distance of 220 feet. At Lancaster assizes, last week, a sentence of five years' penal servitude was passed on Samuel Taylor, late steward of a Chorley burial society, for forging medical certificates of death. The dispute about the charges of the returning officer (the Mayor) at the recent Liverpool election has been settled, the account having been reduced from £2,273 to £1,922. The Mayor and Corporation of Shrewsbury were fined £5 and costs at the borough police court on Saturday, for a contravention of the Locimotive Act by using a steam roller in the street, without having three men ;in charge of it. Dr. Whitmarsh announced on Tuesday night, at a meet- ing of the Hounslow Local Board, of which be is a member, that he intended to withdraw his claim against the rate- payers for damage done to his house, although he wag ruined socially and professionally. At the annual dinner in London on Saturday of the Amalgamated Society of Engineers, the general secretary estimated that the income of the past year amounted to £lBO,OOO. The surplus would be about £25,000, which would increase their accumulated fund to £170,000. A man named Hemmings, a foreman at one of the Lon- don docks, on returning to his home on Friday night, found his wife lying on the kitchen floor murdered. Her watch and wedding ring were missing. Her stepson has been arrested on suspicion of being; the murderer and thief. Early on Sunday morning a fire broke out in an oilman's shop in Oxford-street, Swansea, occupied by a man named Williams. The premises were totally destroyed. Williams, his wife, and others of the family escaped with difficulty. One child died from the injuries, and the charred remains of another were discoverd in the ruins. A policeman was seriously injured in attempting their rescue. Two shocking cases of outrages on women were heard at Lancaster assizes last week. Thomas Hadley, compositor, was charged with the murder of Mary Hayhurst. eceased had been bedridden from a cancer for twelve months, and died from the results of a criminal assault. He was found guilty of manslaughter, and was sentenced to twenty years' penal servitude.—Thomas Costlewaite, joiner, was charged with the murder of his wife at Barrow. He was found guilty of manslaughter, and sentence vies deferred. THE CHANNEL TUNNEL—The works at Sangatte, near Calais, in connection with the Channel Tunnel heading, continues to make very satisfactory progress. There was a break down with the machinery recently, which caused a delay for a few days, but the average daily advance of about eleven yards is being again maintained. The total length of the heading is now understood to be rather more than three-quarters of a mile. The strata through which the boring is passing continuesfavourably to work, but very little water is encountered. A considerable number of Italian workmen are employed. The much criticised compensation clauses of the Artisans' Dwellings Act are alleged to have had a remarkable and very unexpected result in Brighton. Three years ago the medical officer of health condemned an area under the Act, and the Council, accepting the decision, prepared to carry out an improvement scheme. Various incidental difficulties arose to delay its being carried out, until at length within the last few days a new member of the Council urged that the work should nof longer be postponed. It has, however, been declared that the property owners in the condemned district had been so energetic in improving their property, in the hope of getting increased compensation that the neces- sity for enforcing the Act had actually passed away. This view has been adopted by so many members of the Council that there is very little prospect of the scheme being re- vived. The town will thus avoid an expenditure of £130,000, or an estimated loss of £BO,OOO. The low death-rate of Brighton, the increased sanitary inspection, and the good water supply are cited as elements in favour of revoking the decision of three years ago. A PERFECT SAFETY LAMP FOIL MINERS.—A circular has been received from Mr. Thomas Burt, M.P.' stating that Mr. Ellis Lever, of Culceth Hall, Bowdon, has agreed to hand over to the Central Beard of the Miners' National Union £5OO, to be paid as a premium to any person, either ' in or out of the United Kingdom, who shall invent a por- table electric or other safety lamp to be used in mines. The lamp is to be a perfectly portable electric, or other lamp, which working miners can conveniently'carry from place to place in the mine, and which will not, under any circum- stances whatever, cause an explosion of gas. The efficiency of the lamps put in for compaition will be submitted to five gentlemen, composed as follows :—Three scientists to be named hereafter, one to be selected by Mr. Lever, one by the Council of the isoval Society, and one by the Council of the Society of Arts, one person representing the mining engineers, chosen by themselves, and one person represent- ing the workmen, chosen by the Central Board of the Miners' National Union. The offer will remain open until the 31st day of December next. Mn. GOSCHEN AND HIS CONSTITUENTS.—Mr. GOSChell ad- dressed his constituents at Ripon on Monday night. Re- ferring to the county franchise question, he said it was not en account of any fear of the political views of the masses that he was opposed to the extension of the franchise, but becanse it seemed to entrust the power exclusively to one class. He was not prepared to be responsible for the re- opening of the franchise question at present. He would speak and vote against the bill in Parliament, but would not lend himself to any combination tending to attack the Go- vernment on any side issue. Be had also come to the con- clusion that if, when the time came, the bulk of his Liberal supporters in Ripon should wish to be represented by a member who supported the Government on the extension of the franchise he would resign. He hoped that the County Bills would be broad and strong. With regard to Ireland, he pointed out that Home Rule was insidiously making progress which might become exceedingly dangerous. He agreed with Lord Hartington that patience and firmness should now be allowed time to do their work in Ireland. Concerning Egypt, he argued that the Government had no other course open to them than the abolition of the dual control.

SCENE IN A LIVERPOOL CHURCH. An extraordinary scene took place in St. Jude's Church, Liverpool, on Sunday morning. Upon the Rev. Mr. Fitzroy, the incumbent, ascending the pulpit, he said a statement had been made by Mr. Rakes, a member of the Church Association, and also by Mr. Bailey, one of his churchwardens, at public meet- ings in that city, that the incumbency of St. Jude's was about to become vacant. He denied that report, and asked his commutticents to meet him on Wednesday, when he would make a statement with reference to the circumstances which led to those rumours. He further remarked that he Alietrld take the matter before the Archbishop of York, as he id not get fairplay in Liverpool. At this point the rev. gentleman seemed to have noticed that the churchwarden Bailey was laughing, for, turning towards him, Mr. Fitzroy remarked that laughing in church was brawling, and that he would summon him for it. To this Mr. Bailey replied that the rev, gentleman should not indulge in personalities. Some excitement was created by this scene, and was in- creased when a man rose in the body of the church and in a load voice proclaimed that he was a witness as to the charges against the rev. gentlemen Mr. Bailey and about a score of persons, including the man who had interrupted, then left the church, and the service proceeded. ENGLISH PATENTS.—The following patents amongst others published in the Commissioners of Patents Journal We sealed during the week ending January 20th, 1883 : John Ealington Chaster, Manchester, electrician improve- Mtitts in telephonic apparatus; Adolph Isidor Rath, Man- cheater, waterproof manufacturer, for improvements in life- saving and swimming apparatus; Andrew Dix and Thomas. Renry Dix, Rock Perry, for improvements in apparatus for checking cords of blinds and other articles required to be Pulled up or down: John Barraclough Fell, Spark Bridge, Uiverston, for improvements in locomotive engines for railwaya; Henry Lancaster, Pendleton, engiueer, for improvements in steam traps; Eustace Carey and Ferdinand Hurter, Widnes, alkali manufac- turers, for improvements in the manufacture of hisulphite of soda; James Hargreaves, Whines, chemical engineer, for improvements in therm° dynamic engines; Henry Morris, Manchester, for improvements in apparatus, for adjusting ventilators, and for indicating the state of the temperature at any given place at a distance from such Place' Thomas Singleton, Damen, for improvements in the .ponstruction of looms for weaving; John Cowan QatiMn, engineer, for improvements in telephones, --List supplied by George Davies, C.E., Patent Solicitor. 4, St. Ann's Square, Manchester. .„ M. IRVING BISHOP IN LIVERPOOL: EXTRAORDINARY ANemEsrr.—A remarkable scene was witnessed in the large °Pen space ill front of the Adelnhi Hotel, Liverpool, about °tie o'clock on Saturday last. Mr. W.
