Mr. Forster gives a denial to a rumour that he has re- ceived a letter threatening to blow up his house. Mrs. Stanger, the wife of the German baker whose dis- appearance some months ago is known as the St. Luke's mystery No. 1, was brought up at the Mansion House, on Monday, on a charge of perjury. It is alleged that the pri- soner had given false evidence on behalf of the man Stumm, who is suspected of having murdered her husband. She was remanded. THE MISSING BALLOON.—The Balloon Society of Great Britain on Monday received a letter from Paris stating that the balloon Saladin, which was lost with Mr. Walter Powell, M.P., in Dezember, 1881, has been found in the mountains of the Sierra del Piedroza, Spain. Instructions have been forwarded to Paris to have the remnants of the balloon sent to London. The Earl of Durham, speaking at a farmers' meeting at Newcastle on the subject of approaching legislation, said it was imperative that tenants should receive compensation for unexhausted improvements, and it was also desirable in their interests that local taxation should be administered by county representative bodies. Neither of these questions could be called party question, but he was afraid they would be made party questions. A conference of delegates from all parts of North Wales was held' on Tuesday, at Chester, to consider the question of a college for North Wales, towards which the Government has offered a yearly grant of £4,000. It was resolved to accept the grant, and a committee was appointed to consider the question of a site, the meeting determining, however, that it should be in one ef the six counties of North Wales. Eight towns contend for the honour of having the college. COCKFIGHTING IN STAFFORDSHIRE.— The Staffordshire constabulary alarmed a number of cockfighters at Coseley, on Monday Arrangements had been made for several battles to be fought in a stable near a Wesleyan chapel. When sport was about to commence, the police broke into the stable, and succeeded in seizing a cock, and also spurs. The sudden visit cansed a great commotion, and one or two persons jumped through a window. Several battles have been recently fought in Coseley for heavy stakes. ACCIDENTS AT FOOTBALL MATCHES.—During a football match at Enfield, near Accrington, on Saturday, between Harwood and Enfield first team, a player named Thomas Ashton, while making a run, got his leg entangled with one of the opposing team and broke it. On the same day a foot- ball match was being played at Crewe between Crewe Alex- andria Club and Cocknage, when a young man named Buckley, of Davenham, who had secured the ball and was running with it, was " charged " and fell, his leg being badly broken. The game was immediately stopped. THE TICHBORNE CASE: PROSECUTION BY JEAN LUTE.— On Tuesday, at the New LAW Courts, Jean Luie, who gave evidence in the Tichborne case, and who was sentenced to five years' penal servitude for perjury, appeared as plaintiff in an action against Mr. E. D. Lewis, solicitor, for an ac- count of moneys received on his behalf. Defendant swore that the only sum he had received was £25 from Lord Rivers for defending Luie. Baron Pollock gave judgment for defesdant with costs. DEATH OF AN IRISH PEER.—The death is announced of Lord Castletown, of Upper Ossory, in the peerage of the United Kingdon. The late peer was son of John, late Earl of Upper Ossory, whose Irish estates he inherited. He was a Privy Councillor of Ireland and Lord-Lieutenant and Custos Rotulorum of Queen's County. He is succeeded in the peerage by his only son, Bernard E. B. Fitzpatrick, M.P. for Portarlington, married to Clare St. Leger, only child of Viscount Doneraile. There are few better authorities on the condition of the country than bankers. The condition of their accounts shows them to a nicety to what extent condition, customers are enjoying prosperity or are subject to distress. It is gratify- ing, therefore, to note that the chairman of the North and South Wales Bank on Tuesday was able to say that agri- cultural depression had touched the bottom, and that farmers • are now enjoying somewhat better times. This fact in itself gives hope of a not distant improvement in trade. Mr. WARTON'S PROBABLE RETIREMENT FROM PARLIA- MENT. A Bridport correspondent says that considerable political interest has been excited there by the completion of a canvass by the Hon. Baillie-Cochrane, son of Lord Lamington, recently chosen as a Conservative candidate. A canvas at this stage suggests a generally accepted rumour that Mr. Walton, M.P., has negotiated for resignation in favour of the candidate. The Liberals are fully prepared in the event of a bye-election. MR. JUSTICE DENMAIi AND "FINERY."—Mr. Justice Den- man, in sentencing, on Monday, at Durham Assizes, a young , girl who pleaded guilty to obtaining articles of dress by false pretences, .said she had been led away by foolish vanity and love of dress and a desire to look well in the eyes of others, and especially the opposite sex. Let him tell her that the man who cared for a dressy girl As not worthy of a girl's affection. He was a fool, and would not make a good husband, and the less girls bad to do with such men the better; His Lordship ordered the nominal punishment of three days' imprisonment. A middle-aged woman, belonging to the Salvation Army, was remanded at Dewsbury, on Monday, charged on her own confession with having killed a woman in a brawl in Glas- gow, nearly 12 years ago. The prisoner, who still persisted in her accusation against herself, had stated the details of the affair to a policeman, and told him that after she escaped from Glasgow a newspaper report was read to her which said that a verdict of wilful murder was returned against her at the inquest. The prisoner will, no doubt, be found to be suffering from delusions. Coroners' inquests and verdicts are unknown in Scotland.

A cruel murder was committed in Bellhaven•street, Bow, on Friday afternoon week. Mrs. Emma Hemmings, aged 39, wife of a dock foreman, was found by her husband on his return from work lying on the house floor dead, with a fear- ful wound on the temple. The house had been ransacked, the poor woman's rings torn with great force from her fin- gers, and a silver watch also stolen. A young man named Stephen Hemmings, the stepson of the murdered woman, was arrested on suspicion of being the criminal, and was brought up at Worship-street Police Court on Monday, when he was discharged. There was absolutely no evidence against him.

A "raid" has been made by the police in the Euston-road district on the women of bad character who assemble there nightly. Twelve of these women were charged before Mr. Ellison at Bow-street on Tuesday with using offensive language ani creating disturbances. The women had been arrested in consequence of complsints made by the inhabi- tants Mr. Vaughan said he was determined in these questions to do what he could to abate the scandals of the streets, but that could only be done if the inhabitants took up the matter themselves. The prisoners were convicted and fined sums varying from 5s to 40s; but in one case a sentence of a month's imprisonment was imposed. AN EVENTFUL VOYAGE.--The fine ship Harvey Mills re- turned to tne Mersey on Monday after an unsuccessful at- tempt to reach New York. It seems that as far back as the 19th May last the Harvey Mills left Liverpool for New York, under command of Captain Mills. When but a short time out she was in collision with a schooner, which latter vessel sank. The Harvey Mills afterwards put into Queens- town, where she was detained for several months. She then made another attempt to reach her destination, but was again unsuccessful, having become dismasted, in which con- dition she returned to the Mersey. The Harvey Mills is a large vessel of American construction. THE BISHOP OF GLOUCESTER ON THE FEW SYSTEM.— The Bishop of Gloucester and Bristol, at Clifton Parish Church, on Monday, drew attention to the sale of pews at that fashionable church, and said his attention had been called in many a painful letter to announcements-of these sales, by which the House of God was really and practically owned by different persons, some of them not belonging to the, parish, some non-resident, and in the habit of worship- ping in other churches, He had been called upon th do something in the matter, and, believing that that noble church should be in every sense for rich and poor alike a house of prayer, he was forced to speak plainly of this evil, and he was glad to say that a movement had now been set on foot with a view to acquiring for the parish three private rights and tenures in God's House. THE FEARFUL FIRE IN LONDON—An inquest was 6pened on Saturday on the the persons who were burned to death in a tenement house in Bishopsgate, Londm. The evidence showed that a considerable number of people had lived in the house, that it was very old and in a bad state of repair, land that there was only a small cistern, capable of contain- ing about 40 gallons, at the top of the house for the pur- pose of supplying the whole of the inmates with water. In these circumstances Mr. Costello, the legal representative of the friends of the deceased, said he should call witnesses in order to establish a case of criminal negligence against Colonel Haywood, the owner, and Mr. Grafton, Ins agent. Mr. Payne, the City coroner, said that a case Of man- slaughter could not be made out, but the injuiry was ad- journed for further evidence. On Monday the inquest was resumed. Further evidence was given in .support of the contention that the condition and overcrowding of the house had much to de with the loss of life. A verdict was returned stating that the cause of the fire was unknown, and calling the attention of the owner to the state of the houses now re- main* so that something might be done. ALARMING EXPLOSION AT A GLASGOW GASWORKS: SUPPOSED OUTRAGE.—On Satnrday night as a number of people were returning from Glasgow to Springburn, one of ine suburbs of that city, they discovered on the Keppochill Bridge, which carries the Frith and Clyde Canal over the highway, a small oval tin box lying on the parapet. One of the company, a man belonging to the Royal Artillery, named Adam Barr, opened the lid of the box, which he found was full of sand. He pushed his hand in among the sand, when the contents exploded and began to burn. Barr and four others were injured, though not seriously. As the box was destroyed by the fire, it is not known what the ex- plosive substance was. It may be mentioned that had the bridge been destroyed the canal for a distance of 16 miles would have been drained into the city. No clue has yet been found as to the perpetrator of the supposed outrage. About one o'clock the following morning a coal shed at the Buchanan-street Station of the Caledonian Railway wai blown up. On the watchman and a number of policemen running to the place the shed was found to be a total wreck. There were no signs of fire about the place, and as no gas was used in the shed the explosion mut have been caused by dynamite, gunpowder, or some similar substance. The ruins of the building lie just as they fell, and no search has yet been made to ascertain, if possible, the cause of the ex- plosion. An engine shed adjoining the coal shed was slightly damaged by the force of the explosion, as was also a kiln of the Canal-street Bottleworks, a quarter of a mile distant: Nothing is known about the perpetrator of the outrage. A preliminary examination of the gasometer has resulted in arrangements being made for a Government inquiry into the matter. Mr. Thomas Hawksley's opinion is that the explosion was caused by dynamite, or, at all events, was something other than gas.

Che BRUTAL GAROTTE EORBERY.—At the Leicester Assizes, debris of the carriage caught fire. Fifteen persons were

on Thursday, before Mr. Justice Cave, Daniel Gallagher, Michael Gallagher, and John Gallagher were charged with robbing James Kilborn, a Northamptonehire cattle dealer, with Violence. Prisoners waylaid Kilborn, knocke.4 him down, filled his mouth with rags, and kicked him till they got his money. The prisoners were found guilty, and Daniel and Michael were sentenced to five year' penal servitude, and John to 18 months' hard labour. On Thursday morning the leading colliery owners of Yorkshire received a circular from Mr. Pickard, Barnsley, communicating the decision of the conference, held at Barnsley on Monday, asking them to arrange a meeting on Tuesday next at Sheffield or Leeds, jointly or separately, to confer with a deputation respecting the laying idle of all collieries on Saturday of each week, and working eight hours on other days. The circular says it is neces- sary to do something to preserve capital and the wages of workmen. TuE Messiem Heamrss —A Dublin correspondent tele- graphs :—The clerk to the Rathdown Guardians, who re- ceived the missing heiress when deserted on a doorstep at Kingstown, has so many inquiries from people who have deserted children in their service that he finds much diffi- culty in answering them all. On Thursday a Dublin soli- citor wrote for information regarding Mary Ann Carey, who, he is informed, is the very person now looked for. He is directed to take her case in hand, with the view to making good her claim the story of her desertion tallying exactly with that of the missing heiress. At the Manchester Assizes, on Thursday, Abraham Thomas, a young man, who was in service near Bolton, as a butler, was sentenced to death for the murder of Mrs. Leigh, who was housekeeper at the same place. The cir- cumstances of the murder admitted of no doubt, and there was practically no defence. The housekeeper bad made some complaints to the master of the house which Thomas had reason to believe would result in his dismissal, and the morning after the complaints were made he deliberately shot the housekeeper with one of his master's guns, making no attempt afterwards to escape. PETERSOROUGH CATHEDRAL.—At a meeting of the Dean and Chapter and the general committee appointed to con- duct the affairs of Peterborough Cathedral in the present state held on Thursday, it was decided to completely restore the building. Subscriptions for this object have been re- ceived for five or six years past, and, though the central tower principally needed restoration, it was felt that the preset* emergency afforded a good opportunity for under- taking' the entire work. Canon Perowne presided. It was resolved to issue an appeal for the restoration of the whole building, the sum required being roughly estimated at £55,000. THE PECULIAR PEOPLE: VERDICT OF MANSLAUGHTER AGAINST A FATHER.—An inquest has been held in London relative to the death of a child named Cousins, three years of age. The father, who is a clerk in the War Office, and tho mother gave evidence showing that they beloneed to the sect of the Peculiar People, that they put their trust in the Lord, and refuse to have any medical aid in case of sick- ness A surgeon who had made a post-mortem examination stated that, with proper treatment in the earlier stages, the child's life might have been prolonged. The coroner said that the father was legally and morally responsible for the death, and the jury returned a verdict of manslaughter against him. THE MILES PLATTING CASE.—We ate informed that Sir Percival Hey /rood has intimated to the members of St. John's Church, Miles Platting, that a writ of quare impedit was issued on Saturday last from the Queen's Bench Division to the Bishop of Manchester in the case of his lordship's refusal to institute the Rev. Harry Cowgill to the vacant benifice. We are further informed that the writ would be in the bishop's possession on Monday last. We learn that the Bishop has replied to the resolution which was communicated from the meeting of communicants held in the parish schools on Tuesday evening, the 16th instant, and that the chairman of that meeting has since addressed a reply to his lordship. In the present state of affairs it has been decided not to mike the contentsof these letters public.—Manchester Guardian. The Right Hon. W. E. Forster, M.P., presided on Thurs- day night at a banquet given by the Leeds Liberals. He preferred, he said, in addreesing them after the banquet, to look forward rather than to the past, though he would not let the occasion pass of thanking them for their suppert at a time when support was most needed. He thought there was likely to be a busy parliamentary session commenced next month, one in which both Scotland and England might expect to obtain some really beneficent legislation. The right hon. gentleman' then referred at great length to the question of parliamentary reform, and said, though he did not care whether it was dealt with in one or two bills, the question of redistribution of seats Was of such extreme im- portance that it was necessary they should form a distinct opinion upon it. THE DEVELOPMENT OF THE RIBBLE —On Thursday, at a special meeting of the Preston Town Council, the resolu- tions for the purchase of the Ribble, its development, the constructing of docks, and the extension of the borough were confirmed. The Council also had reported to them that the plan for a new high-level bridge over the estuary fer the extension of the Cheshire Lines Railways to Black- pool had been abandoned. The line will be extended from W 'gar to Longhton on the West Lancashire Railway, and will run from Preston to Lytham and Blackpool by the coast. The construction of such a bridge eas that proposed would have been opposed, inasmuch as it would have seri- ously interfered with the scheme of development of the Ribble. The Ribble scheme will involve a very heavy cost, estimated by some at half a million. VERDICT OF MANSLAUGHTER AGAINST A CLEIIRGVMAN.— Mr. J. Rogers, coroner for Tunbridge district, Kent, on Wed- nesday, resumed the inquiry at West Malling concerning the death of Sarah Ann Wright, daughter of a labourer, who died on the 14th December, as alleged, from the administra• tion of oil of almonds to her by the Rev. John Henry Ti mins, vicar of the parish. Mts. killed, and several of whom were burned to death, and 14 others were injured. Further particulars report that 18 pas- sengers and two porters were killed. ARABI AND HIES COMPANIONS.—The Ceylon papers give an account of the voyage and arrival of Arabi and his com- rades. They describe them as being generally in good spirits, and appearing to regard the voyage as a pleasant picnic got up for their amusement. On arriving at Colombo, the Lieutenant-Governor went on board and conversed with the chief prisoners. They expressed themselves glad that Ceylon had been selected as their place of exile. Arabi landed on the morning of the 11th, and took up his residence in a handsome and well•situated house. A great crowd assembled to witness the landing Loss or A VESSEL AND 400 LITES.—A shocking disaster has occurred off the Dutch coast. The Hamburgh and New York mail boat Cimbria, with 380 passengers and 110 sea- men, was sunk by collision with a steamer named the Sultan. The collision occurred in a dense fog, and the Cimbria was cut down to the water's edge and sank in a short time. The officers were unable to launch the boats, and RS a last resource cut away some of the spars and threw the deck fittings overboard, in ordor to give the people same chance of escape. The steamer went down suddenly, and great numbers were thrown into the sea. It is believed 400 per- sons have perished. ATROCIOUS DOUBLE MURDER:A Swiss correspondent writes that an atrocious double murder has just been com- mitted near Bale. The victims are two Jews, father and son, of the name of Meyer, from Wilhelm, in the Grand Duchy of Baden. The two Meyers, men at considerable mean', were on their way to the fair of Kandern when, as they passed through a wood, they were attacked by several men armed with hatchets and brutally murdered. The object of the murderers was plunder, for as the Meyers were in the habit of making considerable purchases at the fair it was supposed they had with them a large sum of money. As it happened, however, they had very little. One man sus- pected of complicity in the crime has been arrested at We, and another at Wilhelm. The accounts received by mail of the hotel fire at Mil- waukee, state that the Newhall House had been regarded as a "death-trap," The scenes during the burning of the house were appalling. The firs department appears to have been almost powerless to stay the prggress of the flames. A con- siderable number of the victinisrere poor servant girls from Ireland. There appears to have been a suspicion awakened at the time that the terrible calamity was due to incendiar- ism. The New York World, in an article on the subject of fires in American hotels, says that, as to the safety of the average summer resort hotel, "it will only be necessary to cite the fact that an expert sent to Saratoga by the New York Board of Underwriters, last year, to inspect the heat- ing and cooking apparatus of the hotels there, reported that only tour were safe." TIM RELATIVE DECLINE or PARIS —The great increase in the cost of living in Paris, occasioned by the enormous and exceptional amount of the municipal debts and conse- quent local taxation in that city, appears, from facts cited in the report of Mr. Plunkett, the secretaay to the British Embassy, to be seriously affecting the rate of increase of its inhabitants. According to the latest quinquennial census while the increase of population in St. Pierre-Calais was over 30 per cent., and that of Nice over 24 per cent., in Paris it was only 15 per cent. In a list of the twenty-two largest towns and cities the capital occupies a tenth place only; and in the opinron of Mr. Plunkett it would have stood lower but for the fact that the census happened to he taken in December, when the passage of strangers through Paris is considerable, and when rich strangers who live in Paris only for pleasure are mostly in town. TERRIBLE EXPLOSIONS IN AMERICA: FIFTEEN PERSONS KILLVD.—The last arriving mail steamer at averpool from New York brought particulars of two terrific explosions which occurred in the United States, and by which no fewer than 15 persons lost their lives. In one case the calamity was caused by two boilers at the works of the Bethlehem Iron Company. It seems that a 9et of ten boilers were located over the engine house of the works at an eievation of 35 feet, and on the 9th instant two of these exploded with tremendous force. The engine house was completely wrecked, and out of the ten boilers only three were left in position. One boiler was hurled through the roof of an old mill some 300 feet distant, and fell in the midst of about about 100 workmen. Two engineers who were repairing the machinery were killed in a shocking manner, whilst a woman named Graft, who was passing through the engine- house with her husband's dinner, was also killed instantly. Two others of the men in the works were killed, and at latest accounts it was reported that several others were missing.— In the second case the disaster happened at Jones and Nesbit's coal mine, near Coultersville, Chicago, and resulted in the death of lb miners. It appears that on the Bth inst. a violent explosion occurred at the mines, and when the ex- ploring parties attempted to descend the shaft they were met by dense volumes of foul air. It 'Was known that 12 persons were in the mine where the explosion occurred, and only two were got out alive—one a boy, and the other Mr. Mason, the foreman. After the foul'air bad somewhat disappeared, the explorers, who were miners, made another attempt to reach their comrades, and this time an entrance was effected. It was found that all the men were dead, the bodies of tvOts be- ing very much burned. The othn bodies bore no multila- tion marks, the poor men having been suffocated. On the bodies being brought to the surface, heartrending scenes were witnessed. Eight of the men had families, who were waiting at the pit's mouth from the time the explopion oc- curred until the bodies were brought up, not knowing actu- ally the fate which had befallen their husbands and fathers.
Clarke, one of the young men convicted of the Graves- end murder, has, it is stated, written to Mrs. Eves, widow of the murdered man, acknowledging his participation in the crime. _ _

WRECK OF IN AUSTRALIAN STEAMER AND Loss OF 16 Livgs.—A Renter's telegram from Sydney of 28th ult., received via San Fracisco, says :—" The steamer New Eng- lend, employed in the Clarence River trade, struck the bar wri the river yesterday evening and became a total wreck, heavy seas breaking completely over her. A number of the passengers and crew managed to reach the shore, but others were left clinging to the shrouds, and were washed off. There were 53 persons in all on board, of whom about 16 were drowned." SAD DEATH OF A RETURNED COLONIST.—A gentleman about 50 Tears of age was found dead on Tuesday at a Ply- mouth hotel. He had given the name of James Harris,.but was otherwise unknown. In his bag was £276 in gold. It has been ascertained that he lately came home from New Zealand, where he had been for 20 years, and where he had amassed considerable property. He returned to England to see his sister, who was ill at Exeter and has since died, and purposed goine•baok shortly, but intended first to procure a wife. He suffered from palpitation of the heart, to which ! his death is presumably attributable. BARROW ROI.ITB TO TIM ISLE OF MAN AND BELFAST.— The rapid development of the passenger traffic by this route has necessitated another addition to the splendid fleet of the Barrow Steam Navigation Company. We understand that the large and powerful new paddle steamer Duchess of Edinburgh, recently built of steel for the South-Eastern Railway Company by Messrs. J. and G. Thomson, the cele- brated Clyde shipbuilders, has been purchased by Messrs. James Little and Company, of Barrow, for their Barrow and cross Channel trade. Some alterations will be necessary to thoroughly adapt her for the trade referred -to, and it is expected she will be ready for the Isle of Man trade by the end of June. It is proposed that she shall take the mid-day service, and the Manxman the evening service. Passengers; will thus have the advantage of travelling by one or other lof two of the fastest steamers in the Channel. The Duchess of Edinburgh is expected to make the run from Barrow to Douglas in *hours.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHTP CANAL BILL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHTP CANAL BILL.
ADVERSE DECISION OF THE EXAMINER,

On Monday, Mr. Frere, one of the examiners for standing orders on private bills, gave his decision in this case, which was argued before him on the previous Friday. It was proposed, as is well known, by the bill to construct from Liverpool to Manchester a ship canal, the cost of which was estimated at about £5,633,000. Memorials were presented by the London and North-western Railway Com- pany, the Upper Mersey Navigation Commissioners, the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, and the Bridgewater Canal, complaining of non-compliance with the standing orders, on the ground that the promoters had neglected to prepare and deposit plans and sections with respect to a low water channel and other works, together with the estimates and the Parliamentary deposit of 4 per cent. on the same. Mr. J. Coates (Messrs. Dyson and Co.) appeared for the promoters, Sir Theodore Martin (Messrs. Martin and Leslie) fer the Upper Mersey Navigation Commissioners and the Bridgwater Canal Company, Mr. J. C. Rees for the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, and Mr. Pritt (Messrs. Sherwood and Co.) for the London and North-Western Company. Mr. FRERE, in giving his decision, said: The allegations in the memorials against this bill, on which I have new to announce my decision, state that the standing orders have not been complied with, inasmuch as "no plan or section of the low water channel, the execution of which is proposed to be authorised by clause 26, has been made or deposited." This channel is several miles in length, and is proposed to be constructed in a permanent manner and with a depth and capacity sufficient to enable ships of a large tonnage to go up to a point on the Mersey where at present there is no water at low tide, only the fresh water dribbling down the sands. This is, I think, acknowledged by the promoters as well as the petitioners to be a work of magnitude and im- portance such as is rare even in the present day, and it is a work which comes under the designation of an allegation of the standing orders of the two houses of Parliament, and is a work of which plans and sections ought prime fade vs be deposited. The arguments of Mr. Coates are twofold. First, he has called attention to the provisions of the Mersey Con- servancy Acts under which the conservators of the river, to whom plans and sections of the work in question are by clause 26 to be submitted for approval, and without whose approval and consent the powers cannot be exercised—that these conservators have powers to dredge and deepen the channels of the river or to authorise the same to be done, and the inference he proposes to draw is that this is not a work beyond the powers so given to the conservators. I consider, however, that the work proposed is beyond the powers of the body to whom the conservancy is entrusted. .The name conservancy is sug- gestive, but I will not dwell upon that. Though the Com- missioners have power to deepen and widen the channels of the river for the purpose of maintaining the existing navi- gation, such a work as is now proposed is not contemplated in their Acts, and they are provided with no funds for such a work. It is a vast and important work in itself, most important as forming a portion and a very essential portion of a magnificent scheme of a ship canal to Manchester, which is to be executed by independent parties. The second ground of Mr. Coates, and the one on which he places most reliance, is the impossibility of laying down a definite line for the proposed channel, and the impossibility of giving plans and sections. In support of this he called Mr. Abernethy, the consulting engineer to the scheme so far as regards the present time. But what did he say in cross-examination? He most candidly stated, "It would be very difficult for an engineer lib lay down the definite line of channel without a good deal of consideration and experience," and "before the channel can be defined careful observations will have to be taken extending over a considerable time, probably a whole year." And again he says: "%e shall commence the canal immediately, because there are many heavy works which will occupy a large amount of time, and then very careful observations will be made so as to define exactly the existing line of current, and then after that we shall determine on the best mode of dredging and the direction of the channel." And "there can be no doubt if two years were given you may define the channel exactly throughout the whole length." Under these cir- cumstances, I can entertain no doubt that before this portion of the scheme was brought before Parliament, plins and sections of the works proposed ought, in compliance with the standing orders, to have been deposited. And although this is not in the allegation, of course it would follow that the estimate of the cost and the deposit of £4 per cent. on that estimate should have been made.

Mr. Coates: I do not know whether you would feel justi- fied in making any special report to the House, seeing that the promoters have, as to all the other parts, very carefully prepared their plans and sections. Mr. Frere : It follows as a matter of course that I shall report to the House. Mr. Rees: The Examiner cannot report specially unless he entertains a doubt.
The Bill will corns on appeal before the Standing Orders Committee at its first meeting after the assembling of Parlia- ment.

div.head: CHESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE.
div.p: CHESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE.

On Tuesday afternoon a special meeting of the Che- shire Chamber of Agriculture was held in the Town Hall' Macclesfield; Mr. H. J. Tollemache, M.P., in the chair. Up to within a few years ago the North Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture held monthly meetings at Macclesfield, the members comprising the agricultural community in the northern part of Cheshire. The society was wound up about two years since, and the Cheshire Chamber, at their last meetimg, resolved to meet at Macclesfield, with the view of obtaining the support of the members of the defunct Cham- ber. Tbis was the first meeting of the Chamber held at Macclesfield. There was only an average attendance, amongst those present being Lieutenant-Colonel T. U. Brocklehurst, of Henbury Hall; who was nominated a mem- ber.

Mr. T. RIGBY, the secretary, read a paper, in which he discussed the report of Her Majesty's Royal Commission on Agriculture. Lieutenant-Colonel BROCKLEITURST spoke approvingly of the paper, and proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Rigby. He was sorry it had not touched upon a matter which must be of much interest to farmers, especially in bad seasons—the system of ensilage they have in America, which is packing the grain crops upon an improved principle similar to the way in which we bog turnips and potatoes in this country. He did not know how far such a system would be workable in our climate, but he thought it might at all events 1),3 done with regard to hay in inclement seasons. He would be glad at another meeting of the Chamber to read a paper on the subject. (Hear, bear.) Mr. MILLINGTON (Henburv) said that though there had been Some impatience manifested that the Government had not dealt sooner with agricultural topics, he thought it was not to be very much wondered at, or indeed regretted. He believed we should now get a more robust measure than we would have done a few years ago. It was high time tenant farmers had better security for the money they expended on the land.

The CHAIRMAN said it was admitted thrcughout the length and breadth of the land that there 'should be com- pensation allowed for unexhausted improvements ; the only question was how it could be best accomplished and upon what principle. Mr. SLATER seconded the vote of thanks to Mr. Rigby for his paper, which was agreed to. On the proposition of Mr. RIGBY, seconded by Mr. MIL- LINGToN, the following resolution was passed :—"That this meeting approves of the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Agriculture as regards compensation for un- exhausted improvements, local taxation, the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, the removal of restrictions on cul- tivation, the reduction of railway rates of height, appoint- ment of a Minister of Agriculture, the alteration as regards tithe re,r,it charge, and the recommendations respecting the adulteration of manures and feeding stuffs and seeds, and desire to see them all soon fully provided for by law • and that a copy of this resolution be sent to the Central Cham- ber of Agriculture, and also to the Prime Minister, as the head of Her Majesty's Government." A vote of thanks to the Chairman terminated the meeting.

div.head: LORD lIARTINGTON AT DARWEN.
div.p: LORD lIARTINGTON AT DARWEN.

The Marquis of Hartington and Mr. Grafton addressed a large meeting of their constitteents on Saturday at Damen. Adverting to measures which he thought might be in the power of the present Parliament to pass before the time for its dissolution arrived, Lord Hartington expressed his opinion that it might deal with the licensing laws. The reform of those laws was a question, he said, which had made considerable progress in the last few years. This was indicated, in his opinion, by the great diminution which had taken place voluntarily on the part of the people in the consumption of intoxicating liquors. It might be argued from this fact that the people were able to deal with the question for themselves in the best and most salutary man- ner, but on the other hand undoubtedly it showed that there did exist amongst the people a strong and ardent desire to ' repress the great evil of intemperance, and it did to ' some extent strengthen the demand " thet Govern- ment and Parliament should come to their assistance." Passing from this subject to personal matters, his Lordship referred to the changes in the Government' remarking that it was with very considerable regret that he severed his connection with the India Office. He acknewledged, however, that it was better as a rule that the holder of the position he had just vacated should occupy a seat in the "serener atmosphere of the House of Lords." • With reference to Egyptian affairs, he maintained that the Government had no alternative but to interfere as they had done. Intervention in Egypt in some form was a necessity. For this the present Goverrmient was not responsible, and he thought it must be admitted that throughout their pro- ceedings no one could say that they had disregarded the just claims of the other States of Europe, the just object of the Sultan, or our special engagements to France. As to the charge that if England had acted more firmly and inter- vened at an earlier period recourse to force might not have been necessary, he pointed out that we had to deal with a State which had relations and treaties with every Power in Europe, and that premature interference would probably have led to active opposition on the part of other States. As it was, we had the warm acquiescence and ap- proval of almost all the Powers. It was true that France looked with some jealousy and disapproval on our proposal to abolish the Joint Control, but he believed France was still under much misapprehension as .to our aims, and that I when the disinterestedness of our policy was made fully apparent all jealousy and distrust on the part of our French allies would pass away. He believed that in the hands of the financial adviser which it was intended to recommend the Egyptian Government to appoint the interests of all the Powers would be as safe as our own.—After Mr. Grafton had addressed the meeting and the usual resolution of con- fidence had been submitted, an amendment was proposed expressing regret that Mr. Grafton had not seen his way to vote with Mr. Gladstone, Lord Hartington and other mem- bers of the Government on the Bradlaugh question.—Mr. Grafton defended his position, and the amendment had only the support of about a dozen persons. Before leaving Darwen, on Saturday evening, Lord Har- tington received at the residence of Mi. W. Snape, a depu- tation on behalf of the Power Loom Weavers' Associations in North-East Lancashire, who asked His Lordship to use his influence as a member of the Government, to prevent the oversizing of cotton yarns and the "steaming " of weaving sheds, by which, it is alleged, the health of the operatives is seriously affected. Lord Hartington promised to communicate with the Homo Office on the subject, adding that Parliament had recognised the principle that adequate securities must be taken for the protection of the health and comfort of operatives, and, if the practices in I question were really injurious to health and productive cf \disease, it was a matter which the Home Office :eight legitimately inquire into with a view to remedy being applied.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

TYE COUNTERPANE WEAVERS' DISPUTE.—The majority of the employers in the Bolton counterpane weaving trade having_resolved to grant the advance of eight per cent. in the wages of the operatives in a fortnight's time, the men have returned to work, and the dispute is at an end. A deputation ot locomotive employes of the North British Railway, on Wednesday, waited upon Mr. Walker, manager, at Edinburgh, and presented a petition hearing 2000, signa- tures for a reduction of the hours of labour. Mr. Walker promised attention to the matter at the next directors' meet- ing. WAGES IN THE ROYAL DOCKYARDS.—NearIy the whole of the established workmen in Ch4.Warn Dockyard have stnt petitions to the Lords of the AdiThralty asking for an in- crease of wages, as it is some years since an increase was granted to the ading trades, and as the value of labour in private yards has increased. Chatham is working in con- junction with some of the other royal yards.

WEEKLY RETURN OF BILLS OF SALE AND FAILURES —ln the week ending Jan. 20, 1893, there were 267 bills of sale in England and Wales, a decrease of 788/over those of the corresponding period last year ; and the failures gazetted numbered 214, a decrease of 10. The totals for portion of year to Jan. 20,1883, are bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 703, a decrease of 2,175; the failures gazetted numbered 613, a decrease of 3.—Extract from Stubbs' _Mr- contile Gazette. MINERS' CONFERENCE AT WIGAN. A conference of mioers' delegates was held at Wigan on Wednesday, to take into cpsideration, and make final arrangements, for the carrying into ciperation the question of restricting the out- put. It was resolved that the district should work five days per week and eight hours per day, and that the Coalowuers' Association for South-West Lancashire and the South-East Lancashire and Cheshire Coalowners'Associations be written to asking their co-operation to bring about a restriction of the output. Thu RESTRICTION OF THE OUTPUT OF COAL.—A Con- ference of delegates from the mining districts in Yorkshire as well as from other places, was held on Monday in Barnsley. There was a larget:ndance, 20,000 miners con- nected with the Association .71M.13 being represented. Mr. Cowey occupied the chair, aad stated that the conference was the outcome of that rately held in Leeds, when the question of the output of coal was fully gone into. The following resolutions were then agreed to :—" That this conference agrees to adopt the resolutions come to at the. late conference held at Leeds; that the miners shall only: work five days per week of eight hours per day, from bank to bank." "That hi the opinion of this conference, Satur- day will be the best day in the week to be taken by the men for the purpose of carrying out the object in view, the restriction of the output of coal:'• LANCASHIRE MINERS AND THE PROPOSED RESTRICTION OF OIIIPUT.—One of the county demonstrations of the miners of Lancashire to consider the question of restricting the output of coal was held on Amberswood Common, near Wigan, on Saturday. The chair was occupied by Mr. R. Whalley, and there was a fairly good attendance. Mr. Finney, miners' agent for Wigan, said if the men must keep the advance of wages they had gained, they must restrict the output. Already there were indications that with the approach of summer the employers intended if possible to take off the advance. All other counties were organising, and they were coming to the conclusion that increased out- put meant lower wages. The follocing resolution was unanimously agreed to :—" That this meeting is of opinion that the whole of the miners of Great Britain ought to carry out the resolution passed at the Leeds Conference to work five days per week and eight hours per day, in order to bring about a better state of things,"

END OF THE CALEDONIAN RAILWAY STRIKE.—The strike on the Caledonian Railway came to an end on Saturday night. The men consented to return to work, the company having offered to re-engage them to fill up the vacancies and to give them their old places, so far as they are able, at the old weekly wages. The men who have continued faith- ful to their duty, and who have been promoted, and the new men engaged will not be thrown over. The company held (that a universal ten-hours day is impracticable with regard. to the signalmen. The company will agree to make the ' working day of mineral brakesmen 12 hours, or 60 bona a !seek, on the understanding that the weekly wages be read- justed ; but the company will only agree to pay overtime, as at present, as ordinary time. The company do not see their way to alter the present arrangements with rtgnrd to mineral engine drivers, who work 10 hours a day. The general manager and heads of departments will meet deputa• tions of the various grades on an early day with referenee to Sunday duty and other matters. TIE LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE.—Concessions in price have still to be made to do any business of importance in the iron market, and although makers are not disposed to give way very much, the tendency of the market is in favour of buyers. Lancashire makers of pig iron, who were on Tues- day quoting le per ton under last Friday's rates, report fair orders having come forward on the basis of 46s 6d, less 21, delivered Equal to Manchester, which is now their quoted price. For district 'orands prices were unchanged, Lincoln. shire being 47s to 483 and ll,erbyshire 483 6d to 50s per ton, • less 21, delivered here; at about is pe^ ton under these figures there are considerable offers in the market for Lin- colnshire, but at the full quoted rates only a small retail trade is being done. There is still only a very limited business coming forward in the finished iron trade; makers, however, although getting very Bhort of work in some cases, are not disposed to quote low prices for- forward contracts, but for present specificallons they are prepared to meet buyers, and £6 5s to £6 is 61 per ton for ordinary bars, delivered into the Manchester district, represents the basis of the actual selling prices. THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE.—Business in the coal trade of this district continues only moderate for the time of the year, with supplies plentiful in the market. Best coal at the pit mouth does not now average more than about lOs per ton ; good second qualities can be bought at about Bs, with common house fire coals about Gs 61 to is per ton. A fairly good demand is kept up for the lower classes of coal for ironmaking and other manufacturing purposes, but trade requirements generally do not show any increase, the ten- dency, if anything, being rather towards a lessening con• sumption. Common round coals for steam and forge pur- poses average, about 68 to Os Gd per ton at the pit mouth, burgy 4s Gd to ss, good slack 33 61 to 4s, with inferior sorts to be got at 38 to 3s 3d per ton. The shipping trade has been only dull, and both at the high level, Livezpool, and the Garston docks steam coal is freely offered at from is 6d to 7s 9d per ton. In the local Liverpool trade prices are also easier, and during the week there Ins been a reduc- tion of 6d. per ton on coAl coming into the Crown-street station from th?, St. Helens district. For coke a fair de- mand is maintained at about late rates.

PITCH AND 7 oss.—A 'ad named Thomas Ford was bronght up in custody, charged with playing pitch and toss in Silver- squa.re, on sunday afternoon.—The pr:soner pleaded not guilty, but the Bench fined him 5s and costs, or seven days' imprison- ment in default.

STEALING A Bootr.—John Egan, of no fixed residence, was charged with stealing from Josh. Taylor, carter, an order blek, value 3s, the property of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co.— The prosecutor was busilv engaged loading his lorry at the Curlers' Arms, Buttermarlset-street, when the prisoner took the book from his nocket. Prisoner was walking away with It, when prosecutor called to him, and he threw the book across the lorry. A constable came up, and the prisoner was given._ Into custody.—Prisoner was fined lOs and costs, or 14 days' mprisonment. " PEGGY "—John Henry Winwick, James Corcoran, Edward Bolton, and W. Furnival, boys, were summoned for playing- peggy " in the streets, and were each fined 2s. DISTURBING INRABITANTS.—Frederick Fairhurst, a boy, was found guilty of disturbing inhabitants of Mersey-street by knocking at their do )1,1, and was fined is including coits. RIGHTING.—John Plunket and Henry Bate pleaded guilty to fighting in Old-ruad, Latchford, and were ordered to be bound over in their ov.n recognisances of £5 each to keep the peace for six months, or go to prison for 14 days. LODGING HOUSE CASE. Mary McHugh, lodging-house keeper, who did not appear, was summoned for allowing over- crowding—lnspector Norman said the defendant had been a pest to the town for the last 20 yeas to his knowledge.—lt was suggested that the woman should be got into the work- house, but Inspector Norman said the relieving officer had tried to persuade her to go there, but she would not.—She was finrd 20s and costs.

_ SCHOOL ATTENDANCE PROSECUTIONS.—The following persons were summoned at the instance of Mr. George Riley, school attendance officer, for neglecting to send their children regularly to school, and were dealt with as stated:—John Gibbons, forgeman, Latchford. fined ss; Pat Kelley, Bank- street, 55 ; Bridget Collins, Town 13ill, 53 ; John Raftery, forgeman. School-street, dismissed; Benjamin Aukland, wood turner, Bank Quay, Se; Adam Davies, fustian cutter, General- street, ss; William Yates, forgeinan. Hall-street, ss; Patrick Doyle. labourer, Clare-st eet. ss; and Martin Layley, labmrer, Orford-street, 58:_
TUESDAY.—Before Mainr Cartwright and Councillor Broadbent.

As EXPENSIVE RlDE.—James O'Donnel. filecotter, was barged with having been drunk in Egypt street on the pre- vious day.—The constable who proved the case said the pri- soner was helplessly drunk, and that he had to obtain the assistance of another constable to bring him to the police station on a hand-cart--A fine of 5s and cos's was imposed. WEDNFSDAY. —Before Alderman Chand!ey. BEGGlNG.—Elizabeth Ann Barker, a married woman, was charged with having been found begging in Palmyra square on the previous day.—P.O. Paice proved the case.—The prisoner stated that she had been compelled to beg as her husband, who was a wireworher, could not get employment. They had come to the town about a fortnight before thinking they would find employment, but they had been unable to do so.—Alderman Chandley said begging could not be allowed, as anyone in (listxess had the opportunity of applying to the Guardians for relief.—The prisoner was then discharged with a caution.

DRUNK OR INEBRIATED ?—ThOMAS Wilkinson, a respectably dressed man, was charged with having been drunk and dis- orderly in Scotland-road on the previous evening —Prisoner said he was not drunk, but he was inebriated.—P.O. 31 slid prisoner was very drunk, and had a crowd round him; could scam ly stand, and he had to bring him to the police station.—A fine of 5s and costs was Imposed. INDECENCY.—Jane Swabs, a married svorna 1, who said she had one child, was found guilty of indecent conduct in Palmyra. Pc:plate, and was sentemed t II days' imps's ,nment, Alder- man Chaudley remarking that it was a very depler:e case. TUURSDAY.—There was no business at the court trirf morning. ERIDA.Y.—The business will be band repwted in another - C )IUMII.

A little boy had been sent to dry a towel before the nun. • gery fireplace. "Mamma, is it done when it is brown ?" he asked, when the towel began to smoke. EARLY HISTORY OF CANTERBIIRY.—Canterbnry was for long a st;nding witness of the triumph of priestly Over regal power ; it is still a worthy memorial of the birthplace of English Christianity. For LOD centuries it has been the seat of a bishopric, and is the oldest among those which claim Augustine as their founder. As a town it is older still. When Canterbury was first founded we do not know. In the writings of earlier historians, the mythical Lud Eudi- btas greets us, as in the annals of more than one other ancient city; Geoffrey of Monmouth assigns its foundation to him, sod informs us that The date was almost 900 years before Christ. This statement, however, by no means meets with general acceptance. It is, nevertheless, probable that a settlement—to which two mourida, mentioned bel I,v, may have belonged—existed before the Romans came. T ry oc- cupied it, and gave to their station the name of Darovernum —or, as it appears in Bede'e writings, Dorobernia—in which, nrobably, some reminiscence of the earlier appellation 34 ern- bahned. When the English invaders came, they called the city Cant-wara•byrg—the town of the men of Kent—whence has come the present name, Latinised by the Normans as Cantuaria. In the Roman time Dorobernia was a city of importance; three roads—one from Dover, another from near Hythe, called Stone Street, a third from Richbormagh —led to it, the first of which, the great Watling Street, went on to London. It was thus on the main highway b tween the °oast and the metropolis of the south, a place through which travellers from Gaul, and from Rome itself, Roman remains bear witness to iwtsouilmdpnoarttuarnaclelyinpara. Many rlydays. The situation is one which would naturally attract inhabitants. It is built in an open and breezy valley, to which the chalk downs decline gently on the south-western side, the opposite one being more steep, and is traversed by the river Stour—a clear, bright stream —which divides above the ttty to form an island on which a part of the buildings stand. After the English had settled in Kent, Canterbury became the chief city of the district, and the re4iderce of their king. Ethelbert, however, on the arrival of Augustine, abandoned it for Reculver—another Roman fortress, from the ruins of which he built himself a palace—so that Canterbury ceased to be a royal residenoe, though retaining its priority, and adding speedily thereto an additional splendour as the seat of an archepiscopal set ald of two important menasteries.—" Our Ot^n Count:,' for January.

It was t° sha greaeft to Mr. GLADSTONE, no person reak —et right than Lord HARTINCIITON vol_i behalf of the Liberal party. His rrteefrosre, with respect to not a few 10,1,11atly questions have been understood a as indications of the views likely to predominate among e, ° thiy, - Cabinet. LordnARIINGTON

is so liberally endowed with that rather rare I gift, common sense, that the common people always hear him gladly, knowing from past experience that the subject which he has in hand will be treated in a thoroughly practical manner, and that there will be no difficulty in comprehending his meaning. It was. of course, impossible for the SECRETARY for WAR to enter into detail upon every subject that he dealt with, but he nevertheless managed to indicate his views on coming questions with retnarkable clearness. To many people the most important passages in his two speeches are those dealing with matters of domestic legislation. No surprise can be felt that this should be the case, for Irish affairs and questions relating to foreign policy have so exclusively monopolised the attention of Government and of Parlia- ment for some years that there is now a positive hunger for home legislation. Weighty, therefore, though Lord HARTING- TON'S statements were with regard to Egypt and to IrelanJ, we propose not to deal with those subjects, but to direct attention to his observations on matters directly affecting the English people. It has been said that a wise man's romance lies in the future. If this be the case it cannot but be a pleasant as well as a profitable occupation to look ahead, and endeavour to shape our course so as the most readily and speedily to reach the position we, as a nation, desire to occupy. Looking for- ward then in this manner it is not difficult to discern, for it stands. right in front of us, the arrival of the period when the county franchise will be assimilated to that already granted to the inhabitants of Parliamentary Loroughs. Though the proposal to effect this assimilation was at first received with dubious silence by many Conservative mem- bers of Parliament, as well as by one or two Liberals who occupy seats in the House of Commons, it is now evident that they feel the hopelessness of any attempt to prevent it being carried out, and are therefore pre- paring to bow with the best possible grace to the inevitable. If any proof of this were wanted it is to be found in a speech delivered on Monday evening by the Hon. ALGERNON EGERTON, M.P., the newly-elected member for Wigan, and secretary to the Admiralty during the last Conservative Administration. That gentleman declared there could be no doubt as to the direction in which public opinion is tending with reference to the pro- posed reform. In speculating as to the effect which the change may have upon party prospects, Mr. EGERTON expressed a belief that it will not operate to the disadvantage of the Conservative cause in this part of the country; at the same time, however, he con- fessed that he looked with some fear as to its effect in the agricultural districts. The reason which he assigns for this is that the peasantry in the south have not much acquaintance with political subjects. The rejoinder is very obvious. If the peasantry of the south had been inclined to Conser- vatism of course they would, in his eyes, have been acquainted with political subjects but as there is reason to believe they have Liberal sympathies. why, then, they must be politically ignorant! Such will, in brief, be the comment of many Liberals upon Mr. EGERTON'S language. It would be interesting to hear what Mr. JOSEPH ARCH and other leaders of the agricultural labourers have to say on the matter. They might, perhaps. be able to convince Mr.. EGERTON that there were some agricultural labourers who were not politically blind, but who, after very care- ful consideration of the claims and policy of each party, had come to the conclusion that the Liberal programme was the one most calculated to improve their own position and benefit their native land But as the time draws nearer for the accomplishment of this reform, Mr. EGERTON may have been led to. see that it is, from a party point of view, injudicious to make such remarks, and also to perceive that, as he has hopes of again representing South-east Lancashire,„it would be best to swallow the pill, however disagreeable it may be, without making any grimace over it in public Another important subject referred to by the Marquis of HARTINOTON is that of county government. It is really surprising, seeing the length of time that the system of repre- sentation has been the basis of municipal government, that so far as the administration of counties is concerned, people should have been willing to leave their interests in the hands of an irresponsible body of men. There are two reasons which explain the long dura- tion of the present system, the first of which is the excellent manner in which magistrates have, as a rule, attended to county affairs; the second being the little attention paid by ratepayers to the business of the county. When one considers the magnitude of the interests which are affected, it seems really monstrous that they should have been left so long in the care of one class in the commllnity Let us take, by way of illustration, the county of Lancashire, which has within it property of the rateable value of upwards of r6,0n0,000. What possible reason can be assigned why charges made annually upon property of this enormous value should not be subject to the decision of a body elected by the ratepayers? But there is no necessity to prove the desirability of a reform in our system of county administration, for the wisdom of a change is admitted; on almost every hand. Lord HARTINGTON, in his speech at Bacup, clearly expressed the view which generally obtains, when he said he could see no alternative—if there was not to be a government of departments—but the creation of strong elective bodies, composed of representatives of considerable areas, to whom could be entrusted many of the powers which are now, with much inconvenience, exercised by central authorities in Lon- dn. We may add to this state- ment our own opinion, that after the proposed county bodies had got fairly into working order, it would be found possible to lighten even the labours of Parliament by referring many purely local matters which now go before the House of Commons, to the consideration of the gentlemen who would constitute the governing authority of the county. It is impossible to pass over another important question which was brought by Lord HARTINGTON under the notice of his constituents. We refer to the licensing laws, a subject which is one of vital interest to many persons, especially to licensed vic- tuallers. Lord HARTINGTON does not attempt to forecast any measure for the reform of the laws regulating the sale of intoxicating drink, but intimates that he is in favour of legislation, which would have the effect of affording to the people, as represented by the ratepayers or representa- tives of the ratepayers, a greater control over the granting and renewal of licenses than that which they now possess. This view of the matLer appears to be fast becoming popular, and from what we can see there seems to be no reason why it should not, if accompanied by a proposal for cpmpensation for any vested

How IT IS WIDNES MARKET *DOESN'T PAY.—Thomas Barton, a greengrocer, was charged at Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Wednesday, with causing an obstruction in Mersey- road.—P.C.'s 111 and 1,254 stated that on Saturday night last, about eight o'clock, the defendant stopped his cart, from which he was selling greengrocery, near the footpath in Mersey-road. His scales and weights were on the foot- path, and people who desired to pass along had to step into the horse road in consequence of the crowd of people which gathered round.—Fined 12s 6d and costs. THE BEGGAR BITTEN AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Monday, James Kelly was brought up in custody charged with begging on Saturday, and also with assaulting P.C. Ross whilst in the execution of his duty. On Saturday the prisoner went to the constable's house and asked -for alms. The lady of the house refused to com- ply with his request, and called the constable. Becoming aware of the predicament in which he had placed himself, the prisoner maintained that he had only asked for a glass of water. He was, however, taken into custody, but he struggled hard with his captor, whom he kicked and struck in a violent manner.—lnspector Barnett pressed for an ex- emplary sentence, and the Bench committed the prisoner to gaol for 14 days. THEATRE ROYAL, RUNCORN.—The boards at this place of amusement have been occupied this week by the cele- brated " White Family," who, on the first three nights, per- formed " The Dumb Man of Manchester," concluding with the spectacular extravaganza " Lurline," in which Miss Kate Gamey and Miss Kate Gwynne took the chief parts in a manner which elicited frequent plaudits from the audience. Wednesday was set apart for the benefit of Mr. George White, who had established himself a favourite, and on that evening Mr. Ottley recited with much dramatic effect the "Dream of Eugene Aram." On Friday Miss Kate Gurney had her benefit. She took the part of Lady Isabel in "East Lynne," Mr. Ottlev fulfilling the character of Archibald Carlyle. The piece was well put on the boards, and equally well sustained. SHOPKEEPERS AND THEIR WEIGHTS: HEAVY SENTENCES ON WIDNES TRADESMEN.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. A. Fletcher and Mr. G. Pilkiagton, a greengrocer, named James Taylor, was charged with being in possession of eight weights which were light.—Superin- tendent Barker said he visited the defendant's shop on the Bth January, and examined the weights. He found a 7-lb. weight one drachm light, a 4-lb. weight a drachm and a half light, and six othets of varying weight, all light.— Fined 40s and costs.—Mary Murphy appeared to answer a similar charge.—The Superintendent proved that she had a 4-lb. weight two drachms light, and the Bench fined her 10s and costs.—Friend Thomas Simcock, who bad been pre- viously convicted under the Weights and Measures Act five times, was fined ,Z 3 and costs for being guilty of a similar offence.—The Superintendent said he found a 4-lb. weight a draeun light, a 2-Ib, weight and a 1-Ib, weight half a drachm light; in fact, all the weights in the shop were slightly light. The defendant was a shopkeeper in Widnes-road.--- Thomas Hawkins, greengromr, was charged with having seven light weights in his shop. Superintendent Barker said he visited the defendant's shop on the Bth inst., and examined the weights. He found a 2-lb. weight a drachm below the standard, and six 1-lb. weights a drachm and a half light. All the small weights in the shop were light.— Fined 40s and costs.

ALLEGED ROBBERY FROII A RUNCORN BEERHOUSE.— At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Captain Hazlehurst, a young man named George Thomas Wheeler, was charged in custody with hav- ing, on the 7th October last, stolen a coat of the value of £l, the praptrty of ;Ernest Knoof, a sailor. Mr. Quelch, solicitor, of Liverpool. appeared for the defendant. It ap- peared that on Saturday, the 7th October last, the prisoner went to the 'Ellesmere Vaults, Regent-street, Runcorn,- to stay the week end, and on the same day the prosecutor ar- rived in the town and also stayed l at the Same place. The prisoner and the prosecutor slept in one room; but in the morning the coat and the prisoner.were missing. Inspector Holliugworth apprehended the prisoner at Kirkdale gaol that morning, and charged him with the offence. He replied "Yes."—Superintendent Williamson said the prosecutor was at present in Ireland, but he had forwarded a telegram that he should arrive in Runcorn in a week, and he applied for a remand until next Monday. Mr. Quelch contended that the evidence was not sufficient to justify a remand. At the utmost it was a case of mere susplcion, as there were other persons in the bedroom.—The Bench considered the evidence sufficient, and Mr. Quelch applied for the prisoner to be ad- mitted to but. The prisoner was a young man possessed or considerable property, and could find substantial securities for his appearance. Superintendent Williamson objected, and the Bench remanded the prisoner without admitting him to bail. IMPROVEMENT RATE CASs: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD DEFEATED.—OR Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, James Chapman, landlord of the Grosvenor Hotel, Widnes' was summoned by the Widnes Local Board for £ll Bs. 10d being amount due from him on the General District Rate.— Mr. Husband appeared to support the summons, and Mr. W. 11. Linaker' of Runcorn, defended.—lt appeared that the defendant took possession of the Grosvenor Hotel on the sth September, it having previously been occupied by Mr. Sankey. The rateable value of the house was £127 103., and the amount due on the rate laid in July until the 31st March was £l4 7s. 61. The Local Board calculated Mr. II Chapman's proportion at the amount claimed, but the de- fendant, since the summons was issued, had paid £8 10s. sd. in settlement, and 2s. 6d. for the costs of the case.—Mr. Wilson, manager of the rate department, was called, and in cross-examination by Mr. Linaker, said he had not served the defendaq with a notice that his name had been sub- stituted for that of Mr. Sankey's in the rate book. Mr. Linaker thereupon said he took objection to the proceedings, basing his objection on the 221st section of the Public Health Act, which stated that notice of any amendment to the rate should be given seven days before payment of the rate was demanded.—Mr. Husband contended that the alteration of a name was not an amendment. The defendant, by paying a sum into court, had virtually acknowledged the claim.—Mr. Linaker read the clause in the Act upon which he relied, and it clearly stated that the erasure of a name and the substitution of another was an amendrnent.—Mr. A. Fletcher (chairman) said the Bench were of opinion that Mr. Linaker's objection was fatal, and dismissed the case. A CLAIM FOR STREET MAKING: THE UNCHARITABLE COMMISSIONERS.—Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Cap- tain Hazlehurst, at the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, John loynson was summoned by the Runcorn Commis- sioners for £22 19s 6d, being the apportionment of a claim for street making.—Mr. Linaker appeared on behalf of the Commissioners.—ln answer to the usual question, Mr. Joynsnn said he went to the expense of laying a parapet 27 years ago. He did not object to pay for the making of the street, but he thought it showed a want of charity on the part of the Commissioners to charge him for making the parapet.—Mr. Linaker remarked that the defendant had not given notice of his objection within the time required, and it oould not now be taken.—Mr. Barker, surveyor to the Com- missioners and Mr. Brookes, the secretary, proved that the ordinary lormalities had been gone through, it being stated that the total cost of making the street was £650 17s 81— The defendant said he did not particularly object to the bill; but he thought there was a want of charity on the part if the Commissioners to charge the owners in the street for the whole of the parapet when 27 years ago they had I borne the first expense, and the town had had the use of it for that length of time. He thought the bill ought to be taxed with regard to the parapet.—Mr. Reynolds: Why did not you enter an objection to the charge in the usual way? —Defendant said he did; but Mr. Linaker remarked that the Act provided that notice should be given in three months, while the defendant allowed four months to elapse. —Mr. Reynolds said the case was clear enough. The defendant had three months in which to make the objection, and it was his own fault he was a month behind. It was a matter in which the Bench had really no choice.—An order for the amount claimed was made, and costs amounting to 15s were allowed

TILE INFLUENCE OF SURROUNDINGS : A YOUNG RUN - CORN THIEF.—A young girl, named Margaret Bowden, was brought up on remand at Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, charged with having stolen 6s 4d, the monies of Samuel Spann, landlord of the Mersey Hotel.—Ann Grady, servant to the prosecutor, said on Friday, the 12th inst., in conse- quence of a noise she heard in the bar she went there, and found the prisoner leavine the money drawer, inside the bar. Witness asked her what she was doing there, and she replied that she came to see what time it was. She saw the girl had something in her hand, and asked her for the money she had taken. She gave her Is. 101, and com- menced to cry, saying" Let me go." -Witness, however, took the girl into the kitchen, where the prisoner gave her a further sum of 4s. 6d.—!n cross-examination by the priso- ner's mother, witness said Mrs. Bowden had claimed is. 7d. of the money, and had received that amount from Mr. ' Spann, who could not identify the rnenev.—P.S. McMichael deposed to apprehending the prisoner, who, in answer to the charge, said "1 did; but Mrs. Spann has got it." He then charged her with stealing 7s. from the same place, on the 7th instant. Prisoner said "I did, and bought sweets with ' it."—Mr. Reynolds, addressing. the prosecutor, said a child like the prisoner could not get into the bar and steal if the servant was doing her duty.—Mr. Spann said the servant was engaged at another part of the house at the time.—Mr. Reynolds remarked that it was not right to leave money in such a manner that a child could dip its hand in without difficulty.—Mr. Spann said he did not wish to press the case against the girl. He thought there yeare other persons implicated besides her.—Mr. Superintendent Williamson said he bad failed to find a place in an industrial school for the girl because the authorities wanted a shilling aweek obtain from s one.ome llt private w s e' pityan d a sh et bcould ti girl's not surroundings m i Be to were not so good.—Mr. Reynolds said, considering the a a s great case, the Bench ordered her to be confined in the cells for youth of the prisoner and that Mr. Spann did not press the two days.
