At the Liverpool County Sessions, last week, Mary Gray- son, indicted for wounding Margaret M'Casin, at Widnes, was acquitted. John M'Cue (26), labourer, and Mary Clarke (25), were charged with having, at Widnes' on the 6th November last, unlawfully wounded John Clarke. Clarke was found guilty, and sentenced to a month's impri- sonment; the other prisoner was discharged. WIDNES SCIDDOL BOARD AT Won.—Mr. J. H. Danby, clerk to Widnes School Board, appeared at Widnes Felice Court, on Wednesday, to prosecute a number of persons for contravention of the Education Act. On the evidence of the attendance officers the following were each fined 6:1 and costs, 4s 6.1 :—Thomas Oates, William Platt, Owen Welsh, Robert Yates, Thomas Roach, John Morris, and Robert Murray.

EVADING THE EXCISE AT WIDNES.—Wm. WalMSley, a shopkeeper, on a small scale, was charged at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, with selling tobacco without a license on the 11th December. Mr. Heal, supervisor, Excise Office, Runcorn, prosecuted, and called evidence which proved the defendant's guilt. Defendant, however, pleaded his ignorance of the law on the matter. He was ordered to get out a license which would cost 10s., and pay the costs of the proceedings. FURIOUS DRIVING AT WIDNIIS.—Thomas Hawkins, greengrocer, was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of furiously driving a horse and cart. It was alleged that on Saturday, the 13th inst., the detendant was in a cart to which was attached a pony. He Was thrashing the animal with the reins, causing it to run at a furious rate up Widnes-road. Defendant called a witness to prove that the horse could not be restrained on some occasions, while on others it would not stir for a quarter of an hour. The Bench, however, imposed a fine of lOs and costs. A FRACAS AT MESSRS. MUSPRATT'S WORKS. Before Mr. A. Fletcher and Mr. G. Pilkington, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Michael Jenkins, who did not appear, was charged with assaulting Win. R. Clarke, who is a foreman rat Messrs. Muspratt's works. It appeared that on.the 16th inst., the defendant, who was employed at the works, went to the complainant's room in a state of intoxi- cation. He was very violent and abusive, and the corn- I plainant twice ejected him. A third time the defendant entered the room and struck complainant on the eye and the forehead. Defendant was tined 20s. and costs. I A Puerec-norsiz Row AT WIDNES. Before Mr. Hol- brook Gaskell, jun., and Mr. John Brock, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, John McGreel, a rough-looking young fellow, was charged with being drunk on the licensed pre- mises of John Webb, and with assaulting Francis Asher, the barman. The prisoner entered the King's Arms, Anne- street, in a drunken condition, and the barman refusing to serve him with the liquor he demanded was struck a violent blow. The prisoner was then ejected, but returned, and after a long struggle, was again ejected. Defendant was fined 103. and costs, or, in default, 14 days' imprisonment on each charge. THEFT OF A TORTOISE AT WIDNES.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. S. B. Chadwick and Captain Hazlehurst, a seaman named Richd. William, whose guernsey bore the word "Cunard," was brought up in cus- tody charged with stealing a tortoise' the property of Jos. Pegg, lodging-house and beerhouse keeper.—ln answer to the usual question as to where he would be tried, the pri- soner replied, "I don't care which; you can hang me if you like." He afterwards pleaded guilty. The prisoner went into the Sloop Inn on Saturday morning about 11 o'clock, and some time after his departure the tortoise was missed. The police afterwards diecoverd that the prisoner had sold it for Bd.' and that the purchaser had given it to the cap- tain of aflat.—The prisoner, who said he was engaged in the "last war," was fined 10s. and costs 75., or, in default, 14 days' hard labour.—He went to gaol. A HARD SMUGGLE AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday at Widnes Petty Sessions, before Mr. A. Fletcher and Mr. G. Pilkington, Nicholas Dignum, whose head had evidently undergone surgical treatment, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and further with assaulting P.C. Barker whilst in the execution of his duty. P.C. Barker said about a quarter past eleven on Tuesday night, he heard the prisoner creating a great disturbance in Wellington- street. He requested him to cease his boisterous conduct, and leave the neighbourhood, but the prisoner seized the constable by the throat and threw him to the ground. A fierce struggle ensued, the captor and captive rolling about on the ground. At last the constable deemed it necessary to draw his staff in his defence, and this weapon he used effectively. But the prisoner's grasp on his throat did not relax, and he called out for assistance. P.C. 1193, who had taken into custody the prisoner's companion, who was taking part in the disturbance, went to his aid. The prisoner was then on the top of Barker, but he was dragged off, and conducted to the police station. The prisoner was very drunk. The prisoner wee fined ss. and costs for being drunk, and 20s. and costs for the assault on the police.

A SIIAMUtiL SCENE: A FAMILY SQUABBLE AT WIDNES. —Charles Percy, the son of a man who is now in custody on a charge of unlawfully wounding his wife, who is at the point of death, was summoned to Widnes Police Court on Wednesday to answer a charge of assaulting his sister, Sarah Jane Percy.—Mr. Husband appeared for the defence.—The complainant stated that about half-past one her sister,whose name is Mrs. Whalley, went to visit her mother, and whilst in the house some words passed between her and the com- plainant. Mrs. Whalley gave her a smack on the face, and the complainant was about to retaliate when the defendant seized her and used her shamefully, pulling a great handful of hair from her head.—James Percy, brother, said the de- fendant thumped his sister about the place for half-an- hour, causing people to collect outside. It was not the first time he had acted in that manner, and he thought it was a shame as his mother was lying in bad in a dying state.—W. Percy corroborated, adding that it was a most disgraceful scene, and he tried his best to stop it.—Mr. Hush end clwacterised the affair as a family squabble, and suggested that the best way was to settle the case. He called a well- dressed woman, who stated that the complainant was the cause of the whole disturbance, and struck the defendant two or three times across the face.—The defendant was fined ss. and costs.

DISTRAINING FOR RENT IT WIDNES: A STRANGE INCIDENT.—On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, C. Bromley (of Runcorn), and J. Wilson, biliffe, were charged with nnlawfully and maliciously wounding Mary Carroll, an Irishwoman. The charge was reduced to one Of common assault. The statement of the plaintiff, which was cor- roborated by two witnesses was to the effect that on the lfith inst. the defendant knocked at the door of the house whore she lived. She asked "Who's there," and received the reply from -Wilson that it was the "agent." She said the agent was there not many minutes ago, and he knew her husband was "not in work now," but she would do what she could for him on Monday. Without more ado the de- fendants burst open the door, and one of them to prevent it from being again closed properly inserted his stick be- tween the door and the jamb. The complainant, with the aid of another woman who was in the house, resisted the inroad of the bailiffs for some time, but the latter at length "threw the door upon both of them, and entering the lobby Bromley struck her in the eye with a stick, and Wilson kicked her on the knee. Her eye was" bunged up " fora week. Bromley, in defence, declared that the complainant's state- ment was all false. When he and Wilson went to the house, and obtained an entrance, the complainant ran into the kitchen and told a woman there to fetch her husband " Patv," and she would swear on her oath that Bromley had struck her with a stone. He had had many warrants for the com- plainant, who had never paid her rent for years. When he found there was nothing in the house on which he could distrain fcr rent, be told her to get out of the house as quickly as she could. That was all that took place. He never touched the woman. He had been in the business 14 years in the same locality, and there had never been a charge brought against him.—Wilson was proceeding to make a long statement, when the Chairman said the Bench were satisfied there was no charge against the defendants, who were therefore discharged. RAILWAY SERVANTS' SUPPER AT WIDNES.— The men employed in the locomotive department of the London and North-Western Railway at Widnes, had their second annual supper on Saturday evening, at Unsworth's dining-rooms, Widnes. There were about 50 persons present. Mr. Joseph Smith, London and North-Western stationmaster, was pre- sent as an invited guest. Mr. Turnbull, the locomotive foreman, presided, and Mr. Carter, the traffic inspector, occu- pied the vice-chair. The Chairman remarked that such social celebrations showed that good feeling and good fellowship existed between the workmen, and it was his earaest desire that this state of things should continue, and that the corn- ing year would be as prosperous to them as the last. He proposed "The health of the Queen and the rest of the Royal Family," which was drunk with musical honours. The Vice-chairman gave "The London and North- Western Railway Company," coupling with the toast the name of Mr. Smith, stationmaster, Widnes. Mr. Smith responded in a neat speech. Mr. Burton then proposed "Tile Donors," followed by the Chairman proposing The Town and Trade of Widnes." Mr. T. Smith, wagon inspector, alluded, in responding, to the remarkable increase in the importance of the town, re- marking that when he first knew Widnes there were only two shunting engines working regularly, whereas there were now eleven shunting and ten ether engines now in constant use, besides 23 private engines belonging to the works. Mr. J. Wilson proposed "The health of Mr. New- ton, locomotive foreman at Datton. Widnes and Garston," alluding in terms of high praise to Mr. Newton's many good qualities, to which Mr. J. Smith also testified. The toast of "'rho Host and Hostess," which concluded the list, was proposed by Mr. Carver. During the evening Mr. Gill performed several selections on the violin, and Mr. Hudson, Mr. Parr, Mr. Carver, Mr. Lewis, Mr. Platt, and Mr. C. Hudson, each gave a song. Mr. J. Smith recited two amusing pieces.

LOCAL Rarrxnurrs, tic.—(From Friday night's Gazetle.)— Liquidations by Arrangement : R. Hinde, Faulkner-street, Manchester, merchant and shipper; F. Kelly, Stockport- road, LevensLulme, commercial clerk, formerly licensed victualler at Nantwich ; M. Healey, Burlington-street, Liverpool, provision dealer; F. 0. Boyle, Burnly. tailor; P. Oak., Burnley, grocer; and J. S. Anderson, Bolton, bobbin manufacturer._( From Tuesday night's Gazette.)—Liqtacle- bioßs hy Arrawyement : Samuel Barrow, Manchester, bleacher ; James Whittaker, Manchester, wine retailer; Mason Loeb. Manchester, commission agent ; James Sutcliffe, Liverpool, licensed victualler; Peter Tyrer, f*:•esco,, Lancs.shire, brass founder ; Richard Orrnerod, Ormskirli, Lancashire, brewer; Richard Eccleston, Black- burn, grocer; William Robinson, Blackburn, grocer; John Gilgar, Blackburn, shoemaker; George Hilton Smith, Man- chesttr, machinist; William Foster, Manchester, draper and smallware dealer; Matilda Cohen, Manchester, millimer and dressmaker ; and Isaac Mawson and Thomas Mawson, Lancashire, stonemasons and buildtrs.
Tins Nrw HIGH SHERIFF.—We (Prestcs Guardia 4) are able to announce that the new High Sherriff of the County will be Thomas Ashton, Esq., of Ford Bank, Dids- bury, near Manchester.

The names of Mr. Charles Broadbent, of Warring- ton, and Mr. Charles Pilkington, of Haydock, were in the list of grand jury at the Manchester Winter Assizes, opened on Monday. A great chess match between Lancashire and York- shire was played at Leeds on Satuiday. The players num- bered 159. Lancashire won 84 games and Yorkshire SI, and 18 were drawn. LANCASHIRE PLATERAY BlLL.—This bill was fixed t• come before Mr. Frere, one of the examiners of the standing orders proofs at the House of Commons, on Wednesday, but the promoters did not appear, and the measure is therefore dropped. We are pleased to announce the success of Master W. G. Turton, of the Manor House School, Frodsham, grandson of W. G. Gibson, Esq ,of Overton, at the Midsummer exam- ination of the College of Preceptors. ACCIDENT AT WESTON.—At Weston Chemical Works, on Tuesday, a man was struck with the handle of a windlass when the cage was descending, and he received injuries which rendered him insensible, and he is, we understand, still unconscious.
WIDNES PARISH CHURCH ENTERTAINMENT.—The seventh of the series was given on Tuesday evening, to a large audience, and a miscellaneous programme was gone through in the usual affective style.

"TILE LAWS OF HEALTH."—Mr. J. S. Jencock read a paper on this subject before the members of the Halton Parish Church Mutual Improvement Society on Tuesday evening. An interesting discussion followed. Mr. J. W. Haddock presided. NEWTOWN MISSIONS, RUNCORN. Mr. E. Marwood, assisted by Mr. W. E. Lea, gave a magic lantern exhibition in aid of the band fund of the above missions, on Tuesday evening. There was a large audience. The band performed several pieces of music daring the evening, and the children sang suitable pieces. RUNCORN BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.— Mr. J. D. Jones, at the weekly meeting ef this class, on Wednesday evening, read an able Paper on the rules of the Wesleyan Methodist Society, and the views he enunciated gave rise to a lively discussion. Mr. T. Simister presided. FIRE AT HALEWOOD.—At Bank Farm, Halewood, on Monday night, a stack 20 tons of hay was totally destroyed by fire, the origin of which is unknown. The damage is estimated at .£l5O, the farmer, Mr. Richard Sutton, having fortunately taken the precaution of insuring the stack in the Royal Fire and Life Insurance Company. LONDON VARIETY TROUPE AT WIDNES.—This troupe of artistes gave a performance in Widnes Volunteer Drill Hall, on Thursday, before a large audience. The entertainment provided was of a most attractive and entertaining descrip- tion, songs, serio and comic, dancing, and "fancy tumbling" forming a lengthy programme. The performance was re- peated last night, and a third will be given to-night (Satur- day.) FOOT AND MOUTH DDiELSE. On Tuesday, the Clerk of the Peace for Lancashire reported that foot and mouth disease exists at present on about 20 farms in the county, and pleure-pneumonia on three. The Lonclon Gazette contains an order in Council declaring areas at Euxon, Ampull, and Little Huhn, all in Lancaster, to be infected with foot-and-mouth diseass, from the 25th instant.

The London and North -Western Railway Company are making considerable alterations on the old Liverpool and Manchester line, between the Sankey viaduct and St. Helens Junction. Additional land has been acquired for sidings, several new under and over bridges are being con- structed, and a new passenger stition is in course of erection at Collins Green. RESISTING THE POLICE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Catherine Sinnett was charged with resisting P.C. Savory in the execution of his duty.— About midnight on Saturday the constable took the defen- dant's husband into custody. The defendant caught hold of his left arm, and struck him in an attempt to rescup her husband.—The charge was withdrawn on the defendant promising to pay the costs, 7s ad.

DEPARTURE OF A SALVATION ARMY CAPTAIN FROM WlDNES.—Captain Elmes, leader of the Widnes branch of the Salvation Army, has been transferred to Hereford, and he departed for that town - from the London and North- Western Station on Thursday morning. During the kw months he has laboured in Widnes he appears to have won the regard of all his followers, who assembled in crowds to watch his departure. Females greatly prepon- derated, and there was mnch struggling to get a shake of the gallant captain's band.

At ACTOR " WANTED " AT RUNCORN. —Herbert Lloyd, the actor who was before the magistrates ten days ago, on a charge of stealing Blue Beard's wig and whiskers, was summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a charge of assaulting Wm. Johnson, who resides at Heath-road.—Johnson said he was caretaker at the Theatre Royal. On Tuesday, in answer to a knock, he opened the door, when the defendant rushed in and knocked him to the ground.—A warranLwas issued for the apprehenbion of the defendant, who did not appear.—We understand that Lloyd has left the town.

ACCIDENT AT WinxEs.—On Thursday evening, about five o'clock, Thomas Hewitt, joiner, and residing in West-street, West Bank, was seriously injured at Messrs. Kershaw and Co's. timber yard. Hewitt was engaged in the erection of a wooden shed in (he yard, and he fell from a truss beam, on which he was creeding, to the ground below a distance of 25 feet. He was conveyed home, and a doctor was called in, but his state was such that hedid not think it advisable to made an examination. The unfortunate man complained much of pain in his back, an.l it is probable that he has sustained some internal injuries.

LIVERPOOL FAIRIES Is TROUBLE AT ST. HELENS.—TWO young women, respectably-attired, but of doubtful appear- ance, named Alice Moore and Edith Wynne, were charged at the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, with having been drunk and disorderly.—P.C. Chrystal said that about 10 minutes to 1200 Saturday ni.4lit he found the two prisoaers, who were drunk, co lduct ing themselves in a disorderly man- ner, in Corporation-street. He gave them half an hour in which to get away, but as they refused to do so he brought them to the Police Station. One of the defendants said they had only been crying, as they were strangers in St. Helens and had no place to go to.—Superintendent Johnston said they both came from Liverpool, and were not known to him. They were each tined 55, or, in default, seven days' imprison- ment.--A man named Daniel Hanley was also tined 5s and costs, on a charge of having been drunk and disorderly in company of the above-named females.

ODDFRLLOWS' BALL AT RUNCORN.—On Thursday even- ing, the seventh annual tea party and ball in connection with the Loyal Wrights Pride Past Grand Lodge of the , Independent Order of Oddfellors' was held in Runcorn ' Public Hail, under the patronage of the leading gentlemen in the neighbourhood. The room had been attractively decorated for the occasion, the arrangements having been carried out by a c)mmittee, consisting of P.P.G.M. Robt. Wright, Robert Roberts, George Crute, John Barrow, Rcbd. Rowles, George Riley ; P.D.G.M. Robert Gorst and H. B. Toone; P.G George Rogers, T. Lvdiate, S. Armstrong, A. Riley, and W. Ford; PS. G. Burrows. P.C.S. C. Cooke discharged the duties of secretary with his usual urbinity l and courtesy. About 250 persons were present at tea, which was provided by Mrs. Waterworth, of the Anchor Inn, who also provided the refreshments for the ball which followed. Before dancing commenced 13:-other C. Reynolds (chairman) glade a few remarks upon the financial position of the Order. The capital in Runcorn district amounted to £5,475, and each member, were the society to be dissolved, would be entitle to £9 4s U. Votes of thanks were ac- corded to the patrons, on the motion of Brother C. Cooke, seconded by Brother H. B. Toone; and the Rev. Canon Bar- clay, M.A., in replying on their behalf, observed that the success of that gathering showed that the working classes were acquiring habits of providence and thrift. He alluded to the diminution of drunkenness in the town, and expressed the opinion that though the struggle between temperance and drunkenness might be a long one, the latter Would eventually be conquered, and the misery, want, and crime, which followed in the footsteps of intemperance, would vanish. He referred to the valuable work which the Free Library was doing .in dispelling the clouds of ignorance, and touch- ing upon improvidence, said the large increase in the funds of the local savings' bank showed that the people of Runcorn were doing something to redeem themselves from that evil. Mr. Wright also replied. A vate of thanks was accorded to the chairman on the motion of Mr. Pritchard, and the chairman having replied, the room was cleared for dancing, and the devotees of Terpsichore tripped it until an early hour next morning to the strains of Bro. T. Wood's quadrille band.

LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE BANK, LIMITED.—The tenth annual general meeting of the shareholders of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Bank was held on Wednesday, in the Memorial Hall, Manchester. The Chairman of the Board (Mr. William Armitage) was in the chair, and, in moving the adoption of the report (which has already appeared in our columns), he said the progress of the bank during the past year had been of the same moderate but constant kind as had marked its history from its commence- ment in 1872. He briefly traced the course of the bank through the ten years since that period, and stated that the Board, after careful and anxious consideration, bad now decided to propose an increase of dividend after making an increase of the reserve fund to £lOO,OOO. The favourable result on the year's working had been helped by the recent rise in the value of loanable capital, but they were convinced that nothing would for any long period maintain the loan rate but an increase in the activity of trade. For the moment the low price of raw materials and some other circumstances gave ground for hope of such activity, but unfortunately several past years had begun with similar hopes, which were not realised. After pointing out the favourable features of the figures of the report, he said they intended still to go on building up Ithe reserve fund, to Which the Board attached great import- ance. No new branches had been opened during the year, but the bank had now 24 offices, with every appli Ince for a greatly extended business. Having urged that the share- holders had the power to make and maintain their own divi- dends, the chairman moved the adoption of the report,which was seconded by Mr. Goldschmidt, and passed unanimously. —lt was moved by Mr. Notton, seconded try M. Jesse Howarth, and resolved unanimously, that the directors re- tiring by rotation, viz., Sir Joseph C. Lee and Mr. W. E Melland be re-elected. The auditor, Mr. David Smith, chartered accountant, was also re-appointed; and after a smanimous vote of thanks to the manager and other officers, moved by Mr. George Ashworth, and seconded by Sir Jeseph C. Lee, the meeting terminated.
STORM AT WIDNES AND RUNCORN.
GREAT DAMAGE.

IA gale of wind and rain of tremendous violence swept over this neighbourhood on Thursday night. Houses seemed, to the occupants, to be shaken to their very foundations, so much did they oscillate with the force of the wind as it rushed wildly on. Slates, chimney pots, windows, and shutters were continually falling into the streets daring the whole of the night, and the pavement in the morning presented a curious sight. Widnes suffered greatly from the storm. Early in the morning the chim- ney of Messrs. Wells and Galloway's works, which have been closed for a considerable time, fell with a crash to the ground. It was 60 feet high. Near the works runs a railway siding, and on this at the time were standing two coal trucks. Upon these the chimney alighted in great force, smashing them to atoms, and driving the metals and the sleepers about a foot into the ground. The line was blocked, but Mr. Timmins, of Runcorn, who re- presents the owners of the works, was quickly on the spot with a gang of men, who cleared the debris away. At Simms Cross, a heuse, which was being built by Mr. John Phillips, and which was completed with the exception of the roof, was almost entirely wrecked. All the top storey, and part of the basement, were demolished, the bricks and stones being scattered in all directions. Fortunately no damage was done to other propertyin the neighbourhood. The firm of Messrs. Mort, Liddell, and Co. were somewhat heay sufferers. Three of their sheds now occupy a somewhat peculiar position. These sheds are made of wood, with iron supports, and the force of the wind partly overtwined them. But for an old building at one end, they would probably have been totally demolished. The end shed is leaning upon that building, and thus prevents the other two from falling over completely and becoming mere ruins. The roofs are broken, and will have to be removed and re- paced; but it is thought that the other portions can be righted as a whole. We under-stand that none of the plant inside was damaged. At West Bank H)tel a chimney pot fell through the roof into the bedroom where the manager and his wife were sleeping, but they sustained 'no injury; and at the Market Hotel a large plate glass window was blown from its frame into the bar, and smashed to pieces. Its value was about 20 guineas. The roof of the Vicarage at Ditton was partially destroyed, much to the inconvenience of the inmates; and the resi- dence of Mr. Neil, at Farnwortla, sustained considerable damage. At Runcorn the workshop of Mr. Far. rail, builder, lies in a complete ruin. The build- ing occupied the arch adjoining the one throngh which foot pasaengers ascend to the bridge ; and it appears tl have received the full force of the wind. It was a large two-storied brick erection, and the top storey has been cleanly blown over and crashed down through the floors. The lower part bulges forward, and gives indica'ions of a speedy collapss. Had the accident occurred a few minutes later than it did--a anarter to six on Thursday morning—it is possible that several deaths would have had to be recorded, as the men commence work at six o'clock. We have been unable to obtain an estimate of the damage, but the erection is eet'r ly wrecked and the joiners' tools and the plant will very likely be in a similar state ; and several hundred pounds may be stated as a moderate figure. The chimney stack of the Congregational Manse in Greenway-road, occupied by the Rev. J. D. 'Thomas, was blown down. Part of the roof of Norton Arms, Halton, was blown off; and the Round Horse, Weston, which never escapes damage in a storm, had a large hole made in the roof through the chimney stack fa'ling through into the bedroom below. About five o'clock 30 trusses of hay were thrown by the wind from one of the waggons of a passing goods train, just as it emerged from the latticed portion of Runcorn Bridge. The tarpaulin which covered the waggon was carried by the wind to the end of Church-street, a distance of several hundred yards, befere it alighfed. No accidents to human life are reported.

Fidler, Hall, Newsome, Pobell, Jackson, Buckley, Gerrard, Leatherbarrow, Syder, Griffiths, Birchall, Lowe, Eatock, Sadler, P. Longton, Huhne, Penketb, and S. H. Hartley (clerk).

The better plan would be to move for a return from the relieving officers, showing the number of cases relieved, how long they had been relieved, and for what period they were to receive relief. Mr. JACKSON said there was one case is Parr which had beer! on the books for many years.— The Rev. T. T. CHAMBERS assured Mr. Fidler that he intended nothing to the _detriment of the chairman of any cernmittee.—No resolution was proposed, and the subject dropped.

ECCLESTOW LANE ENDS. Mr. HALL. remarked that soma time ago there was a pay station at Eccleston Lane Ends, and he moved that it be restored.— :be matter was referrfA to a committee. There was no other business of importance.

div.head: VAGRANT WARDS AT ST. HELENS,
div.p: VAGRANT WARDS AT ST. HELENS,

At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee, on the 18th inst., the Clerk read a letter dated 4th January, from the St. Helens Corporation, asking that a casual ward or other suitable accommodation for vagrants, be provided at St. Helens • also a letter from the clerk to the borough justices, and copy of resolution in favour of the action of the Town Council, adopted at a meeting of the borough magistrates, on the 12th inst.—On the motion of Mr. Hall, seconded by Mr. Fidler, it was resolved that the committee are not aware of the necessity for the erection of vagrant wards in St. Helens, but would be pleased to consider any information which the Corporation of the Borough Bench might think fit to submit.—The minutes were confirmed, the matter remaining in the hands of the committee.

div.head: SI7RPRISE-CONTEMPLATED RESIGNATION OF !lIM MASTER.
div.p: A SI7RPRISE-CONTEMPLATED RESIGNATION OF !lIM MASTER.

The CLERK read the following letter from the master and matron of the workhouse:—" We beg most respectfully to ask you to give us a testimonial to assist us in our applica- tion for a more lucrative appointment. We have had the honour to serve as master and matron of your workhouce for more than two years, and have to acknowledge much kindness at your hands, and at the hands of Mr. Hartley, the Union clerk. Our only reason for making this application is a desire to improve our position. We have the honour to be, gentlemen, your • obedient servants, W. 11. and E. B. BICKNELL."—The Rev. T. CITAMBERS said the letter rather came upon them by sur- prise.—The CHAIRMAN: We cannGt refuse to give the testi- monial asked for.—Mr. NEWSOME moved that a testimonial l» drawn up by the clerk, and that the seal of the Beard be affixed to R.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS had very great plea- sure in seconding the motio.n, but while seconding Mr. Newsome's motion that an excellent testimonial, and one of the best kind be given to the master and matron, he asked whether the Guardians should not consider the propriety Of giving them an increase of ' salary because they all recognised their excellent services, and if their only reason was to better their position the question of another increase of salary should be entertained. —The CHAIAMAN did not think the letter was being used as a scheme for getting a better salary from that Union.— The Rev. T. CHAMBERS did rot suggest or suppose that it was.—The CHAIRMAN said they should give the testimonial. The master and matron were merely applying to another Union where there was a larger salary. Preseot Union had been regarded for some time past as a stepping-stone to something better, He supposed there was no objecion to the application being complied with. ("Certainly not.")— The motion that a testimonial of the highest kind be given to Mr. and Mrs. Bicknell was carried unanimously.

div.head: GUARDIANS AND THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT litoArtn.
div.p: THE GUARDIANS AND THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT litoArtn.

The Rev. T. Cluathens said with reference to the letter of the Local Government Board with regard to the extraor- dinary expenses of Guardians, and to the motion which in his absence Mr. Dobell had given notice of on his behalf at last meeting, he hid read the letter of the Local Govern- ment Board with a great deal of surprise and regret. He fully shared the indignatien which the chairman (Mr. March) had expressed on the subject, although he did not go so far as to agree with him in consigning that august body, the Local Government Board and their communications to his satanic majesty.—Several Guardians interposed with a denial that the chair- man bad done so.—The Rev. T. CHinBERS was glad to hear it was not so. He was not present at the time, and was only repeating what he had read. A Guardian remarked that it was a mistake of the reporters. The Rev. T. CliAmBERs, resuming, said with regard to the letter of the Local Government Board, be had never read a more shilly-shally. evasive production since he had been a Guardian, and it was utterly unworthy of the:office from which it emanated. After reading it lie consulted Colonel Biackburne, who advised him to write to Sir Richard Cross. He wrote at once and the right honourable gentleman replied that if Mr. Hartley would forward him all the correspondence lie would write at once to the new Presi- dent of the Local Government Board. He had seen Sir R. Cross since, and the right honourable gentleman had told him that he had written to Sir Charles Dilke expressing very strongly his views on the subject, but that the new presi- dent being at present on the continent, it might be a fort- night or three weeks before an answer could be obtained. Tne Guardians could therefore do nothing but remain in g.atu quo, and hope that the reply would put a different complexion on the situation. (Applause.) He agreed with an observation which had been made that the work of the Local Government Board Office seemed to be done by subordinates, for, judging from Mr. Dodson's demeanour when the deputation waited mama him, be (Mr. Chambers) was certain that if Mr. Dodson had bad the courage of his convictions. he would have consented to the allowances they had asked for. Let them hope that Sir Charles Dilke, the new broom, would make a clean sweep. THE MAINTENANCE OF DESERTED WOMEN.

The Rev. T. CHANUIECIits said, that having received a ' second list of outdoor poor in the different townships of the Union he had made an analysis of the several townships. It would be in the recollection of the Guardians that a rule had been passed that women deserted by their husbands, and women whose husbands were in prison should not receive encouragement from the Board by the receipt of outdoor re- lief. It was very desirable that there should be uniformity of action among the relief committees, but the rule had been broken by several committees. In the Windle district 09 9s. 3d. had been paid to women deserted by their hus- bands, or whose husbands were in prison, and of that sum only £2l had been repaid. In the Widnes district the relief committee had disallowed everything except in one case where £5 Ss had been paid to a woman whose husband had been in penal servitude for four years. Mr. Hartley, clerk to the Guardians, asked for an order for 49. A week; and Mr. Stewart, relieving officer, having deposed ta defendant's ability to pay that amount, the magistrates made the order asked for.

- VAGRANCY IN PRESCOT UNION. Several tramps were brought before the Pressot magistrates on Tuesday charged with begging, sleeping out, and acts of vagrancy, in the neighbourhood of Barnhill and Whisbcn. Superintendent Barker stated that since the workhouse authorities had adopted the plan of detaining tramps tro nights and making them work for the relief given to them it bad become common for vagrants to avoid the workbouve and loaf about the country. Each of the prisonert was sentenced to seven days' imprisonment.

UNLICENSED HAWKING AT ST. HELENS.—AI the St. Helen's Police Court on Saturday an elderly woman named Maria Naylor, was charged with having been hawking fire- stands and bill-files in Westfi:ld-street on Friday without the necessary license. P. C. Houghton proved the charge. Prisoner's husband produced a license for hawking in his own name, and said the reason why his wife had done so was that he ha l been toe ill himself to go about.—The Bench, in consideration of this fact, dismissed the prisoner, but informed her that she must obtain a license in her urn name if she wished to hawk.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

An order has been received at Chatham Dockyard inti- mating that it is the intention of the Gwernment to close its lead and iron mills after the end of the financial year, the material required being in future obtained from private firms. A large number of men will thus be thrown out of employment... . _ _ _ _ _

A memorial is in course of signature in Burnley, strongly, supporting the action of the Bishop of Manchester in re- fusing to institute the Rev. Harry Cowgill to the living of Miles Vatting. The memorial, which is. strongly in support of the Bishop, is signed amongst others, by the Rector of Burnley.

At a meeting of the Glasgow Gas Committee, yesterday, it was intimated that Major Magendie was of opinion that the gasometer of the south side had been wilfully fired, and that such would be the purport of his report to the Home Office. The Corporation to-day offered a reward of £lOO for the discovery of the perpetrators. At Middlesbro' Police Court yesterday, Mr. Frank Corn Jones, son of a leading ironmaster, was charged with an aggravated assault on five young ladies, daughters of the principal inhabitants of the town, whom he bad stopped on the way home from scbool. About 20 serious informations were laid and five cases entered upon. Prisoner pleaded guilty, and was fined £2O in two cases, and he was further ordered to find recognizances of £5O pounds, and two sureties of £5O in each case for his good behaviour. HORRIBLE WIFE MURDER NEAR BOLTON.

Another terrible tragedy has occurred at Maley Bridge, a Inilo and a half from Bolton. An operative cotton spinner named Hugh Calderbank had been quarrelling with his wife through her intemperate habits. Yesterday morning she was fouud lying in bed dead, with black marks on her neck, and the husbAnd acknowledged that he had strangled her. .
RUMOURED WAR BETWEEN FRANCE AND ENGLAND,

The Daily Noes correspondent at Cairo telegraphs that in consequence of ridiculous rumours of a coming war between France and England there has been much excitement in the native quarters of the city. The excitement increased on Thursday because of the march of some companies of Eng- lish troops to selected positions within the town for the purnose.of
hit PROSEAJTION OF MR. DAVITT.-REFUSAL. TO FIND SURETIES.

Yesterday's Freeman's Journal announces that Messrs Healy and Davitt have determined not to give sureties re- quired by the Queen's Bench, and will therefore have to go for six months to prison, while Mr. Quinn will similarly refuse, and will be incarcerated for three months. The JouPnal adds that the wisdom of this course is being freely discussed, as a good many persons feel that men like Davitt and Healy can be ill spared by the country just at present.
HEAVY MERCANTILE FAILURE. LIABILITIES, £53,500.

At the London Bankruptcy Court, yesterday, an applica- tion was made to Mr. Registrar Ilazlitt, sitting as chief judge, to grant an injunction retraining suing creditors in the matter of Eugenio Pella& The debtor has filed a peti- tion for liquidation, descrioing himself as of 66 and 67, Cornhill, general merchaot, trading as "E. Pell ts and C.," land of Argenoia ltaliana, late a partner in the fl in of Pella, Gerly, and Co., of 39, Lombard-street. The liabilities are stated at £53,500. Mr. Robert Wells applied On behalf of the debtor for an injunction aglinst several suing creditors. It appeared, however, that a receiver and manager bad been recently appointed under bankruptcy prcceedings presented against the debtor prior to the liquidation ; and his honour, after hearing Mr. Boxall on behalf of the petitioning creditors, made the order and directed it to be drawn up under the bankruptcy proceedings.

div.head: TWO WOMEN KILLED AND OTHERS INJURED AT OLDHAM.
div.p: TWO WOMEN KILLED AND OTHERS INJURED AT OLDHAM.

Yesterday morning a terrible accalont occurred at Mems. Bagley and Wright's, Belgrave Mills, Honeywell-lane, Oldham. The high wind blew a heavy stone out of ittl place on to the roof, which fell in, killing two women and, injuring several others. The women were not extricated for several hours. The names of the injured are Elizabeth Russell, 24, and Heathcote, 17. The mill is a new one, work having only recently commenced. Two sisters are badly hurt about the head. The four are Emma Booth, Clara and Louisa Rawlinson, and Rosa Mills. The damage done to the mill is to the extent of about £5OO. and it is not insured. A large coping stone, on which the full weight of the wind ctme, fell in on the roof of a room where 100 operatives were working, and struck down the two girls, killing them imm,diately, and crushing them terribly. A large iron beam was literally smashed, about four square- yards of the roof falling in.

div.head: GREAT LIBERAL MEETING,
div.p: GREAT LIBERAL MEETING,
MR. McMINNIES, M.P., AND HIS CONSTITUENTS.

When some time ago the member of Parliament for the Borough of Warrington addre:sed a meeting at the Liberal Club, there was an impression on the minds of many per- sons that Mr. MeMinnies did not intend to address his con- stituents during the prorogation of Parliament. Indeed, so prevalent was the impression that it was found necessary to publicly correct it, and it was then promised that the borough member would meet the electors early in the new year. This promise was redeemed on Thursday eveaing, when a meeting eves held in the Public Hall, and was in every way a great success. So strong was the desire on the townspeople to be present at the gathering that the tickets which were issued were speedily disposed of, and the pos- sessors of them were early in attendance on Thursday evening to secure seats. The doors were opened about half- past six o'clock, and theca was a steady influx of auditors who soon took possession of the vacant benches. In half-an-hour every available seat was occupied, but the audience still continued to increase, and long before the commencement of the proceedings the hall was pecked in every part. Meanwhile the assembly joined in singing the songs which bad been distributed about the ball. To the accompaniment of the organ, presided over by Mr. T. Mather, they took up the sympathetic air "Auld Lang Syne," and then heartily sang the chorus of the in- spiriting "Pilot of the State," which was rendered by Mr. George Wallington, jun., "When 'Mac' goes marching in again," a parody on a popular song, being given with a gusto that created much amusement. The appearance of the hall was much 'enhanced by the effective and tasteful decorations, which consisten simply of mottoes relieved with a few flags. Most prominent, in front of the organ were the words, "God bless the Gran.lold Man, Eneland's true patriot ;:' and at the opposite end in the centre gallery was inscribed, "A noble trio—Derby, Duke, and Chamberlain." Mottoes indicating the Liberal programme—. Free land and cheap food," "Electoral reform," "Justice to Ireland still," and "County franchise," were placed round the gallery, and in the centre was the wish of all present, "Long life to John Gordon Mc Minnies, our member." The finishing touch to the decora- tions was added just before the meeting began, and con- sisted of the three memorable figures, '520," representing the Liberal majority at the last election, which were placed in front of the chair amid cheers. Punctually at the ap- pointed time the chairman made his appearance on the platform, followed by the speakers and others, who were re- ceived with much enthusiasm, and the utmost cordiality prevailed throughout the meeting. The following is a complete list of the ladies and gentle- men who occupied seats on the platform :—The Chairman (Mr. Charles Broadbent, J.P.), Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P., Mr. H. Broadhurst, M.P., Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P.' Mr. John Crosfield, J.P., Mr. John Rylands, J.P., Mr. Alderman Holmes, .LP., Mr. Alderman Burgess, J.P., Mr. C. H. Cart- wright, J P., Mr. J. N. Peak (chairman Stoke Liberal Asso- ciation); Revs. EL Lloyd Jones (Rhyl), John Yonge, Rd. Filcher, 8.A., Thomas Rippon, J. A. Beet, E. Moore, J. Moreton' W. Pilling; Councillors F. Monks, J.P., John Platt. John Brown, P. Caldwell, J. Barker, J. Greening, F. Dixon, W. Pierpoint ; Messrs. G. H. Powell (South-West Lancashire Liberal Association), William McMinnies, Far- rington), E. Brewtnall, E. Guest, 8.A., Joseph Jackson (Garstang), Julian Winser, Franklin Winser (Kegworth), F. A, Roberts, John H. Cornell, C. S. Burgess, F. W. Monks, W. Cartwright, F. J. Cartwright, J. H. Flem- ing, George Blackhursti M. Bowden, William Longshaw,W. Burn, John Bounell, George Plumpton, A. H. Crosfield, John Crosfield, jun., Thomas Morris, Thomas Birchen, Noah Legge, P. Roberts, Samuel Jones, Samuel Barlow, J. J. Sanderson, E. Ford, John Chappell, James Woods, John Mullins, Thomas Flood, Samuel Woods, S. Kenyon, S. Beaman, Robert Evans, Henry Whitham, B. Sewdon, John Toft. E. Wallington, A. H. Perris, F. Brown, J. Summersgill, P. Clare, J. W. Hall, H. Thornton. T. Dayies,W. Grimshaw, W. Y. Lawton, A. Rathbone, W. Jeffreys, Jos. Mounfield. jun.' Richard Dowd, A. H. Dunn. John Gandy, J. P. Hud- son,J. Mackay' James Monks, J. P. Donoghue, Edward Twiss, Charles Suelow, William Wright, James Urmson, John Critchley, Charles Plinston, George Holford, Richard Siddall, S. Dunbubin, Jno. Cralk, jun., and other gentlemen. Mrs Peter Rylands and the Misses Rylands, Mrs John Rylands, Mrs E. J. Guest, Mrs J. Winser, Mrs F. W. Monks, Mrs T. Birchall, Mrs Gornall, Mrs E. L. Jonas, Mrs F. Monks, Mrs H. Roberts, and Mrs Briggs (Crewe). The CireixerAx who was cordially received, said he bad been called upon most suddenly and unexpectedly to fill the position of chairman that night, in the unavoidable absence of his friend Mr. Samuel Rigby. (Applause.) Ho could not hut feel it a great honour to preside over that great meeting of their great party. (Hear, bear.) He cer- tainly should have enjoyed the meeting very much more had be been allowed to take a less conspicuous position. They knew Mr. Rig.by's manner, and his smiling face, which he could not emulate any more than he could his white beaver and white coat. (Laughter.) Mr. Rigby had often been there and cheered them in the boar of adversity—kept up their spirits when they were apt to be feeling rather low. Happily, he (the chairman) had not to cheer them in the hour of adversity. It was rather the hour of triumph for the Liberal party. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He thought few of them could remember any time when the Liberal party was in a more satisfactory position than it was at the present. (Hear, hear.) The party was united, both the great bulk of it, and also so were the leaders of the Go- vernment. He had not known a time when the Govern- ment and the leaders of the Liberal party had worked more harmoniously together, Nth what they might call the Radical section, and the more moderate section. Whether it was that the Radicals had become a little more moderate, or that the moderate men had become a little more Radical, he would not undertal' eto :ay. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) But certain it was that they were working well together and doing good service for the country. (Hear, hear.) He was afraid he was unable to pay their opponents a similar compliment. There had seldom been a time when the Tories had been more--[At this point Mr. P. Rylands, M P., entered the room, and received quite an ovation, the audience cheering lustily and singing a portion of "Auld Lang Syne."]—The Chairman continuing, said they had received a most pleasant interruption. (Hear, hear, laugh- tee, and applause.) However cheerful they might have felt a few minutes ago, they felt still more cheerful now. (Hear, bear, and applause.) They were honoured not only by the presence of Mr. Rylands—(A woman : " God bless him,")—but still more by the presence of Mrs. Rylands. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Returning to his subject, the Chairman said there had seldom been a time when their opponents. the Tories, had been mire thoroughly disor- ganised. He did not think the Liberal party need rejoice in that fact at all—(hear, hear)—for he thought it was an advantage to the country and to parliamentary government when the Opposition was united, and consistent, and patriotic. The leaders of the Tory party were somewhat troubled by a number of free lances which were thrown in their sides; and also by a particular kind of individual— who perhaps the audience understood, but which he did not —called the Tory democrat. (Laughter.) The Chairman referred to the coming visit of Sir Robert Peel, remarking that he was not able to say whether he would succeed in adding to the consistency and wisdom of the Tory party, but they might safely say that he would con- tribute to the brightness and amusement of that meeting whenever it was held, and he (the chairman) should be very glad to be present (Hear, hear, and applause.) He was sure that they could make that meeting much more pleasant than the last meeting held by the Tory paity—(laughter)— when upon that celebrated occasion a certain telegram was received from Liverpool--(langhter)7-which fell like a bomb-shell in the middle of the party, and did not contri- bute to the cheerfulness and success of the meeting Happily for him he need not address them at any length, for he was surrounded by three members of Parliament—(applause)— and many others, who' would occupy their time yen- plea- santly and very profitably. Two of them were well known to them, and most favourably known. They all took pride in the member for Burnley. (Hear. hear, and applause.) They hed known him as long as they could remember, and they regarded him with great favour. As to their own mem- ber, he did not know what to say about him—(applause)— excOpt that each year's Acquaintance with him made them esteem him more highly. (Applause.) Then there was Mr. Broadhurst. ( Applause.) He was a stranger whom they were proud and happy to see present. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) Mr. Broadhurst was known in the House of Com- mons as understanding those questions connected with work- ing men and with labour perhaps better than any other man in that assembly. (Applause.) It was particularly appro- priate that they should have him amongst them that night in that centre of manufacturing industry. (Hear, hear.) Mr. McMemetns, M.P., who was received with loud cheers, the audience also rising and singing "For he's a jolly good fellow," spoke as follows : Mr. Chairman, ladies and gentlemen, I am sure I need not say that I have great pleasure in meeting you to-night. It always gives me pleasure to meet my constituents in this hall, for I never receive anything from them but good feeling and kindliness, I think a great deal of blindness to what I fear are many faults, and a great deal of kindness to what I fear are very few merits. (" No, no.") It is always a pleasant experience for a member of Parliament to come into the provinces. (Hear, hear.) After the apathy, and pretentiousuess, and self-sufficiency of London politics —(hear, hear)—it is quite delightful to get into the more robust and earnest elements of provincial politics—(hear, hear) ; and I think that a member of Parlia- ment enjoys having his opinions strengthened and his efforts encouraged by meeting with his Liberal constituents, and he goes back to his duties in London with the sense that he has enjoyed a season of re- freshing from the presence of his constituents. (Cheers.) I need not take up your time by speaking of the last session of Parliament. I have had on two occasions to do that, and on both occasions the remarks I made have been reported by the local Press. I think that that session was a session of considerable disappointment, perhaps to everybody, and Ido not think that we need say very much more about it. We began that session, as yon are aware in the midst of very foreboding predictions on the part of the Tory party as to the future of the Liberal party. (Laughter.) We were said to be on our last legs ; to be losing favour throughout the country. The election of 1880 was a great mistake. If another election could be brought about the. Tories would go in and possess the Treasury Benches. (Laughter.) That was the prediction at the beginning of the session. Well, we ended the session with the Govern- ment in a stronger position than, I dare say, it ever occu- pied—(hear, hear)—with the country having greater confi- dence, greater affection in our great leader than, perhaps, ever it had—(hear, hear)—and with the prospect in the future of great measures being carried by that great man, and by the majority behind him. I think we may look for- ward with great hopefulness to next session. (Hear, hear.) I dare say this fool's paradise—(laughter)—into which the Tory party were lifted at the beginning of the session arose in great measure through the conduct, the eccentric conduct, the disloyal conduct, of certain members of the Liberal party in the House of Commons. You will always have connected with our party, and I dare say with every other party, vain men, disaffected men, and men who don't believe that their virtues are properly appreciated by other people; and I think it is not at all unlikely that these men in the House of Commons, whom I need not name, did a great deal to put the Tory party in the position of believing that through dissensions the Liberal party was vary likely to fall to pieces. These straws which the Tory party caught up turned out to be nothing, and the Tory party at this moment, as the chairman has just said is, if anything, sink- ing. Ido not think that during the session upon which we are about to enter we shall have any very heroic legislation; but we seem to have promised by Government some very great measures almost immediately. We are promised a Bankruptcy Bill, a Corrupt Practises Bill, a County Government Bill—(hear, hear), a London Corporation Reform Bill, and it is very likely that the land question will come up, and the question of compensation for improvements in the land by the tenant farmer. (Cheers.) Now, these questions concern principally England, Scotland, and Wales—and I dare say we are all of opinion that the time has come when legisla- tive measures affecting these kingdoms should engage the attention of the House of Commons—but we shall make a great -mistake if we believe that everything has been done for Ireland that ought to be done. (Hear, hear.) There is no doubt at all that it seems to be the opinion of many people that it is desirable to wait and see what the result of those remedial measures is that were passed during the last session of Parliament. (Hear, hear.) But we have not done everything yet that will enable us to say that we have done justice to Ireland. (Cheers.) There are questions relating to the franchise, county government in Ireland, and to education in Ireland, which will have to be dealt with before we can expect that Ireland will be satisfied with the legislation of this country towards Ireland. (Cheers?) For my own part, I am descended from Irish ancestors. (Cheers.) I have near and dear relatives in Ireland, I have sincere sympathy with the wrongs and with the requirements of that country, and I can say that whatever measures come before Parliament that are at all likely to work for the benefit of that country, those measures shall have my sin- cere, and earnest, and constant support. (Cheers.) Well, now, there is another great measure which is looming in the future. Not in the next session, perhaps not in the next session but one, but certainly it will come before Parliament before the general election, and that is the assimilation of the county and borough franchise and the redistribution of seats. (Cheers.) I myself have some doubt as to whether that change will at present work for the advantage of the Liberal party. The farm labourers have not much know- ledge of political matters, and ignorance is not a good thing as regards Liberalism. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) It seems to me that both parties are committed to this as- similation of the franchise; but I have no doubt at all that Lord Salisbury and the Tories will oppose it. I dare say they won't oppose it directly, but they will oppose it by some side issue. There will be a difference of opinion as to whether the franchise bill and the bill for the redistribution of seats shall be considered in one measure, or whether they shall be two. Ido not know, of course, what determina- tion Government will come to, but I have no doubt at all that whatever determination tney come to they will be opposed by the Tory party. (Laughter.) If they bring in one measure embracing both the franchise and the redistribution of seats, the Tory party will say that it is very much too weighty a matter, and it ought to be divided into two bills. If they bring in two bills, the Tory party will say that this is the first time that ever the two measures were dealt with separately—(laughter)—and that it is very much better that they should be introduced as one treasure. (Laughter.) Now, they are sure to say this, because it is not true. (Laughter.) The re-distribution of seats and the franchise were dealt with separately by Lord John Russell, in 1866. His bill was thrown out, but the ministry cer- tainly dealt with the two measures seperately and:distinctly. Well, it is just possible that this measure for the rc-distri- bution of seats, and fee the extension of the household suffrage to the county, may be thrown out by the Tories, and if so, that is very likely the question upon which the next general election will turn, and if it does. I think it won't be for the disadvantage of the Liberal party, but I think it will be for the disadvantage of the Tory party. (Cheers.) There is another question which I should like to see dealt with. It is now thrust very much into the back ground, and I should like to see it much more talked about, and I should like to see it dealt with heartily in Par- liament, but despair of ever doing so, and that is the ques- tion of the expenditure. the imperial expenditure of this country. (Cheers.) If you deduct the cost of the Post Office and the Telegraphic Department, which are really not expenditure, but which are great businegs departments earning very good profit for the Government, you have still an imperial expenditure of eighty million pounds sterling. It is enormous. Many years ago, Lord Derby said that the Government that could not conduct the rule of this country for less than sixty millions was not fit to rule it at all, and some years before that Mr. Cobden proposed that the expen- diture of the country should be reduced to forty-five mil- lions. The expenditure at that time was fifty-five millions, and it has gone on iecreasing ever since constantly and rapidly ; and still the cry of the spending department, as my friend the member for Burnley knows very well is the cry of the daughter of the horse leech "Give, give," and they say not "It is enough." I believe there is no one more anxious than the Prime Minister is to reduce the expendi- ture of this country—(hear, hear) ;—but he is powerless in this direction so long as the coun- try remains apathetic. Some day or other the country will awake with a start and we shall see a great re- duction in the expenditure. (Cheers.) It is no business of mine at present to say where this reduction ought to take place, but I do not think it needs much sagacity to say where some of it might be found, when we remember that the warlike armaments of this country costs 27 million pounds sterling a year, and the smallest standing army he Europe costs more than the largest. (Hear, hear.) There is another consideration that I think will aff,ct the country, and perhaps statesmen before long, and that is the evident falling off of revenue arising from consumption of intoxi- cating drinks. (Cheers.) If this revenue had increased during the last two years in proportion to the population there would have been now arising from the sale of intoxi- cating drinks a revenue of 51 million pounds sterling a year. The fact is that there is less than 47 million pounds a year. Now the chairman has referred te a meeting that was held in this-room not very long ago. He has told you that it was held on the day when the Liverpool election took place. It was held on that day with an object. (Hear, hear.) I be- lieve it was postponed on purpose for that day,—(hear, hear)—and it was intended that in the middle of the meet- ing a telegram from Liverpool should arrive with an ac- count of the elect:on of the Tory candidate by a majority of 2,000, which was to be received with loud cheers and thungers of applause by the audience. (Laughter.) But Burns has told us years ago that "The best laid schemes o' Mice and men Gang aft a-gley," and on this occasion, at any rate, one thing was lacking. There was the meeting, and there was the chairman, and there were the speakers; but, instead of the telegram an- nouncing a victory of the Tories in Liverpool by a majority r 2,000, it was a defeat by a majority of more than 300— (cheers)—and insteadlof a meeting with countenances full of sweetness and light, there was nothing in the assemblage but long Nees. Everybody was disheartened, our genial friend, Sir Gilbert, even almost forgot to be gracious, and he scattered blessings round the platform with not more than Profuseness and generosity—(laughter)e one half his usual separated,,,m%mafroertaiong and then, I think, they with saying in tremulous terms one another and it i united." because a(Loud f laughter.) Well, now, at this meeting,it was said that the this that r have referred to it, work- ing classes in this country, are, the majority of them, Con- servatives. Now the authority for this assertion was rather curious because it came from a gentleman who not long ago said that the result of the election in the town in 1880 arose from the votes of Irishmen and ironworkers. He seems to have changed his opinion as to whether the work- ing classes are Conservatives or not, 14 at that time I

(Loud cheers.) Well, now, sone public men, in referring to this motion, had objected to it on the ground that it " smacked " of Socialism. He was not dis- posed to quarrel with men who ride off at a tangent upon a comparatively new subject. The members who were pro- moting this resolution might, perhaps, during the course of discussion, see some means of im- proving or making it more acceptable to those whose support they sought. But he entirely objected to the theory of socialism which was applied to the resolu- tion, or at least upon that objection being set forth as a rea- son why it should not be passed. If they wanted an illus- tration of something near akin to socialism in the land question, they had only to refer to the Land Act of 1881 and to the Arrears Bill of last session. (Hear, hear.) If they said there was a smack of socialism in those measures he should not be prepared to dispute the charge, and he did not see that those measures should be in the least condemned because there was a smack of socialism about them. (Hear, hear.) If a good and wise and just law, calculated to do some good to large classes of the community, was of such a nature that it partook of the likeness of socialism, by all means call it socialism it they liked, but pass the law. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) We had done many things in our country that had had some relationship on the face of them to socialism. What were the grants in aid but something of a socialistic character ? The central Government gave grants in aid of local rates in every county in the United Kingdom, and what did the grant in aid of local rates mean? It meant that a part of the maintenance of rural policemen was paid out of State funds, *and these rural policemen were instituted to act in the main as gamekeepers to their great territorial landlords. (Prolonged cheering.) It was not Socialism in the objec- tionable sense so long as the landlords were obtaining an advantage from the measure, but the moment they proposed to lend a helping hand to the poor hopelss agricultural labourer, then there were no terms sufficiently strong with which to denounce it. But then even for the proposal which he had read they had a very high authority, a very influential and welcome supporter in the person of the member for Ripon, Mr. Goschen. (Cheers.) The other ',dav he made a speech in which he said he could not agree to the motto which was displayed on the walls, namely, the county franchise. If Mr. Goschen honestly believed that the majority of the people would rule badly, he was perfectly justified in taking up his position, and he (Mr. Broadhurst) did not see that they should go out of their way to quarrel with him over it when they had such a very overwhelming majority on the other side. Mr. Goschen, in a speech at Rugby some twelve or eighteen months ago, referring to peasant pro- prietary, said it was not only a financial question but a great social question, and it was mainly upon those two grounds that they would support the proposal when it came before the House. What they wanted was this—that in agricultural districts where there were men evidently of energy, of character, of industry, and thrift, who had some little savings about them whether they were villagers, farm labourer, or village blacksmith, and who could by a little assistance acquire a small holding of land, say of ten or fifteen acres, that the State should, if necessary, assist them in the purchase of those small holdings. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) That was an illustration of what they wished to accomplish, and he would now tell them why they wished to accomplish this. His experience was that in a country like this, where they were so pressed together in great cities and in great communities, that they did not cultivate on the small holding system so much as they might, and that many large farms would be much more valuable, not only to the owner of the land but to the community at large, were they broken up into small holdings. Every year they imported into this country from France and the Mediterranean ports something like £10,000,000 werth of fresh vegetables and other garden pro- duce. Did they not think that the greater part of this , £10,000,000 worth could be as well grown close to their own towns as in France and the Mediterranean ports? (Hear, hear, and cheers.) He believed it could, and he be- lieved also it would answer the purpose of many a large landowner to let portions of his farms, that were now absolutely unoccupied, out to small holders, than it would he to continue them under the present system of letting. (Hear, hear.) There was another object also in the resolu- tion, and that was that if they could distribute about the country say 10,000 small owners and cultivators of these small holdings, an enormous amount of labour would be retained upon the land and in the villages which was now constantly floating and migrating towards the great towns. Every one of the great cities was being daily recruited in numbers of unskilled labourers from the rural villages, from which they were driven because there was no employ- ment for them. What he wanted to ask was this, whether hundreds and thousands of those who migrated to the great -manufacturing districts would not be better employed on the land at fair and remunerative wages, from whence they would be sending to Lancaehire for cotton goods, to Leicester for stocking goods, and to Northampton for boots and so on. Instead of overcrowding the market, they would be demanding increased supplies from the manu- facturing districts. That was the object they had in view in proposing to Parliament and the country an attempt to establish a peasant proprietary. (Cheers.) He knew it would be bitterly opposed by many landlords, but what he asked them to remember was this—that every reform accom- plished in this country had not been a reform having for its object or its result the destruction of their best and truest interests, but every reform had been, if he might so term it, a buttress to further strengthen the present fabric of society. (Hear, hear.) He appealed to them, and he appealed to all influential people, to consider well the pro- posals for land reform of this moderate character as the time would come when larger and more extreme proposals should have seized hold of the minds of the people that there would be no resting place between their present position and a complete revolutionary overturning of the present system of ownership in the property of land. (Cheers.) He feared he had bad to hurry over this subject, which was one full of interest ;—every feature of it was subject for thought, and he earnestly appealed to his fellow workmen and to every- one who had the welfare of the country at heart to take Up the subject, and to force it on to the consid9ration of Parlia- ment at the earliest possible date. It could no longer be permitted that a few families should, by birth of course, in many cases by accident—and in some other cases by more questionable means than that (cheers) continue to monopolise for their own pleasure and for their own interests the land which God gave to his children for an inheritance (Loud cheers.) They had established school boards in every village nearly, and certainly in every town in the United Kingdom, and the day these institutions of light were established in their midst, that day commenced the period when these anoma- lies must certainly have their days numbered. (Cheers.) With a reading and thoughtful working people throughout , the country, he ventured to say that when they got thoroughly to understand this great and important subject they would make very short wm k indeed with the opponents; of reasonable reform in the land laws. (Hear, hear.) He was not saying that they would do anything wrong or un- just to the present owners, but they would see that justice was done, and that very speedily. The Teter party of course would obstruct this measure. It was their mission. (Laughter.) The object of their combination was to band together to prevent good work being done, but, if the rules for the facilitation of legislation passed last November and October should not be found strong enough to prevent them stopping its progress, they might depend upon it that the ' country would demand that Parliament should further re- form itself in order that legislation should not be eternally set hack from session to session, from year to year, and that their reasonable desires should not be continually defeated. There was only one party in the State who were likely to do this work thoroughly. They, the etorkingmen, had been appealed to many times upon the platform and in the press to support the Conservative party. They were told that their interests lay as much in the direction of Coneerva- tivism, and more so, in fact, than they did in Liberalism. He should certainly like to see that made perfectly clear, because with all the reading and all the listening be had been able to give to the subject as yet, he had not been in the least convinced of it. He was constantly being attacked by the Conservative press and Conservative speakers because he, a workingman, voted and worked with the Liberal party in Parliament, and they said that he ought, from the very nature of his calling, to assume an independent position in Parliament and to pledge himself to neither party. He knew the sort of independence which they required. On questions where he honestly differed from the Liberal party he voted ahead of them. He often found himself with Mr. Rylands land Mr. McMinnies, voting ahead of their party. But the Tories meant by an independent position, a man who sat constantly on the Liberal side of the House and spoke and voted as constantly on the Conservative side of the House. He never knew what were called independent politicians in his life, but they were Conservatives. He never knew an independent newspaper—(loud laughter and cheering)—his friend Mr. McMinnies assured him that they had one in Warrington. (Loud laughter.) He was not aware of that, and he certainly •did not intend to be personal either to the proprietors or to the press. But what he was going to say was this—that if they went back, as Mr. McMinnies had done to some extent, over the history of the great measures that had made them and himself (Mr. Broadhurst) what they were that day, he would ask which party gave them those measures. div.head: Xetterl to tlit editor.
div.p: Xetterl to tlit editor.
IS "PIG AND WHISTLE" A CORRUPTION CS pLTNI,"-CRUEL SPORT.

Sir,—! have received the following from a talented authoress, whose name is well known in literature all over Win civilised world :—" Dear Mr. —, I think from piga maws had Pig and Whistle ' is a probable derivation, or rather corruption; but there is one that suggests itself to use. You know the Scandinavian belief in a witch's power of whistling for a wind. ibis used to be, I ueiele, rather * lucrative Uuslnee, awl It Jo .tal Then, you know, a pig is supposed to see the wind. 'A straw in a pig's snout' is a sure and ready barometer to the popular belief. May not the sign, which is frequently found in seaport towns, be a kind ef hieroglyphical combination of these two notions ?" With reference to the word" Wins," ii" Newtonian" will consult valuable dictionaries, he will it'd that though obsolete, it has no connection with archi- tecture or artisanship, though it is sometimes used by cooks. It may also be applied to a person in drink, in the sense of fullness. See the Imperial Dictionary. As an instance of bow a vernacular word or term gets corrupted, in a letter I have this week received from a very old friend in Lanca- shire, who very seldom commits a mistake he uses the word " chowterved " for blockhead. Now, I always thought " chotty " was the correct Lancashire term, and the glos- sary of the English Dialect Society confirms my opinion. But a truce to the discussion of corruptions, technicalities, ice., and plaee sex dames! The Princess of Wales is using her influence to put down the cruelty of shooting pigeons from the trap, and it is said she has succeeded in getting her right royal husband to share her views. Will the ladies of Newton in particular, and Lancashire in general, join the standard of the gracious royal lady and exemplary mother, and set their faces against all " gate-money" or demoralis- ing exhibitions of so-called sport? The action of the Princess will ultimately prove the death-warrant of pigeon shooting and coursing matches got up for the sake of profit. In conclusion, I would refer those who take an interest in legitimate field sports to the current number of the Entr'acte, in which they sill rind the subject dealt with in a manly way by a writer who is evidently a genuine sportsman in the English sense of the word.—l are, sir, rim. Newington, London, Jan. 21. ANGLO-SCOTUS.

div.head: PROPOSED ACCIDENT HOSPITAL FOR RUNCORN.
div.p: THE PROPOSED ACCIDENT HOSPITAL FOR RUNCORN.

no doubt in common with many other residents in the town, have recently received a circular from Mr. J W. Lightburn, hon. secretary to the committee that has been formed to promote the establishment of an accident hospital for Runcorn and the neighbourhood. I presume there will be few of the inhabitants who will be inclined to dispute that any necessity exists, for such an institution, and I am sure many will gladly contribute towards its acquisition and maintenance. But whil:t I am far from wishing to throw cold water on such a praiseworthy under- taking, I cannot but think that, seeing the many calls that ar3 made upon the purses of shopkeepers, and the depressed state of trade in the town, they would be acting wisely and considerately in delaying their replies to the circular until they know what the large employers of labour, and their employes, are willing to do in the matter, because they are the parties who will be mostly benefited by the establish- ment of an accident hospital. I would also suggest, if it has not already been done, that a circular be sent to that extensive trading concern, the Co-Operative Society in Church-street, which is composed principally of the work- ing classes, and yet, notwithstanding its wealth, seldem, if ever, contributes to any fund that may be started for phil- anthropic purposes. If this question were brought under the notice of the members at their approaching annual meeting, I cannot but think that they would be willing to vote a considerable sum out of their large income for this

object, and also subcribe liberally towards its support in ' the future. I would also suggest that the subscription list be published from time to time in the local papers, in order that those who may not have already subscribed be thereby stimulated to do so.—l am, Sir, yours truly, A SIARKEEPER.
Runcorn, January 24tii, 1883.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Barclay. There were also present Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. Ashton, Darbyshire, Weir, E. A. AN morptcomE PRopoSILL.—TARMIRS AND DISEASED MEAT.

A telegram was read from Mr. W. H. Brook, town clerk of Warrington, with reference to the appointment of the Corporation's nuisance inspector to the oversight of Walton Inferior, Walton Superior, Appleton, Acton, and Whitley.— Mr. RIGBY opposed the appointment, remarking that he thought the Authority was quite capable of looking after its own affairs.—The Rev. J. LOCKWOOD said this was a matter which should be seriously considered. He, personally, was in favour of the proposition made by the Town Clia-k. It was impossible for the Authority's inspector to get to the remote parts of the Union, and as there was a kindly good feeling existing between the two sanitary inspectors, they could, by acting harmoniously together, do the work more effectively.—lt was stated that the object of the proposed appointment was to facilitate the seizure of diseased meat; but Mr. C. RIGBY said the interests of the farmers would be jeopardised if they had "a man like Norman " coming into the Authority's district. For instance, if a farmer had a cow suffering from milk- fever, it would have to be immediately slaughtered, and could not Ise taken into the town. Tha beef was no good as that of a well fed beast, but they allowed Mr. Norman to exercise two powers in the district, he would condemn that tow and say the carcase must be buried. It was a perfect farce to allow Mr. Norman to come in.—The Cmetnataer : I speak in ignorance, but is such a cow !It for food.- —Mr. RIGBY : Yes; as well as a well fed bullock.—The Rev. J„ LOCKwOOD pointed out that in the case which gave rise to the proposal the meat was in a vile condition, and con- demned as unfit for food by Mr. Farrington and the Medical Officer.—Mr. RIGBY : It will he a great injustice if you allow Mr. Norman to step in. I fcr one protest etronaly against him being permitted to have anything whatever to do with our business. We have an inspector, and if he is not qualified have another.—The CHAIRMAN : If no member moves the appointment the thing falls to the ground.—Mr. RIGBY : I move that we have nothing to do with him in any way or siipa W'Etn : I eonrl that.—The proposition was declared unnecessary; and the CHAIRMAN said Mr. Brook would be informed that the Authority had discussed the question, but had passed no resolution thereon.
