div.head: INFECTIOUS PAUFERS.-A. GOOD SUGGESTION.
div.p: INFECTIOUS PAUFERS.-A. GOOD SUGGESTION.

A letter, dated the 17th instant, was read from Dr. Mouritz, medical officer, Runcorn, in which he stated that he must decline to attend paupers at Runcorn Infectious Diseases Hospital at so much percale. He would attend them at 103. per day, or at a salary of £5O per annum.— Mr. HANDLEY observed that the last case coat the Guardians £2 or £3. There was a previous case to that which cost £lO for attendance. He did not think any case would cost more than that.—Mr. ASHTON inquired how many cases there were in a year.—Mr. HANDLEY replied that dim were only the two he had mentioned.—Mr. NontteN thought the Board had better appoint the doctor at 10s. per case for the first year. The terms could easily be altered if they were found unsuitable.—The DEPUTY CLERK said the Board had recently expended £2,000 in building a hospital at the Workhouse, and now the members were considering how much per case they would pay to have their patients provided for at Runcorn. He thought the best plan would be to expend the money in purchasing an ambulance in which the patients could be removed to the Workhouse hospital. A horse could always be got when wanted.—The CLERK: All you want is a properly- constructed ambulance.—The DEPUTY CLERK: And dis- infected each time it is used.—The letter was referred to the Visiting Committee, on the motion of Mr. WEIR, seconded by Mr. JACKSON.
GRAYS CHARGES AGAINST THE UNION DOCTOR FOR STOCKTON HEATH.

The following report was read by the Deputy Clerk The committee appointed to investigate the charges of neg- lect or inattention to pauper patients by Dr. Willett met at the Saracen's Head Inn, Wilderepool, on Wednesday. January 17th, 1883. Present :—Messrs. R. Aehton, T. Norman, Edward Wallington, W. Handley, and W. R DePrez (relieving officer) The committee had before them Thomas Clark, who osaffcrirasf.,Cl• 5Vg, 04,4501 bc. thorn El,. following particulars :=-On November Ist last, on returning from work, he slippedlis foot on the kerbstones in Latchford and falling broke his leg. He was conveyed home, and as the family were in poor circumstances his wife applied to Mr. W. It De Prez for a medical order. He offered to give her one on loan. On informing her that this meant the repayment et a medical fee of £3 she returned home without the order, but Dr. dharrocks happening to be in attendance on a patient near to was requested to see Clark. He advised his removal to Warrington Infirmary, and obtained from him an order for admission. At the end of a month Clark returned home con- valescent, but b-ing unable to follow any employment he applied on December 20th for relief. Mr. DePrez gave a medical order so that if necessary he could legally give relief or bring the Case before the Guardians. Mrs. Clark took this order to Dr. Willett, and saw him. Hespoke unkindly to her and upb aide! her that she had cheated him out of £3 and her husband had better go to the workhouse, On Mr, DePrez examining the medical report on the 24th December he could find no record of his paying any visit to Clark, and thinking it might have been aa oversight, called the following day at Clark's house, and was told that Dr. Willett had not called He at once wrote a note to the doctor urging his atten- dance, which was at once taken by Mrs. Clark to Dr. Whet, who told her that he would not mine to see her husband. He, however, called en the following Friday evening, aeout eight o'clock, but would not examine or attend to him in any wars as he said he should be under a penalty it he did so, and again nvelt'oned about the ices o' £3. He has never called at Clark's house or seen him since, alth ugh the Committee were In- formed that he had been in attendance on a Union patient living only two do-rs away from Clark's house. Clark stated that he had not yet b ea able to work, and had not earned a penny since his accident. The Committee next had before them John Davis, a man seeminzly very ill and weak. In this case the doctor had stated that Davies was able to follow light employment. Davies stated that vying to the doctor's irregular attendance he had been compefled to obtain medical aid since November 33rd as an out patient of the Warrington Infirmary. He had, however, been in the habit of going by Mr. De Prez's directions to the dcotor's surgery fortnightly, so that his name could not appear on the report. The doctor gave him no medicine, as the doctor said it would not do him any good. The committee next saw Sarah Clark. a paralytic, who had been confined to bed a long time, and although in receipt of relief, had net been seen by Dr. Willett sines May, 1881. He had occasionally given medicine on being applied to for it, but, It was stated, complained of the great expense of the medicine. She has since beers atteded by Dr. White, of War- rington. The committee have also seen Stephen Roughsedge, of Whitley Superior, who was reported well by Dr. Willett, on December 23rd last, having suffered for several months from a lacerated foot. In consequence of this report the relief granted by the Board was withdrawn, but the man Is still unable to obtain or foliow any employment. During the earlier part of his ailment he was attended by Dr. Willett as a private patient, and paid for such attend- aece by Stephen Itrughsedge. The committee saw no reason to doubt the truth of these statements as an examination of the rued:cal reoorte goincided with them, and they drew attention to the irregularity in their filling up, as in one of the cases the column stated that patient had been attended at the surgery and medicine given, whereas the patient was confined to the house. They were of opinion that the cases were suffi- ciently serious as to call for an explanation from Dr. Willett, and further, that his res*d.nce, so far,from the centre of his district, materially increased the difficulty of paupers receiving early or continuous medical attention. Mr. MCINTYIII4 said he should like to answer a qnestion with regard to Clark's case. He understood that Clarke broke his leg, and was lying on the highway a night. Did the committee ascertain if this statement was correct or not? —Mr. HANDLEY : It is not true. He was removed by a passing cart after lying there au hour or two.—Mr. Mc- , INTYRE said he understood that there was no order given the medical officer to attend Clark in the first instance; that he was virtually taken out of his bands and I taken to the infirmary and there treated. Dr. Willett oh-

jected on these grounds to have anything to do with the case lest he should ba involved through interfering with another doctor's treatment.—The DEPUTY CLERK pointed out that it was only when Clark came from the infirmary that an order was. made,because Mr. De Prez could not give relief un- _ _

less Dr.Willett certified that he was unable to work —Mr. Mc INTYRE : That he failed to do.—The DEPUTY CLERK : That he refused to do, the report says. -- Mr. HANDLEy : That is true. Dr. Willett, however, has not been called upon to give any explanation. Mr. MCINTYRE : I merely ask these questions in the interest of an absent man.—Mr. HANDLEY said he should be glad to answer any questions.— Mr. MCINTYRE : The report contains a serious accusation

against a medical man.—Mr. NORMAN: It is a serious thing. As long as the Board paid a medical officer, he thought that gentleman ought to attend to any order he received from the Board's officer,—(hear, hear.) whether it was £3, £2, or Ll. They had heard in the report that the doctor at- tended a pauper case next docr but one to Clark's, but into his house he would not go, because he had had his leg set by some one else. He thought such conduct abominable when human nature was suffering.—The Rev. J. LOCKWOOD

moved that a copy of the report be sent to Dr. Willett, and that he be requested to attend the next meeting of the 80-Ird. Mr. MCINITRA secoaded. Mr. HANDLBY said it was misleading, for Dr. Willett stated in his reports that he had attended people at the surgery, when the committee bad incontestable evidence that the people were fast in bed. He thought his attention ought to be specially called to that. If he was only to give a verbal reply, he ought to be ques- tioned on the matter at the next Beard day. It might be better if he gave some statement in writing, so that it could he referr3d to at any future time.—The motion was carried.

div.head: FATAL COLLISION ON THE BITER.
div.p: THE FATAL COLLISION ON THE BITER.

The DEPUTY CLERIC said they would see from The Examiner that on Friday midnight, the 12th instant, a sailor was killed on a smack which was coming up to Run- corn, somewhere about Garston. The body was brought to Runcorn, the police communicated with the coroner, who , held the inquest on Monday, and a verdict of "Accidental death " was returned. An order was given for the inter- ment of the body, which was then lying in the mortuary at the Cemetery in the clothes the man wore at the time of his death. He had no money, and no friends, and Mr. Wright was requested to give an order of burial for a pauper He declined en the ground that the man did not belong to Runcorn, and that his death did not occur in the Union, but in the channel. On Thursday Mr. Salkeld called upon him (Mr. W. H. Linaker), and said the Burial Board could not I interfere. The body was decomposing and ought to buried, ; and he understood Mr. Barker had to give an order for burial. He (the speaker) said the Commissioners had no power to do so. " T,hen," was Mr. Salkeld's reply, "the body mast lie there." He (Mr. Linaker) said that would cause a great public scandal, and be offered that if the Burial Board would charge single fees, instead of double fees, which were charged for a man who came from without the district, he would, to avoid the scandal, undertake to pay the cost of burial. He would bring the matter before the Board of Guardians, and see if they would give an order. He now did so, and if they would not, he would pay himself. The costs were , £1 18s. Gd. This was one of those cases for which the law made no provision for burial. If the body had been drowned and washed ashore, the Board could have charged the county with the expense. Me asked the Board to order the amount he bad expended to be paid by the re- lieving officer, and write to the Local Government Board, asking them to give their sanction. He thought it was a disgraceful thing that any poor man should be lying in the mortuary in a state of decomposition, and there was no one but himself who would take the opportunity c.c. burying it. —A resolution embodying Mr. Linaker's request was passed, on the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. Watts.

SEVERE STORM AT EART,ESTOWN On Thursday ni!,ht and early yesterday (Friday) morn- ing, a severe storm of wind and rain passed over Earles- town and Newton. The wind blew almost a perfect hurri- cane, and great damage has been caused in the neighbour hood. So violent was the storm, that the roof of the shed connected with the Vulcan Ironfoundry was seriously damaged, and owing to the felling slates, glass, 4fic., it was not considered safe for the men to be allowed to 3tart. As a consequence they were turned back yesterday (Friday) morning. A large number of the hands are thus idle. When I tell you after going through the accounts, and the clerk is in a position to contradict me if he thinks proper, because everything is eerried out to the letter in regard to the expenditure of this house, that absolutely the whole cost of the rations for the whole of the officers of this house is £l2B 53 4d, is it not strange that a gentleman should get up in this place and say that two or three children are costing this Union £lOO a year? I say it is totally unfair, and it is a report that ought to be. contradicted; and I hope that Mr. Longshaw will to-day make the amencle honorable.— The CLERK said the rations' account for the officers for the half year ending September 30th was £225 15s 7d.—Major CARTWRIGHT: That includes those at the twe institutions? —The CLERK: Yes, and that is for the half year.—Mr. Da.xasysHlßE asked hut, many umcers mere 'me at the Workhouse ?—Mr. BROWN thought the Major's figures would be for the half year.—Major CARTWRIGHT was at a 108 S to know whether the rations for these children Came out of the rates, and whether they were numbered amongst those who reeeived rations.—The CHAIRMAN: Mr. Mackey will be able to answer that.—Major CARTWRIGHT remarked that when an accusation of that kind was made it was only fair the Board should give the officer an opportunity of ex- plaining matters.—Mr. LONGSHAW could only say in regard to the management of the house that so loose was it , that they had no dietary tables, and they could keep half-a- -' dozen persons without having to make any return out. There were not only four children, but three persons in attendance upon them, according to the information he had. Those attendants had to be kept, and, from what he had learned, such was the loose manner of management that they could keep half-a-dozen more persons in that house without it being perceived by the ratepapers or from the returns. The house was conducted in a loose sort oh way that was not all satisfactory to him as a ratepayer or a.s a Guardian, He knew there were scores, if not hundreds, of ratepayers who believed that Mr. Mackey paid for his children, and he thought it was hoodwinking the ratepayer' altogether. It ought to be finally settled that Mr. Mackey should pal for his children and Mr. Mackey placed in a more independent position. He was a ratepayer, and he did not want to keep any of the Master's children or their attendants. Let the Master pay for them ; he was quite as able as he (Mr. Longshaw) was.—Mr. WooLEALL Does Mr. Longshaw wish the Board to understand that there is no dietary table P—The CLERK said there had not been an officers' dietary table. The Local Government Board had written to the Board calling their atten- tion to the fact. He wrote to the Local Government Board and asked if they would give the Guardians some informetion of the dietary tables in other unions, and they sent the Board a list of them and they were referred some months ago to the House Coin- mittee.—As to the maintenance of children the CLERIC read the following from "Glen's Poor Law Orders " In reference to their children, if they have any, the Poor LAW Board, in a circular dated the ith December, 1256, have stated that where necessity may seem to require, they will assent to their being allowed to have their children residing in the Workhouse, under proper restrictions. But, they add, in such case they will think it right to require some equivalent for the cost of maintaining each child to be paid by the Master to the Guardians." —On the motion of Mr. BURN, the Master was at this point called into the room. The CHAIRMAN referring to the entry in the journal, said as far as he could gather the .clerk could find no such resolution entered in eny book. Could the Master tell the Board what the arrangement was f—The MASTER stated that some years ago the Matron applied for an increase of salary to the House Committee. The matter was entertained and the Committee then took into consideration her children, and said they were not, and had not been, plying for their children. That was so. They decided then and arranged that instead of giving an increase of salary, the children should be censidered and that no charge should be made for them. That was in the recollection of many old Guardians, and he dared seer in the recollection of many of those present.—The CHAIRMAN: Do you consider that a legal arrangement f—The MASTER: Most decidedly, so far as I am concerned.—The CHAIRMAN thought to put an end to these unseemly discussions week after week it would be much better for the Guardians to enter into some arrange- ment whereby the Master would be put on a proper footing. There was no resolution of the arrangement described. and therefore it was a private arrangement between the Master and two or three members.—The MASTER: It is not a private arrangement; it is a public arrangement.—The CHAIRMAN: It is not a public arrangement, as it has never come before the Board.—Major CAR TWRIGHT : Have you a dietary table P—The MASTER : It is understood we have.— Major CARTWRIGHT: Have you a dietary table for the officers 'a —The MASTER: There is.—Major CARTWRIGHT: Do you draw so much per week P—The MASTER Yes.— Major CARTWRIGHT : Is there any carelessness in regard to the rations f—The MASTER : Certainly not ; everything is weighed daily.—Major CARTWRIGHT: And are you in the habit now of drawing rations similar to what you have had since you were appointed by the Board P—The MASTER : Yes.—Major CARTWRIGHT: Have you passed muster with the auditor ?—The MASTER: Yes, I have never been sur- charged in my life, and I have had 14 different auditors.— Major CARTWRIGHT : I think that will prove there is not that carelessness some gentlemen would like to make out.— The CHAIRMAN: Is the dietary ecall that you are speaking of the dietary scale approved by the Local Government Board P—The MASTER: It is the dietary scale that is approved by this Boird.—The CHAIRMAN: You see there you come to it again. The Clerk: It should be approved by the Local Government Board. The MASTER: I protest against you interfering. You have the books and the dietary scale, and everything that you can cheek uie with. If lam one ounce wrong you can point it out to the Board. The CLERK said it was not possible in an institution with 106 sick people to keep such a check--In reply to questions, the MASTER said it was not correct that there were three persons attending his children. The cost of maintenance for the whole of last year for all , the officers in the House was £l2B ss. 7d. There were; seven officers at the house, including tbe matron and him- self.—The CLERK said in his ledger the cost of the officers' rations for' the half-year ending September was £225 15s. 7d.
FINANCE.

The Finance Committee-recommended accounts amount- ing to £549 lie 8d for payment. Since their last report I 253 6s 2d had been paid into bank. The committee sub- mitted a statement.of accounts, September 29, 1882, which showed that there was in the hands of petty cash keeper, &c., £8 17s 4d, due from overseers, £1,150; due from Educa- tion Department (Government grants) £1,597 Os; total, £2,756 65 4d. The outstanding liabilities: Account over- drawn at the bank, £246 14s 9d ; orders of the Board not paid by treasurer, £lO 19s 3d; proportion of Govern- ment grant due to teachers, £662 7s Sd : estimated interest on loans, £350 ; outstanding accounts, £4; audit stamp, £5; £1,299 is 8d; balance, £1,457 4s 8d ; total, £2,756 65 4d. The general receipts for the year ending September 29, 1882, had been as follows: —School fees, £1,202 94 3d ; Government grant, £1,597 Os; other sources, £57 is lid; rate authorities, £2,300 ; total, £5,157 Os 2d. The costs for the year had been as follows : —Expenses of administration, £722 lie id; maintenance of public elementary schools, £3,288 35 ; contributions to industrial scheols, £B4 101; repayment of princip tl led interest on loan, 411.310 135 7d; total, £5,40:5 17s Bd. The estimated expenditure at Simms Cross school for the year ending September 29, 1883, was £1,219; at Warrington-load £727 ; at West Bank, £l,2ll.—The minutes were passed. TRH BOARD'S lizsrosy RIVIEVIRD.

Mr. SII/W said as this was the last year of the present Board's existence, it would perhaps be interesting to briar glance at the work which the Board had accomplished. The Board was constituted on the 4th Nov., 1874, and the mem- bers soon found that they would have to provide accommo- dation for 2,000 children. It was decided to build three schools capable of accommodating 2,400 children, and the town was mapped out into three districts. Plans upon which were shown the then existing schools and the population in each district, as well as the school deficiency were prepared and submitted to the Education Department, who signified their apprnr.l_ Tho pinn3 of the proposed school were also approved. On lulu try let, 1877, two years from the formation, the first school called the Warrington-road school, WAS opened. It gave accommodation to 800 children, and was built at a cost of £O,OBl 15s. 3d. On September 10th of the same year West Bank school, which cost £10,128 103. 3d., and gave accom nodatiou to 800 children, was opened; and on Nov. Ist of the following year Simms Cross school, which ale) provided for 800 children, was opened. 'I he cost of that school was £11,527 17s. 4d. They would thus see that during the first four years of its existence, the Board erected three large schools at a cost of £30,738 is. 3d. and they had the satisfaction of finding them occupying a place amongst the first in the country for efficiency, and the amount of grant obtained per head. Although at the commencement there seemed to be great misgivings as to what the result of the action of the Board would be on the schools maintained by the religious bodies of the town, he had no hesitation in saying that since the formation of the Board the denomina- tional schools bad been greatly benefited. Mr. SifaNv re- ferred to the harmony and good feeling which existed be- tween the Board and the managers of denominational schools in the town, and he concluded by moving that a precept be served upon the overseers for the sum of £2,300, being the estimated amount of the deficiency in the school fund up to the Nth September, 1383; also that the precept be signed and sealed and made payable on or before the 31st March next.—The CHAIRM&N seconded the motion, remarking that Is,lr. Shaw had lost sight of the fact that the Board prior to the erection of the present schools rented a school, where they instructed about 000 scholars. Referring to the expenditure, lie observed that though the Board spent a great deal of money, the ratepayers had extremely good value for their money. And they should bear in mind that the expenditure which the Board had now was not for the present generation. There was a large sum Put away in a sinking fund to pay for the schools, which at the end of 50 years would belong to the township free of chare. There would then be a very small School Board rate.—The CMAIRMAN explained, in answer to Mr. Deacon, that the balance of £1,400 was not a cash balance. It was merely a statement of how the Board stood with the world.—The precept was ordered to be signed, and the Board rose.

—The MASTER, replying to the chairman, said if they took out the items they would find the cost at the Barracks We! more than double what it was at the House. The CHAIRMAN : Then they must be very extravagant at the Barracks. Mr. BROWN said the children had not been introduced into the house surreptitiously, and their existence being in the knowledge of the Guardians, it could not be imputed that they bad been kept by the ratepayers without it being known to the Board. (Hear, hear.) He felt strongly that Mr. Mackey's evidence was strictly and literally correct—that an arrange- ment was entered into by the Guardians in reference to the cost of the children. Whether that was a wise tking was another matter. He himself would prefer that a sum of money be paid to the master equivalent to the cost of the children's maintenance. Eut he thought they ought not to treat any ()Meer in the manner in which Mr. Mackey had been treated that morning. He held that the chairman did not treat My. Mackey fairly in the manner in which he put Ida questions. It was his duty—The CHAIRMAN : Never mind what my duty is.—Major CARTWRIGHT : How very touchy you are, Mr. Chairman.—Mr. Bnowx : I can tell you it is your duty—The CMAIRMAN : I do not want to know my duty.—Mr. BROWN: You are in that chair, and you must listen to what I have to say.— The CHAIRMAN : I am sorry to have to listen to such rubbish !—Major CARTWRIGHT : I think that is an ex- pression derogatory to your position.—Mr. BROWN : It is derogatory to the chair.—The CHAIRMAN remarked that Mr. Brown was like many other gentlemen—be was very fond of dictating to the chair, and he should not allow it. There was no member whose opinion he valued less than Mr. Brown's.—Mr. Bnowx said it was the chairman's duty to ask the question in the manner in which Mr. Burn pro- posed it. It was a simple question, and did not need a pre- face of half a column of a newspaper ! He did not think because Mr. Mackey was an officer, and Mr. Blaelahurst the chairman, that the latter should brow-beat the master. (Hear, hear.) The Board should come to some definite arrangemer.t respecting the remuneration of Mr. and Mrs. Mackey, and at once sponge out the possibility of this sort of thing—Mr. BotiNELL thought it was very degrading that this matter should be brought Up at all, seeing that there was no record of it in the minute book. He thought the discussion was quite uncalled for.—Major CARTWRIGHT Llieu nolsta th.t Lau been nanaea rennet to the members should be read.—The Clerk read it as follows :- 1, Fennel-street, Warrington. January 18th, 1883.—Madam, —I hear that the subject of the maintenance of your children was drawn into another discussion at the Board meeting last week. As I was a member of the Board when the affair of your salary, Ac., was settled, I think it is only justice to you to write you particulars as far as my memory will allow. In 1871. I think it was, you made application for an increace of salary. You stated that you would prefer paying for the board f your children. I remember Messrs. C. H Cartwright and Joseph Harrison, and many others who I can't just call to mind, were present at the discussion, and no d..,tibt will remember. You were wishful to have an increase of salary, but we decided that your salary should remain as before, and the children boarded by the Guardians in lieu of an advance. There ought to be a minute to that effect. I think there is. I should not have troubled to write you an the question, but knowing when I heard read the report that the subject of boarding your children was discussed and settled some years ago, I thought it was as little as I could do to furaish yon with these tow particulare. You are at liberty to use this as you mey think am, yours truly, WILLIAM WO6DS.— Mrs. Mackie, The Workhouse.

Major CARTWRIGHT said that was very straightfor- ward.—Mr. BURN said it should have been read before.— Mr. GRRRNING did not think it was Mr. Mackey's place to come there and ask whether such an arrangement was not made. He thought the chairtran and the clerk ought to see that these things were done. As to the accounts being kept in the loose manner suggested by Mr. Long- shaw, he had seen the books, and must say he never saw books kept more cleanly and orderly than Mr. Mackey's were. From questions he had asked the master several times, he learned that the rations for the inmates and officers were all weighed oat each day, and there certainly could net be any loose way of keeping the accounts. He thought if Mr. Longshaw would take the trouble to go into the matter he would find he was mistaken.—Mr. LONGSHAW said so far as he could gather at the Barracks tho officers had five meals a day, and he thought they were extraor- dinarily good meals. If officers could have five meals a day, it was merely eating and drinking and very little work. That was his opinion of the matter, and he believed that things had been kept so loose that they could keep in that house a number of persons without being per- ceived.—Mr. BONNRLL gave notice that he would move at the next meeting a resolution that the matter be settled by an arrangement being come to.—The CHAIRMAN was very glad that the que9tion had come to a point because he thought it would be put on a satisfactory basis for the future. It had been a vexed question, and had arisen over and over again, but new Mr. Bonnell had given notice to put it in a proper position. Notwithstanding what Mr. Brown had said, he defied him or anybody else to say he had made a wrong remark to Mr. Mackey that morning or brow- beaten him.—The subject then dropped.

div.head: WIDNES WOUNDING CASE.
div.p: THE WIDNES WOUNDING CASE.
IMPORTANT ST4.TENIENT BY THE PRISONER,

William Percy, the Moss Bank farmer, was brought up, on remand, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. A. Fletcher and Mr. G. Pilkington, charged with unlaw- fully wounding his wife, Margaret Percy, with intent to do her grievous bodily harm —Superintendent Barker said he thought the woman was sinking. The prisoner had been re- manded from time to time in the hope that Mrs. Percy might become conscious, and her depositions could be taken in the presence of the prisoner. He did not think there was much h.pe of that now, and he asked for the prisoner to be remanded for eight days.—Dr. Cooper said Mrs. Percy was now very weak and almost unconscious. She showed a little reasoning power, but could not speak much or tell anything about what had happened. When he was called in on the 7th January she was suffer- ing from concussion of the brain and paralysis of the right arm, and since that time she had been just sufficiently con- scious to soy a word or two, but not to connect any sen- tences.—Superintendent Barker (to prisoner): Have you any qaestions to "ask Dr. Cooper ?--No, I don't know that I have; but it is under false evidence that I am here.—ln- spector Barnett said from information he received he took the prisoner into custody on Sunday the 7th instant. T.`le prisoner in answer to the charge said he had been away from home, and when he returned about eleven o'clock on Saturday night, his wife commenced " calling " him, and threw a chair which struck him on the legs. He then either struck her or pushed her, lie could not recollect which, as he was "far gone in drink." "She had a bad temper and many a one would have killed hec years ago." The Prisoner: All I have got to say is that it is false evidence altogkther. It is the servant who gave wrong evidence, and the Inspector and Sergeant know it is SO.— The prisoner was remanded for eight dave.

Bri±hton has been selected by the Volunteer Colonels as the scene of the Volunteer review at Easter. The Council of the National Rifle Association htve, after deliberation, come to the conclusion that the Snider ride shall be used at the next Wimbledon meeting as heretofore.

A lad named Christopher Thomas Horrocks was on Thurs- day morning committed by the Bolton magistrates for trial at the assizes on a charge of sacrilege. On Sunday night he forced open a window in the school attached to the Noble- street Wesleyan Chapel, and then entered the chapel, broke open the offertory-boxes, and took away the contents. When apprehended Horrocks had 103. in his possession. A Liverpool undertaker named Chapman was fined 20s. and costs on Thursday, under singular circumstances. He was in the hab;t of hanging about the Office of the registrar of deaths, touting for orders, and following and annoying p.ople by his persistency. He had been warned to discon- tinue the practice, but took no heed of the warnings, and the registrar therefore summoned him for causing an ob. ' struction in the thoroughfare. div.head: DII7I7TATION AT THE NEW SCHOOLS,
div.p: A DII7I7TATION AT THE NEW SCHOOLS,

The SUPERINTFINDHST of the Barracks reported that a deputation from the Ormskirk Board of Guardians visited the temporary schools on Monday last, and also inspected the homes at Padgate. The deputation consisted of nine members of the Board and Mr. Parr, their clerk. They ex- pressed much pleasure at what they saw, both at the tem- porary .chool,s and at Padgate.—The CLERK said he had rq- ceived the following letter trom tie ciertc to the Ormskirt Union, dated 23rd inst. :HI I write to you to express the thanks of our Gardians for the pleasure they had yesterday in visiting your temporary schools in Wilson Patten-street, and your new school buildings at Padgate. Mr. Mines was most obliging and useful to us, and the information he gave us was really valuable. From our own observation of the management of the temporary schools, we obtained sever al wrinkles which our Guadians will not fail to turn to account here. Indeed our Guardians seemed rather to be envious of your superintendent. We had the pleasure of meeting with your chairman after our business was concluded. Our Guardians fully appreciate his kindness in saying that he would have been very glad to accompany us and assist us with every information in his power if we had only given timely notice of our visit."—ln the course of a brief con- versation, Major CARTWRIGHT hoped no Union would make , the mess of it they had in regard to the school buildings from beginning to end.
THH TRIINNIAL BLmenow.

The following letter from the Local Government Board, dated 12th inst., was read :—" I am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 24th November last, and tc transmit to you herewith the enclosed copies of an order which they have issued directing tbat from and after the 15th April next the elective Guardians of the poor of the several townships comprised in the Warrington Union, shall continue in office for three years, instead of one year, as heretofore."

div.head: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT THE HOUSE.
div.p: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT THE HOUSE.

The MASTER reported, under date, 23rd inst. :—" Nurse Watkins sent for me in a great hurry, about a quarter to eight o'clock last night. When I got to the hospital I found her by John Taylor's bed side, and saw a quantity of blood which upon examination revealed the fact that it was from self-inflicted wounds on the neck and breast. Sent directly for the doctor who attended to him. The wounds are not considered dangerous. At the time he did it there was another man in the room with him.—The Master and Matron on behalf of the aged and infirm inmates, beg to acknowledge, with thanks, a quantity of tobacco and snuff from Mr. Taylor; also a number of comic papers.

div.head: SURCHARGES.
div.p: SURCHARGES.

The CLERK informed the Board that the auditor had made several surcharges, the most important of which was respecting the furniture purchased for the Master's room. He remarked that there was no doubt he would get the sur- charges remitted without much trouble, but he expected considerable difficulty in the surcharge for the furniture. This was all the business.
STABBING CASE AT -WARRINGTON.

Mr. J. Fairclough, J.P., had before him on Monday, at Wallington Borough Court, a case the like of which is fortunately of rare occurrence in the town. Gennaro Faccenda' an Italian, was charged with having unlawfully wounded William Yates, by stabbing him with a butcher's steel.—The Chief Constable stated that the circumstances of the case were as follows : The prosecutor is a butcher's assistant, and lodges at Mrs. Connor's common lodging- house, Bank-street. The prisoner is an itinerant musician, who had lodged for the past few days at Monks's common lodging-house Ship-yard. On Saturday night, about a quarter past 10 o'clock, prosecutor was at the stall of John Backhouse (by whom he is employed), in the Market Hall. Prisoner, along with one of his countrymen, passed through the hall, and went to the stall occupied by Tho'mas Hatton, next to Backhouse's. He priced some bones, and then went to Backhouse's stall, where he also priced some bones. Someone said something to him by way of a joke, and all at once the prisoner picked up the steel produced from the stall of Mr. Backhous' e and plunged it twice" at the prosecutor, striking him in the left breast and then in the fleshy part of the left arm. There was an inch wound in the arm, and a 11 inch wound in the breast. The wounds were as cleanly cut as if done by a sharp instrument, and Dr. Richmond, who was attending the prosecutor, said he could not understand how the steel produced could make such clean wounds. He (Mr. Hunt) would, however, be able to produce conclusive evidence, but as the prosecutor was unable to appear he asked for a remand.—Prisoner was remanded until Friday. The prisoner was again brought up yesterday before ' Major Cartwright and Alderman Webster.—The prosecutor stated that he is a butcher's assistant, and lives in Bank. street. He was in the Market Hall on Saturday evening, about 11-15, and saw the prisoner walking about. He came to the stall where witness was standing and snatched up the steel (produced) from the slab, and stabbed him three times. A young man named Thomas Daintith seized prisoner by the arm, and Mrs. Backhouse snatched the steel from him. Witness could not seize because he had only ene hand. He had had some drink, but was not drunk. •He did not know he was stabbed until a short time after it had been done, when he found blood trickling down him. The police took him to the Infirmary, where the wounds was dressed, and he was still under the care of the doctor. Mrs. Backhouse stated that on Saturday she was serving a cus- tomer, and on looking round from the stall she saw the prisoner take up the steel and stab prosecutor about three times with it. She did not see any quarrel between prisoner and prosecutor before the latter was stabbed. Thom. Dainteth got hold of the prisoner, and she took the steel from him. Prisoner was afterwards roughly handled. She remembered prisoner buying some meat from her on the previous Wednesday.—Thomas Daintetb, labourer, Latch-

ford, corroborated last witness, adding that he did not get hold of prisoner until after prosecutor had been :Fl9-bbed. Dr. Richmond, house surgeon at the infirmary, said that he examined prosecutor when he was brought to the Infirmary, and found on the left side of the chest an incised wound about half an inch long in a horizontal direction, the outer end of it being a quarter of an inch below the left nipple. The depth of the wound ex- tended for an inch'and a half inwards across the body to the right. On Sunday night he found a somewhat lace- rated wound, about half an inch long, partly healed, under the left arm. He had examined the clothes (produced) and found the holes in them to correspond with the wounds. The wounds were not of a dangerous character, but were in a dangerous situation, and had they teen straight instead of oblique, they would in all probability have caused death. The steel must have been used with great force to "cause the wounds.—The prosecutor was drunk when brought to the Infirmary. The prisoner, through his interpreter, was then cautioned in the usual manner. His statement was to the effect, that on Saturday evening ha went with a friend to the Market Hall to make some purchases, and he priced a piece of meat on a stall where prosecutor was standing, and the person who was attending at the stall said it was 4Th per pound. Prose- , cutor hearing this said, "put it down you Italian—; you should be charged Sd. for it." He left the stall and went in search of meat more suitable for him, and while he was doing so someone came behind him, caught him by the coat collar and knocked him down, and he got the steel and used it to defend himself.—The prisoner then called George Leather, of 47, Lord Nelson-street, who stated that he was a coal dealer. He was in the Market Hall on Satur- day evening and saw the prosecutor hit prisoner four times, and the witness Daintith hit him twice, and then a crowd gathered round. Prosecutor and Daintith got hold of prisoner and pushed him with his back on the bench of the stall, and prisoner was apparently about to get hold of a piece of meat, but seeing the steel lying on the stall picked it up and struck prosecutor twice with it. The quarrel lasted about eight or ten minutes before prisoner used the steel. Both prosecutor and Daintith were drunk. Prisoner wds a stranger to him, but prosecutor and Daintith were not. —Prisoner was then committed to the Liverpool Assizes for trial.

- The two pensions of £B5 a year, vacant by the death of retired Captain David and retired Captain Walter Reid, have been awarded to retired Captain Richard Brayke and retired Captain George H. Clarke respectively. At Durham Assizes, on Monday, M. Justice Denman sentenced to eight years' penal servitude John Neillan, labourer, who had killed John Brennan, with whom he lodged, by stamping on his chest. Neillan's wife was acquitted.

- MANCHESTER COEN, THURSDAY. —(From Messrs. William Warburton and Co.'s Circular.)--The trade has perhaps been aliglitly less active since last market day, but prices have been well maintained, wheat realising extreme quotation, flour commanding an advance, and spring corn being steady. Wet onfavourable weather has again prevailed. At Liverpool re- to an average extent of other articles. There was no special feature requiring remark at this morning's market. With an average consumptive demand, wheat in some instances was held for Id per cental over last week's quotations. Flour was geqerally 2d per cental higher. Oats and oatmeal were unchanged. Beans and peas firm. Ittai7e varied greatly in condition, but dry samples brought Id per cental over the cur- rencies of Thursday last.

div.head: STOCK AND SHARE MARKET.
div.p: STOCK AND SHARE MARKET.
Messrs. Joseph R, and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 13, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Jan. 25th) :

, The movements to be reported this week ate somewhat con- flicting. The foremost securities show enhanced figures as a rule, although notwithstanding the anticipated reduction in the Bank rate and its occurrence (not without sonic good effect), some of the most speculative railway stocks do not show best points reached as now ruling. Egyptian stocks suf- fered somewhat from Paris prices: and the threatened disturb- ances there, but have recovered from the worst and united on balance, exhibit a decline of only A meagre business is re- ported in the other classes of investments, none showing any activity, but on the whole prices keep fairly steady. Com,. /flow, &0., AND MINING —.A. trifling amount of business concluded for the week Quotations show some dlqinct changes, but not sufficiently one-sided to mark any decided tendency either way. Canadian Copper and Sulphur quiet, sad toilers stAing trifle lower figure. Fanners' Shipbuilding A exhibit an advance on buyers' offer, but no corresponding movement on the part of sellers; the B issue mark a quotable advance. sharp Stewart and Co. have regained another 1 of their recent fall. Bolckows and Ebbw Vales quiet and not much changed; the latter, however, are somewhat lower. Naety-y-Gte and Blaina preferred mark a sharp fall, with no dealings marked. Higher: Carnmells to lf, Sharp Stewarts 1, l'almers Ship- building 15 to Park Gate Iron 1, and Telegraph Construction and Maittenance f. Lower: Nanty-y-Glo and Blaine preferred If to 31, Rio Tinto fto W Cumberland Iron, &0., fto InOlaa Phoenix Gold Ebbw Yale Steel, &c., /to I, and Bolckows fully paid /.
